Hogg, the Ettrick shepherd, happened to be seated at dinner next to a daughter of Sir William Drysdale. She was a charming young lady—unaffected, affable, and clever. To some remarks which he made, she replied, "You're a funny man, Mr. Hogg," upon which he in- stantly rejoined, And ye're a nice lassie, Miss Drysdale. Nearly all girls are like a bundle of pens, cut by the same machine—ye're not of the bundle." A Scotch nobleman of no bright parts, chatting with the late Duchess of Devonshire, she asked how it hap- pened that the Scots in general made a much better figure from home than in Scotland. "Oh," says he, nothing is so easily accounted for. For the honour of the nation, persons are stationed at every egress to see that none- leave the country but men of abilities." "Then," returned she, "I suspect your lordship was smuggled." A CONCEITED BIRD.—An undeserved character for con- ceit has been thrust upon the woodpecker by the pea- sants of Normandy in consequence of its habit of knock- ing at one side of a tree and then running round to the other side to see if any insects have been startled out of their homes. Their opinion is that the bird has so high an idea of the power of its bill that it has no sooner struck a blow than it runs round to see if it has pierced right through the tree. How TO SILENCE AN Ass.—Few people know how to prevent asses from braying. Two travellers in China were distracted by the continual braying of one of their asses throughout the night, and appealed to their mule- teer to put a stop to it. He put a speedy close to the nuisance by what appears to be a customarycontrivance in that country—viz. by lashing a heavy stone to the beast's tail. It seems that when an ass wants to bray he elevates his tail, and if his tail be weighted down he has not the heart to bray. Ais ODD MEMORY.—AN Irish porter forgot when sober what he had done when drunk, but, being drunk again, distinctly recollected the transactions that had occurred during his former state of intoxication. On dne occa- sion he had mislaid a parcel of some value, and in his sober moments could give no account of its locus in quo. He again became intoxicated, and then clearly recol- lected that he had left the parcel at a certain house, and, having no address on it, it had remained there safely,and was immediately given to the party who claimed it. A MOHAMMEDAN Lroin.m.—A tree grows in heaven, say the inhabitants of Mohammedan countries, upon every leaf of which some man's name is written. When death is at hand, the leaf upon which the dying -man's name is inscribed falls to the ground, and is picked up by Azrael, the Angel of Death, who then proceeds to the abode of the sick man and awaits /the parting of soul and body. When the soul leaves the body, if it belongs to a good man, the angel takes it in his hand up to heaven; but if to a bad man, he receives it on the point of his spear. LITTLE JANE'S GRAMMAR.—R is a pathetic sight to watch the meanderings of the childish mind through the intricacies of English grammar. Little Jane had repeatedly been reproved for doing violence to the moods and tenses of the verb "to be." She would say "I be" instead of "I am," and for a time it seemed as if no one could pre- vent it. Finally Aunt Kate made a rule not to answer an incorrect question, but to wait until it was corrected. One day the two sat together, Aunt Kate busy with em- broidery and little Jane over her dolls. Presently doll society became tedious, and the child's attention was attracted to the embroider,' frame. "Aunt Kate," said she, "please tell me what that is going to be ?" But Aunt Kate was counting, and did not answer. Fatal word, he! It wad her old enemy, and to it alone could the child ascribe the silence that followed. "Aunt Kate," she persisted, with an honest attempt to correct her mistake, " rllease tell me what that is going to am 2" Still Auntie sat silently counting, though her lip curled with amusement. Jane sighed, but made another patient effort. "Will you please tell me what that is going to are" Aunt Kate counted on, perhaps by this time actuated by a wicked desire to know what would come next. The little girl gathered her energies for one last and great effort, "Aunt Kate, what am that going to are?"

ACCORDING TO CIRCUMSTANCES.— We Were driving down the winding mountain round. The sunshine was golden and the air was direct from the Gilead balmworks. "One never wearies of the mountains," said the Pro- fessor, "nor of the sea. Changeless, yet ever changing; always the same, yet ever varying in mood and expres- sion,i n dimple of sunlight and shadow, in calm and in storm; we love them with a sort of worship; we never weary of them, and we would lovingly linger in their shadows for ever." Nine miles further on the stage went to irredeemable smash, the blistering sun escorted the party back to the hotel, and when they struck the seventh mile up the grade, the Professor stood still for a meiment to say, with uncovered head: "If I had known what kind of rock-patch this barren, foredoomed, aban- doned mountain country was, I would have gone to the great Sahara for the summer. I would rather live ten thousand years in the middle of a desert alkali Prairie nine million miles wide, without even a cactus on the whole reservation, than to own this whole mountain range and have to live on the prettiest bit of it three days a year. Of all the eternal blights that warp and wrinkle the fair face of Nature with a warty excrescence of lightning-scathed rocks and fire-swept pine barrens, there is no desolation this side of Gehenna equal to a mountain range." And then he b iled clear over because we laughed at him, and he went away behind a big granite boulder and kept the recording angel so busy for the next fifteen minutes that there wasn't a single entry from Texas made in that period.—Brooklyn Eagle. BOYHOOD OF SIR WILLIAM ARMSTRONG. —From the days of his childhood Sir William displayed the pos- session of inventive genius, and even in die matter of his toys indulged in mechanical arrangements of his own devising, which were far in advance of his years. He was a delicate boy, and in order to protect him from the rigours of the northern climate his parents used to keep him confined to the house for months together during the winter, when he took advantage of his en- forced seclusion to exercise his ingenuity upon such un- promising materials as happened to be at hand. When only five or six years old he was accustomed to amuse himself with setting a number of old spinning wheels in motion by means of weights descending on strings from top to bottom of his father's house, over the staircase railings, making the wheels perform evolutions in imita- tion of pumping water and grinding corn. The days passed pleasantly enough to him while superintending these diverting operations, and so long as his mechanical playthings served to make WI confinement acceptable to him his parents looked on with gratification without, however, for a moment suspecting that in gratification, early evidences of ingenuity there was foreshadowed the strong genius of the inventor. Friends and relatives bought mechanical toys for the little prisoner, but they could not bring themselves to regard. with unmixed satisfaction his mania fol pulling them to pieces. With him this was a matter of simple investigation not to be resisted; to them it looked much more like pure mis- chief. When the cold winds had gone, and the atmos- phere was tempered with sunshine, he was allowed to leave the house, and would often pay a visit to the estab- lishment of his maternal grandfather, who was a builder; and in the joiners' shop there, where "Old John Fordy" was the presiding genius, young Armstrong would spend hour after hour in working out his mechanical notions, with wonderful patience and industry, for, though as yet his vision had not extended beyond the realm of toy- land, he showed the true spirit of invention in all he un- dertook, and improved upon most of the toys that were presented to him. Sometimes he would pretend to assist "Old John" in the regular work of joinering, and, happy in the thought that he was rendering useful ser- vice, would look up into the face of the old workman and ask, with an earnest gravity there was no mis- taking, "How much money do you think I could earn, John ? " The kindly joiner had to confess this to be a question beyond the power of his answering, but, as he scanned the pale face and transparent hands of the little workman, and called him his "canny bairn," he would smilingly encourage him to further efforts, much as he desponded regarding the lad's health.—" Fortunes Made in Business" in London Society. The virtues of a dead townsman are thus recorded by an Arizona editor :—We drop a tear as we record the demise of poor Billy, Muckrow. His genial presence and ' hearty laugh added a new grace to the most exclusive saloons of the town. We say it without fear of contra- diction that Billy was as square as a chessboard. He was na chump. He never killed a man without cause. He never forgot to settle his score on the slate. He never refused to go out on a hunt for hoes thieves. And he was a rustler when out with the boys. But his crowning virtue was that just before his death he paidais a, three years' subscription in advance for the Howler, and we assure his!viidow that the paper will be delivered to her on time:every week. Stranger' go thou and do likewise. PRODIGY AND POODLE.--SiT John Lubbock, at the British Association, on the "Intelligence of the Canine Species," told a good dog story. He has a black poodle, I Van, who, out of various cards imprinted with so many words, such as "food," water," "tea," &c., picks out the' one naming what he wants, and brings it, by way of request, to his master. Here is indeed a' clever dog. He . has at least acquired the first It; he :can read, and with a little more instruction his power of reading may be capable of extension beyond English letters. Sir John Lubbock, perhaps, will succeed in teaching Van a dead language, and training him in classical scholarship suf- ficiently to enable him to understand dog-Latin.—Punch. CHINESE WODIEN.—A Chinese woman walks just as well as you or I. She even runs upon her little feet, and, to add the last drop to the story-teller's bitter cup, she goes out walking, or in her palaquin, and has not •-even a veil to hide her from indiscreet gazers. What a curious book, for the Chinese, might be made with all that is said about them! Certainly, they do not resemble -women in the West; but they: are women notwithstand- ing, with all those qualities impossible to define; and, with some slight shades of difference, all are atighters of Eve, if by that expression is to be understood the in- stinctive disposition which impels them to henpeck the male sex. Man and woman, as members of the family, have special duties, to which different systems of educa- tion are adapted. Their social position is settled before- hand, and each is brought up to follow the fitting direc- tion. Man and woman then receive a separate education. The one is occupied with studies leading to State era- loyment ; the other adorns her intelligence with useful kA owledge, and learns the invaluable science of the h sehold. Our women may be unacquainted with the ante. 'hambers of Ministers and fashionable receptions, in win 'eh the European woman assumes all the seductions of her k lex to charm the society of men; but they have no need . to regret the loss. An old Dutch farmer in America, just arrived at the dignity of justice of the peace, had his first marriage case. He did it up in this way. He first said to the man: "Veil, you wants to be marrit, do you? Veil, you lovesh dis voman so goot as any voman: you have ever seen?" "Yes," answered the man. Then tojthe woman; , "Veil, do you love dis man so bettelas:any man you have ever seen ?" She hesitated a little, and he re- peated: "Veil, yell, do you like him so yell as to be his vife ?" "Yes, yes," she answered. "Veil, &it ish all any reasonable man can expect. So you are marrit ; I pronounce you man and rife." The man asked the jus- tice what was to pay. .." Nothing at all; nothing at all; you are velcome to it if viii to you any good." • CANADIAN v. AMERICAN FLODRS.—Samples of flour milled in Winnipeg from Canadian North-West No. 1 hard wheat have recently been tested with six samples of American flour. The water absorbed by the Cana- dian North-West sample was 13i drachms, as against 13 drachms absorbed by Pillsbury's Best and Minnesota,ftwo of the leading American brands, all the other American samples absorbing considerably less. The number of 41b. loaves made from a sack of 2801bs. was 108 i, as against 105 from the highest American samples. On the , point of strength, the Canadian sample standing at 100, 98 represented Pillsbury's, 96 Minnesota, 95 ,Long John flour, the other American flours being of lesser strengths. On all these points, therefore, Canadian North-West flour is entitled to a foremost place as against samples of the best known American brands. INFLAMMATORY ATTACK IN Honses.—"A.G." says "One of my cart horses was taken ill last Saturday evening with what I thought to be colic, so I gave him one of Day and Hewitt's colicdraughts, and about two o'clock he appeared much better, although he did not feed, and his ears and legs were vory"chilly. I then left him, thinking he would be all right next day; but when the horse-keeper came ift the morning he was quite dead.. The *knacker' said that inflammation of the bowels was the cause of death. Does this always kill a horse in such , a short time?" The length of time a horse will livejwith an attack of inflammation of the bowels varies very considerably In different cases. This variation depends upon the age and constitution of the animal attacked; also upon the severity and cause of the disease. It some- times happens that the mucous membrane of the bowels only is affected sub-acutely. In such cases an animal may linger on for several "days, and then die. But in ' acute attacks, which are most common, the sufferer I generally dies in from 12 to 48 hours. noose is Catyys.—At this season of the year this troublesome complaint shows itself, and it is advisable that all rearing-calves should be brought at night into an airy dry yard, with some cover, and fed on good hay, chop beans, and a pound of linseed cake. Those out in damp, low-lying pastures, however full they may be of grass, are almost certain to take the complaint, and lose more flesh in a month than three months of high feed- ing will put on again. At the first symptoms it is desir- able that they should be drenched in the morning after a night's fasting. The mixture, simple in itself, may be procured in any village. Two parts olive or Gallipoli oil and one part turpentine, well shaken. Thebest way to drench is with cone of the large, flat, long-neck sauce bottles, eighteenpenny size, which may be given full as a dose, and eepeated three times a week ifArequired. It is certain to effect a cure. In many parts of Stafford- shire and Derbyshire rearing calves are always broughtl in at night in the hottest weather to avoid thq damp atmosphere aiways present in large riverside pastures. No one will doubt that some of the best young stock in England are reared in these counties, which is saying much for the system.—F. AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION IN Wates.—Some:Carmar-- thenshire farmers, in view of the great agricultural de- pression existing in Wales, have issued a manifesto, in which they say:—" That in order to meet the great de- pression of stocks and crops a general reduction of rents must become imperative. It is not only the present, but the future prospects of the tenant farmers that are gloomy, if not alarming. Oats, wheat, and barley are imported into this country cheaper than the farmers can grow them even if the rents were half their present value. Beef and mutton are likewise largely imported, so that the prices of fat and store cattle 'fiave been re- duced to a ruinous extent. If a general reduction of 30 per cent. be made on land,, the owners at the present time would be as well off as they were ten years ago when receiving increased and full reats, for £7O at the present day is equal to, if not more than £lOO at that time; £2O to-day for a plot of land is equal to--£27 years ,ago. The reduction, therefore, would inflict nopiardship on proprietors of land, since the cost of living and prices of commodities have already been reduced to that ex- tent. We hope that the landlords and agents will take the matter under .their immediate consideration, and make timely and liberal concessions in the rents to their respective tenants. We ask for an equitable adjustment of rent to the present value of commodities." NORTH LANCASHIRE FARM NOTRS.—Miserable harvest weather has attended us since the night of Saturday, the sth inst. Up to that time we had got on fairly well with a deferred ripening. Some of the grain was much laid by the storms of a fortnight before. In some eases the machines could be used for the cutting, in others resort had to be had to the scythe. On the night of the sth heavy rain and wind set in, stooks were thrown'clovrn, and standing grain was still worse laid. Since then the rain and the winds have visited us at regular:intervals of two or three days, little cutting has been done,!and as fast as the stooks are set up they are blown down again. On Saturday last we had a day of continuous heavy rain, with high winds. In many places the fields were flooded, the sheaves of grain were afloat, and had to be carried out. Sunday was a bright, fine day, with a dry- ing wind, and the water was blown off the graip quickly; but next day we had again a downpour of rain, wah stormy wind, and the work of setting up the Stooks had to be again repeated. Fortunately the low'temperature that has prev)iled has prevented the grain from sprout- ing, and whefe care is taken to,prevent the sheaves lying too long on the wet ground, the grain takes a lot of spoil- ing. Oats seldom take much harm, but barely loses its brightness as a malting sample. It is to be hoped that what is lost in the grain by the present bad weather will be recovered in the good done to the root crops.—R. If rural want their boys to like apiculture a,s an occu- lion and to become expert cultivators and farm'inan- ,gerd, they should pursue a liberal course towards the yonngers. instead cf treating them as if they had no rights whatever. Those who desire to keen their sons at home to become their successors, should not only ren- der home pleasant and attractive, but give the juniors 'optiorturilties to learn how to manage for themselves. It is easy to get them interested and make them ambi- tious. This may be done in various ways. Treat them i:fairly and liberally, and they will not abuse your confi- dence and generosity. A little encouragement will have great influence in shaping their future, and may .often keep, boys from leaving the farm and seekMg uncertain occupations. Wise fathers are usually both just and gen- erous towards their children. They are wont to stimu- late the industry, skill, and ambition of their boys by as- signing to them plots of ground to cultivate for their own benefit, ail giving them animals to raise and train for themselves. ' No farmer who pursues this course )will "miss it" in the rearing of his sons, but be very likely to find it redounds to both his own welfare as well as that of his boys, •

HEREFORD AND SHORTHORN Caosses.—All:things con- sidered the cross between these two famous breeds is perhaps the best rent-paying animal that can be pro- duced, whether regarded from a beef o*nilk point of view, or, what is better still, as possessing M combina- tion of the two qualities. If we cast our eyes across the Atlantic for a moment, in order to take note of what is going on there, the aspect of affairs is seen at a glance. The Americans on a gigantic scale are cross-breeding their cattle. In the first ;place we must not omit to point out the foresfyht that has guided the American breeders in taking this step. They desire better beef, and more of it, and a hardier race of cattle, without any deterioration of their milking properties. All these essen- tial conditions are secured by using Herefords on their vast foundation already acquired from shorthorn crosses on native stock, termed somewhat contemptuously by our cousins over the water "scrubs" or common' cows. There is, however, very considerable shrewdness, or say sound judgment, exhibited in crossing with the white faces. Cross-bred beef cattle having Hereford markings bear unmistakable evidence of the cross by which the animal was produced. If the markings of the Hereford are not perceptible, the animal has not in his looks that which commands a little extra value in America as well as in this country. A difference in value of one half- penny per pound in beef cattle is a most important item to every breeder and grazier, and it is one of the main secrets of the Hereford's employment amongst American herds. Quality out there is winning in the field of im- provement, and as all know that Hereford beef is 1 superior to shorthorn, it would not pay to use the gray variety of Hereford on shorthorns, for the reason that there would not be a sufficient impress of the first-named transmitted to the grade offspring, which should always carry about the marks that entitle them to additional value. If cross-bred Herefords and shorthorns had the characteristics of shorthorns stronger, or more in the ascendant than those of Herefords, it would be a very great mistake on the part of the breeder to encourage the perpetuation of inferior markings. To do so would operate against the animals when fattened and on the market for sale. In producing cross-bred animals it is an invariable custom to cultivate the appearance of the breed that has the greatest salable quality or value. But if shorthorn type were produced and Hereford subdued as not to be traceable, the cross would certainly lose much that enhances its value. Hereford markings, then, should be plainly indicated. GENERAL. RIMER FOR DAIRYING.-Mr. J. li. Broornell, of Aurora, a successful factory man, gave, at the Illinois Dairymen's Association, the following general riles for dairying :—I. Decide on your line of dairying—butter or cheese, or both. 2. Select your cows according to the line of dairying chosen. 3. Test each 'cow separately, and reject all not suited to your line of dairying, or that fail in quality or quantity of milk. 4. Feed liberally; have pure water always accessible,nd keep a mixture of equal parts of salt, ashes, and sulphur within, reach .f the cows. 5. Be sure your stables are well ventilated; remove all droppings promptly; freely use absorbents and deodorisers, such as sawdust, dry earth, or cut straw, not omitting a liberal use of plaster. 6. Be scru- pulously clean in every particular, both in keeping the cows and in milking and handling the'inilk., 7. By all means avoid exposure of the-milk to the hot sun and foul air. 8. Air and cool your milk as fast as possible down to at least 70 deg., if you carry it any distance to a factory or creamery. Do the same if you make it into cheese at home, though you need not go below 80 deg. if made up 'immediately. 9. When tnilk is kept over night to be carried to a factor, the temperature should be reduced' below 60 deg. His rules for butter making are :—lf the milk is set at home for cream, the sooner ,it can be set after milking, and the higher the tempetature, the better, as cream rises best and almost wholly while the temperature is. falling. Never reduce the tempera- ture below 40 deg., as a lower thmperature has a ten- dency to chill the product and injure the keeping quality, and it also expands the water, rendering its relatively greater density less instead or increasing it. To go 5 deg. below 40 deg. would have practically the same effect as raising the temperature 5 deg., and to that ex- tent retards the rising of the cream. Skim as soon as the cream is all up, or so much of it as you wish to take from the milk. Keep your cream, if not churned imme- diately, at a temperature of 64 deg. or below, but no below 40 deg. Churn at such temperature between 55, deg. and 64 deg. as experience shows you is best. Con- ditions vary the tomperature.for churning. Stop chutn- ing when the butter is in granules about the size of wheat kernels. Draw off the buttermilk and wash in clean water before gathering the butter, until the water runs clear. If one washing is in brine, it is all the better, as brine coagulates the cheesy matter, which dis- solves, and is then washed out. Salt to suit customers, using none but refined salt made for dairy purposes. The best American salt is as good as any. Put up in such packages as are demanded by your market.

div.head: LABOURERS' VOTE.
div.p: THE LABOURERS' VOTE.

"A Voice from the Plough," generally recognised as that of Joseph Arch, writes to the Agricultural Gazelle: —"Presuming that the welfare of the agricultural la- bourer may be considered as within your province,'. I beg to say a few words on the subject of our vote. The public at large are much concerned about it, and are anxious that we should use it 'with discretion, and at times offer us some wholesome instruction ;:and some with very strong Political opinions temper a little per. suasion with their instruction ,and tell us which way to - vote. To these latter we listen and consider, and when the polling time comes we shall use our own judgment; There are a few (and I am pleased to say a very few) who use pressure. To these individuals we *say little, but think much. Some tell uethat in the past:we ;have been, neglected and oppressed.llawever that may be, our skin is too thick and our liver too healthy to retaliate, or lose time in resentments; and from the big town guar- temwe hear that the farm labourer is ignorant and stupid—we acknowledge our ignorance, but it is not al- together our own fault, and it is very easy to'inistake patience for stupidity. Why should our vote be con- sidered by some as dangerous to the State beetause we arennlearned ? Wisdom is not always found withlearre ing. Wisdom without learning is like a plough without a coulter ; but learning without wisdom is like a coulter without a plough. How should we be a dangerous class because we are simple, so long as we possess the virtues in common with other men? The vote is a new thing to us, and it bothers us uncommonly. We know it's a responsibility, and for that reason some of our chaps won't vote. A few will vote Conservative, some will join the Liberals. But most of us shall go in for Radi- cals. Why?" Because we think in the past the Conserva- tives have done nothing for us, only under pressure, and. the Liberals can't have, done much for us, or we should not have been so kng neglected. We are unlearned because in the past we have been left out in the cold. The Radicals promise us everything we want. So that's how most of us shall go. Not as we value promises overmuch, for we shall vote for agriculture and our bread-and-cheese, if 1 we know 'which way we cam get it. The Radicals tells us what they are going to do for us; while the other parties only tell us what they have done for us. Our political knowledge is like most other kiiids of know- ledge. It begins in doubt and will likely end in doubt We find it a 3ob to get much true politirial knowledge ;out of political speechds. If a Conservative wishes to show you the great world of politics, he puts a piece of coloured glass before your eyes, and everything appears yellow. In the Liberal glass it's all blue.. In the Radical red. And each of their separate glasses are so besmeared with the froth of 'personal abuse that the political world seems to our unlearned eye to be not altogether an un- corruptible world. We don't expect as the vote will give us everything we want. But some of us are poor, i and poverty s usually hungry and thirsty. Some of us just now hunger for land. I can't say exactly how thirsty we are, as we have only just got our heads above i water. We can see as the land s in, too big lumps, and there wants a little redistribution of wealth, as great , wealth is too often like a great muck heap, it only en- ' riches one spot. As a rule we shall vote for our per- sonal advancement, so far as it is just and right to our country and fellow-creatures. We don't take so kindly as the mechanic to working men's clubs, bat that is not because the agricultdral man is less intelligent, but be- cause, he is less communicative and loves individual liberty, and that will prevent him going with a body to the poll. Like the mechanics, we have a few Socialistic chaps among us, who would smash up everybody and everything, but they are too few to be of any danger. It's said by a few that our votes can be bought; perhaps they may, but it's said by Sam Slick that for two dollars you can buy a dog, but all the dollars in the world can't buy the wag of his tail. I shan't give advice as it suf- fers just now so very much from over-production, but I think the farmer and his man should be not only in the same field of politics but in the same furrow. We shall never go long with the mechanic—hang them self- binders—they take the bread out of our mouths. But now I'm getting one-sided, and to be one-sided is as bad as being one-eyed. We all view things from our own standing point. Oh! would the Lord "the eyes to gi' us, to see ourselves as others see us."

ON THE BANKS OF THE DOUGLAS. By J. J. (From The Blackburn Times.) Believing with Solomon that "He who observe:h the wind shall not sow; and be that regardeth the clouds shall not reap," notwithstanding the threatenlng aspect of the weather, and the heavy clouds which seemed about to dit- charge themselves in copious showers upon the parched earth, several members of the photographic section of the Blackburn Literary Club assembled at the stationnne gloomy Saturday afternoon, and proceeded to Longton by the West Lancashire train which leaves at 1-45. On reaching their destination, the party walked down to the village, passing in succession on their way thither, the entrance to the Grove, bright with gay parterres of flowers, and sheltered by umbrageous trees ; the peculiar-looking building which has evidently once been a windmill, but now, judging from ap- pearances, does duty for a house; and comfortable-looking cottages, each with a well-kept, attractive garden before the door. The whole party being strangers in a strange district, a council was held at the 'Golden Ball," to decide which was the most desirable route to take, and it was finally determined to walk on towards Southport, and trust te cir- cumstances for suitable subjects for the camera. The party were abundantly rewarded for their courage, in undertaking ;he excursion, regardless of appearances, for as they jour- neyed on,

The sun uprose through opening clouds of grey. And at his touch the misty hills unveird. The country, though flat and almost treeless, was not by any means devoid of interest. The hedges were festooned with delicately tinted wild roses, and masses of honeysuckle, and over all The purple vetch its breathing garland flung. At iutervals they came upon PAchers. and rakers, and merry haymakers. and sunlit ricks of bay that filled the air with a fragrance as sweet

As the perfume of Araby'. shore. ,while quaint, old-fasnioned thatched cottages lent a charm and variety to the scene. Phcebus, having conquered in his battle with the clouds, shone out in all his effulrent glory, and the entire landscape was radiant with his smile, as the party journeyed op, breathing The pure, sweet ozon'd air of heaven. Pursuing their way through Weimer Bridge, where there was scarce a sign of human life, and where the number of untenanted houses reminded the visitors of Goldsmith's Deserted Village, they stopped a few minutes to admire a picturesque cottage at the bend of the road, then travelled through the village of Little Hoole, and shortly afterwards were traversing the hamlet of Much Boole, where the at- mosphere was laden with the breath of flowers, and every cottage, as well as every mansion they passed, reminded them that

The time of the roses had come. On arriving at the church of St. Michael situate at the southern extremity of the straggling village, a halt was made, and the cameras were for the first time unpacked. The parish church of bole is an ancient and time-honoured structure, but although interesting on its own account, it is chiefly famous, and will ever continue to be famous while one stone rests upon another, as being the scene of the labours of the celebrated astronomer, Jeremiah Horrocks, who, when Hook Was part of Croston parish (Which it con- tinued to be till 1641), and the nucleus of the present build- ing a chapel-of-ease, was curate of the district. On ap- proaching from the village, after descrying the church, with its painted, brisk walls, and weather-beaten stoue tower, the attentien of the visitor is arrested by the inscription which runs round the clock and reads as follows:—" In Memo- riam Horroceii, 1639.-1859. "Ut hora, sie vita." " As is the hour so is life." The first date refers to the old clock, and to the year in which the young but ardent astronomer observed the transit of Venus over the sun's disc, and the second to the year in which the memorial clock was placed in its present position. Having spent some time viewing the building from the road, the party entered the church- yard. A large sun-dial, bearing date 1815, occupies a Pro- , minent position on the south wall of the tower, above which Oa the legend—" Sine sole tileo." "Without the sun I arn I silent." Immediately above the entrance to the substantial porch, on the south side of the church, there is a square re- cess, which, it is said, once contained a stone on which was an intimation to those who were in the habit of using it (i.e., the porch) for gossiping purposes, " to leave off 'Mating, and go inside and confess their sins." The old stone has now given place to a marble slab, ow which are the ,words:—" Prepare to meet thy God. Believe. Love. ;Obey." The last three words formed the text from which the Rev. Robert Brickel, the late rector, while suffering acutely from pain and weakness, preached hie last sermon to a deeply-affeeted congregation. By the time the fore- going inscriptions had been copied, the person who has charge of the church arrived with the key, and the photo- graphers having finished their operations with the camera, the party availed themselves of the opportunity, to inspect the interior of the ancient fabric, by means of the" dim re- ligious light" that steals in through the stained-glass windows. The year (1628) in which the churoll was re- built confronts the visitor, on the lintel of the door, as he , enters the building. When inside, the stranger is struck with something like astonishment, on beholding the massive pillars, and ponderous arch which sustain the eastern side of the tower. The gallery extends along the south wall, and seems at first sight to touch the ceiling, which most effec- tually conceals the pointed roof from view. The interior is scrupulously clean, and, notwithstanding the peculiarities mentioned, internally the church, although small, and with- out side aisles, has a singularly cheerful, impressive, and venerable appearance. At the western end of the nave, several of the old seats remain in their original state, and good, honest specimens of the joiner's work they undoubtedly are, albeit somewhat an- tiquated, and rugged in form and finish. They are each about nine inches broad, with a narrow strip of wood at the top,, intended for a support to the back. How- ever long and tedious the set moo, and however drowsy the listener might be, it must have been next to impossible for the weary one to enjoy anything like a comfortable sleep, while occupying such a seat. Adjoining the entrance is an octagonal stone font, on one side of which is the inscrip- tion :—"Des donant, Johan Stones. An. Darn, ." "A gift to God. John Stones. A.D. 1633." It may be as well to mention here that the donor of the font, lived at Carr House, Bretherton, that he was the first patron of the living. and that the Communion Plate still in use was presented by his wife, Catherine Stones. On the north wall there is a hatchment emblazoned with the coat of arms of the Marquis de Rothwell, one of-the lords of the manor, the other being Lord Lilford. The next object of interest is a handsome marble tablet, with a gothic border, erected by the clergy to the memory of Horrocks. As the inscription written by the Rev. Canon Jelin Owen Parr, vicar of Preston, is at once an eloquent and a loving tribute to the youthful genius whose untimely death it notices in touching terms, wa give It entire as copied from the tablet :—" Jeremiah Horrocks, born at Liverpool,. edocated at Cambridge, the curate of }Resta, died in the 23rd year of his age, 1641. The wisdom Of God in creation was his study from early youth; for his wonderful genius and scientific knowledge, men speak of him as 'One of Englatal's most gifted sons." The pride and boast of British astronomy.' Amongst his discoveries are— the nearest approximation to the sun's parallax, the correct theory of the moon, and the transit of Venus. But the love 'of God in redemption was to him a yet nobler theme ; the preaching of Christ crucified a yet higher duty ; loving science much, he loved religion more, and turning from the wonders of creation to the glories of the Cross, he expressed the rule of his life in these memorable words Ad majora atmealus, puce &see parerga negligi non davit.' Called 'away to higher duties, which ought not to be neglected for these ornamental pursuits.' In memcry of one so young and yet so learned i so learned and yet so pious, this church, in which he officiated, has been enlarged and beautified.-1859." In one of the divisions of the window east of the tablet, a telescope is represented resting on a Bible, within a circle, round which is the following inscription:—The Word of our God shall stand for ever. MD.—Religion and Science in fellowship.—ll 3,74." Flanking this window are the reading. desk, and antique canopied pulpit, the latter, the same from which Horrocks preached "Of oin, and of righteousness, and of judgment." The Bible and Book of Common Prayer are noticeable on account of the words printed in gilt letters ,on the outside of each, which are as follows :—" Ad Glariam AU. In Memoriam Horroccii, 1639.-1574." "To the glory of God. In Memory of Horrocks, 1630-1874." The .first date refers of course to the transit of Venus, observed by Horrosks alone ; the second to the year, when Astronomers all over the world, watched the same planet crossing the sun's disc. Opposite the pulpit on the back of one of the pews are the letters R 0: F 0:, and the data 1631. Immediately behind the lettering is a stained-glasa window, placed there by the Asir. Robert Brickel, in memory of his sister, Ann Brickel, and of the Rev. Miles Barton, who was for 36 years rector of bole. Contiguous to the window, the eastern wall, on the south side of the nave, is relieved by a white marble tablet, en- closed in a red granite frame, erected to the memory of a man who was loved and reverenced by his parishioners when living, who is still held in affectionate regard by all who knew him, and whose daily life, it has been well said, "was a commentary upon the doctrines which he taught, and his death was a confirmation of the truths, he so firmly believed." When he went to live at Hoole It was, he says, the roughest ilace between Preston. and Liverpool, the village was literally undrained, a cesspool stood before every door, vice ' was rampant, and such altogether was the state of the neigh- bourhood, that he declared "the morality of the parish was becoming very like that of Sodom and Gomorrah." All this is now changed, the people are as respectable as any in England, the village is thoroughly drained, fruits and flowers adorn the front and side of nearly every house, and ' though Much Hook may not be as picturesque as many villages, it is as clean and cheerful a hamlet as any in Lan- cashire. The change for the better is due in many respects to the piety, the zeal, the courage, and to the untiring in- dustry of the Rev. Robert Brickel, while his work entitled "The Transits of Venus 1633-1874; or, A. Chapter of ' Romance in Science," is a valuable contribution to litera- ture; and the pamphlets, and printed addresses which he sent out periodic illy to his parishioners, are well worth a perusal. In view of what we have said, we give the inscrip- tion in its entirety, as copied from the tablet—" In memory ' of Robert Brickel, BA., Trinity College, Dublin, for 33 years rector of this parish, who died Feb. 18th, 1881, aged 68 years. This tablet is erected by public subscription in remembrance of one greatly beloved and deeply regretted, a kind neighbour, a faithful friend, a student delighting in :he works and word of God, a pastor whose last message to his beloved flock was Repent, believe, obey.' He was a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost, and of faith, and much people was added unto the Lord. He was followed by his beloved wife en the 2:ith day of May, 1881." •. .GE GARDEN. How To Pal '*ir APetts AND Pans.—Peel and core the apples, anc , them on to boil in a brass pan, with half a pint of ivrater to every 61bs. of fruit. When the apples have boiled tender, add 31bs. of sugar, and 'mix well together, boil again for three quarters of an hour, stirring them all the time. When reduced to rather a thick paste, put into pots and cover over with paper, pasted round the edges to exclude the air. This is called apple marmalade, and will keep for years. Pear mar- malade is made by boiling 121bs. of: pears and 81bs. of sugar in one quart of water for one hour, the fruit having of course been previously peeled and cored. In this case, the pan should have a cover on till the fruit has boiled tender, when the sugar should be added and the whole kept boiling and stirred till they sare worked into a thick paste. Another method is to bake the pears in the oven till they are tender, then math them and add the sugat; and boil over the fire till worked into paste. Put into the pots whilst hot, and finish • off like all other preserves. Some impair the quality of their jams by z.teglecting tupick out decayed portions before the fruit is put on to boil. Apples and pears are sure to have some portion in an incipient state of decay, which should be cut out when the fruit is peeled and cored. LETTuca.—ln order to have these early in the season small plarits should be pricked out now in a suitable position, the most likely being against the wall of the residence or other building facing South or S.W. Build- ings not provided with spouts to conduct the water off the roof are not adapted for the purpose, as in that case the water would fall on the plants or near by, and create a worse position for them than if they were in an ex- posed portion of the garden. The plants may be pricked 3in. distant if they are as they should be, only just large enough to handle. It is not wise to extend the planting more than a foot or 18in. from the wall, because of the inconveniehce of supplying them with some screen during severe weather. Even a few boards over the bed' leaning against the wall will afford more protection than some people imagine. There are other protective articles, such as oiled paper and Russian mats, but the best un- doubtedly is glass, as light may be admitted, and during frosty nights some kind oftextile may be fixed on the glass frame as an additional screen. Las FRONT GARDEN.—FOT the first time for some , years we have seen the Gladioli flowering this season in I a cottager's front garden. No doubt there are other in- stances of the plant pushing its way into gardens that have been barred against it. The plant at one time was pestered with a disease not yet extinct that destroyed the bulbs or roots wholesale, which no doubt deterred amateur and professional horticulturists from taking up its culture. No one, however, need fear giving the scarlet Bronchlyensis a trial, and some of the commoner sorts of Gaudavensis. The first may be purchased at the rate of ss. per 100, or a dozen for is. The usual practice is to take up the bulbs after the tops. have en- tirely decayed, and preserve them in paper bags till March, and then plant them in well-manured ground, which should be annually changed. We are, 'however, acquainted with a batch that has been left in theground undisturbed for two years, and they have flowered equal to those treated as above. As soon as the stems turn yellow (which they are now doing) some may be tempted to take them up, but such a proceeding must tend to debilitate the bulbs, as the fibrous. roots are still fresh, and will not have performed their functions for quite another month. We are disposed to think that they will keep better in pots with moderately dry sand or soil round them, and as they survive an cfrclinary winter in the ground we may reasonably conclude that these and a cool, moist cellar would be more fitting sur- roundings than the paper bag method of storing them. THE WlNDOW.—Primulas are apt to decay just above the soil if they receive too much water at this season, more especially if the pots are not full of roots. Over- heat' watering must be discontinued, and whatever water is applied must go direct on the soil. The leaves and their footstalks are so woolly that they retain the moisture for a considerable time unless the room is warm, and when that is the case the Primula bloom is only, of short duration. Each time the plants are watered the particles of soil on the top should, when pressed with the fingers, have a dry feel, and they must remain separate, and not become pasty from the pressure of the fingers.

His Excel- expressed to them his gratifacation of the proofs i";ceived of their loyalty to the Indian Croyeenment, add- he would never forget their conduct during the 7itine_otCrisis. THE RISING IN ALBANIA. The Rews that the Miridite Albanians have risen in arms iscoerdrmed. Last Saturday they captured 200 horses and a convoy of ammunition and provisions on the way to the Turkish frontier garrisons at Crussinje, Playa, and Upek, rhe Miridites, who are Catholics, 35,000 strong, inhabit a district accessible only by three narrow mountain defiles ; and they are all the more formidable as they command the Prisrend and Tyranna roads—the only ones that can be used by the Turks in case of war with Montenegro for com- municating with Upper Albania. They are the only Alba- nian tribe that have a military organisation.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. Sir Rowland Blennerhasset recently offered his Killarney tenants their holdings at 20 years' purchase. This offer was rejected, but thetenants now agree to accept them at 14 Years, The Roman Catholic Archbishop of Dublin on Tuesday refused to accept the official managership of St. Patrick's Training School, Drumcondia, while the Model Schools were retained in Dublin in defiance of the sentiment of The Loyalists Protective Association intend organising a fund for the protection of all who stiffer through their resistance of boycotting. In this connection they intend making an appeal to England for funds. Subscriptions are being already raised for the purpose, and liberally responded to. Late on Monday night a shot was 'fired through the bed- room window of Matthew Morrisey, living between Bansha village and Tipperary. Mrs. Morrissey was the only occu- pant at the time, but was not struck. Morrissey is in the employment of a landlord who is stated not to have given any abatement in rent. The Kildysart branch of the National League, at a meet- ing held on Wednesday night, presided over by a local priest, passed a resolation calling noon all percons to cease speaking to or dealing with Mrs. Morgan O'Connell (niece of the Liberator), who is being`hoycotted on account of her .conduct as a' lan'downer. On Sunday, a reporter from a Cork Natienaliet paper at- tended the Fermoy branch of the League to report the pro- ceedings, bat he was by an unanimous vote expelled, owing to his having a week previously spoken to •persons who are not members, and which the League considered unfitted him for giving an impartial report. Theliorth Dublin guardians on Wednesday adopted a resolution calling ou the landlords of Ireland to give their tenants an abatement of 50 per cent on rents. A guardian stated that unless landlords gave large abatements, in a few years they would get no rent at all, for all the land would be lying waste on their bands. A sheriff's sale of cattle was held on Tuesday, at Ennis. An emergency bailiff from Belfast was in attendance, and was declared the purchaser of all the cattle at very high prices. 'There was much excitement. The sheriff and the auctioner were roughly handled, and the police charged the 'crowd. Several arrests were made. At Dublin Castle on Monday evening a consultation was held between the Lord Lieutenant, the Chief Secretary, and the Lord Chancellor with reference to the great extension of boycotting throughout the country. Several resident magistrates from various parts of 'lreland where the prac- tice is in full force were in attendance, and gave full infer- mationvith respect to the state of things existing in their "respective districts. After celebrating mass recently at Templeboy, the Rev. Mr. Cosgrove mentioned the great competition which the 'farmers were subjected to by the importation of foreign agricultural produce. The tenants, he said, should forward a statement to their landlords setting forth their claim to a reduction of rent consequent on the depression of the times, and demand not merely as a gracious concession, but as a matter of justice, a substantial reduction of their present rents.

A crowded and boisterous meeting of the National League was held on Tuesday night in Waterford to consider the ' letter Mr. Harrington giving his opinion as to the legality of the expulsion of Mr. Alderman Smith, vice-president. Mr. Harrington states that, in his opinion, after reading the reports and resolution oc the meeting, the whole proceed- ings were irregular and illegal. Mr. Alderman Smith at- tempted to speak, but was refused a hearing. The proceed- ings terminated in great disorder. BOYCOTTING ENGLISH GOODS.—A public meeting of trades has been held in the Town Hall, Killarney, for the purposetoof adopting a resolution condemning the sale of English ready-made clothing, and manufactured boots and shoes, as very injurious to both parties. The president of the local b anch of the National League presided. The reso- lution was carried; also one strongly protesting against the unpatriotic conduct of local drapers in their innovation of having foreign manufactured goods.

div.head: FATAL RAILWAY COLLISION.
div.p: FATAL RAILWAY COLLISION.
A DRIVER AND POINTSNIAN CHARGED WITH
-MAN-SLAUGHTER.

At the Present Police Court on Tuesday, before l'sfr.'F. W Earle, Peter Pomfret, a signal may, residing at Broad Green, and Thomas Hulme, an engine driver, residing at Wavertree, were cnarged with the manslaughter of James Knight, a brakesman, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company. Pomfret was defended by Mr. Neale, of Liverpoel, and Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for Hulrce. Superintendent Barker swid the two prisoners were charged with the manslaughter of lames Knight, of Warrington, and the prisoner Pomfret had been committed for trial by a coroner's warrant on the '2lst ult. On the 2nd April last Pomfret was a signal man employed at the Roby signal box, and he allowed a light engine to pass without having sig- nalled. The consequence was that it came into collison with a goods train of which James Knight was the brakes- man, and he was so injured that he died on the 12th Sep- tember. Efulme was the driver of the engine, and he so disregarded the signals as to run into a stationary goods

train: Eliza Knight, 13, Elizabeth-street, Warrington. deposed that the deceased was her husband. He attended his work on the 2nd April, and the next time she saw him was en the .sth April, when he was at the Royal Infirmary, Brownlow Hill, Liverpool. He was suffering from injuries to the head , and body. For several days before be died be could not speak. Previous to the 2nd Lpril her husband had always been a strong man. He was 44 years of age.—By Mr. Neale: Dr. Fox had told her that her husband died of :con- sumption. She still maintained that he was a strong and healthy man. Dr. Edward Austin Fox, curgeon, Warrington, deposed that from the 24th April he attended the injured man, who was suffering from a shock and general debility. He bad a mark on his forehead which bad, evidently been a scalp wound. He attended the deceased up to his death on the 12th September. On the 17th ult. be made a postmortem examination of the body. In his opinion death was from consumption, accelerated by injuries received in a railway accident. He would probably nave lived longer had he not received any injury.—By Mr. Swift: Judging from the post- mortem examination alone, consumption was quite sufficient to account for death. He attended the deceased for bran- ehitis four years ago. Dr. Arthur William Dawson, house surgeon, Royal In- firmary, Liverpool, said deceased was admitted to that in- stitution on the 3rd April. He was suffering from a scalp wound on the forehead, a bruise on the nose, and a shock. Deceased was in the Infirmary for two or three weeks, and then suffered from erysipelas, arising from the wounds. He noticed no consumptive appearances about him.—By Mr. Swift : When he left the Infirmary the injuries were cured. Thomas Harvey, of 31, Nichelsort.street, Warrington, , said he had been 32 years in the •ernploy of the railway compacy, and for 22 of which be had been employed as an engine driver. On the 2nd April he was driving an express goods train from Warrington to Liverpool, which was stopped by one of the signals after passing Roby signal box. They were waiting forth° signal to be pulled off when wit- ness felt something run into the rear of the train. He found that a light engine, driven by the prisoner Halms, had run into the guard's van, which Was thrown off the rails, as well as the waggon next to it. He assisted to get the de- ceased out of the van. Ile was injured about the forehead and nose, and complained of an injury to his side. He was afterwards removeu to the Royal Infirmary at Liverpool. Witness spoke to the prisoner Heinle, who slid, " It is a bad mess, but through the weather being a bit hazy I could not just twigs,the signal." . .

div.p: nnaam or LORD SEAFTESBUEL—Lord Shaftesisary died at Folkestone at a quarter before two o'clock on Thursday? afternoon. His last moments were of the most peaceful character. The night curse had been with him until an early Dart of the morning, when Isle valet (Goldsmith) re- sinned duty at the bedside. During the morning his lord- ship dictated two letters to his daughters. Three members of his family—Lady TemptemOre, the HOB. Edith Ashley, and the Hon. Cecil Ashley—Were in constant attendance upon hims and he conversed with them in the most affec- tionate and cheerful manner. Up to the last be retained consciousness, and conversed with the utmost sensibility.: He expected death, and his gentleness with his: children in the last hour was Most touching. His lordship, who was born April 28th, 1801, had thus considerably exceeded his 84th year. He Ii succeeded by Lord Ashley, born in June, 1831, and be leaves three other sons and two daughters, the second son being the Hon. Evelyn Ashley, M.P. He was renowned throughout the world for his zeal in all good simiks, and espeoially for his labisurs on behalf of factory operatives. Messages of con- dolence are being received by the family from all Darts of 'the country. The deceased nobleman will be buried at St Giles, Dorsetshire. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S Cocos to close tests, and the result has always proved its great endue as & sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imit.stions.- 1 Advt.

div.p: Wiltywo TIIE-EXAMINER. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1885.
TRE ELECHON CAMPAIGN.

Mr. Darlington, the Conservative candidate for the Rugby Division, having staaed that Mr. Gladstone was convinced of the value of the ballot by the commission appointed by Mr. Disraeli to inquire into its working, the right teem gen- tleman was writtereto on the subject, and has replied "that there isnot one word 9f truth in the statement made by Mr. Darlington." During the canvass of Mr. Childers, M.P., at Pontefract, he discovered that some misapprehension existed as to the disposal of time-expired clothing. It is explained, on the authority of a minute from the War Office, that a Conserva- tive Government were the firet to deprive the military of the privilege of disposing et their time-expired clothing, end Mr. Childers merely carried out the principle adopted by his predecessors. " I hear," writes a 'London correspondent, " that the Commission on Trade is likely to fall to pieces. Several of its members were not consulted in regard to the absurd questions addressed to Chambers of Commerce, and they have threatened to withdraw from the Commission. Other members are now discovering th,at the ininiry will he futile, and they do not care to waste time 'in an investigation which can have no result." AXATTON.-.-A Nottingham correspondent sere the atten- : tion of Mr. Chamberlain aud Lord E. Churchill having been called to the burden of the income tax felt by strug- gling tradesmen and professional men, Mr. ,Chamberlain replied by forwarding a copy of his speech e the 14th Of r January last, approving Prince Bismorck's proposal for tine tax to be graduated according to the amount, and to vary according to the character of the income. Lord Randolph Churchill-sayarthe subject is receiving his attention. Mat. $. H. WHITBREAD AT BOOTLE.—Kr. S. H. Went. bread, the Liberal candidate, addressed his constituents for the first time on Monday. The meeting was very enthusi- Win. The speaker spoke principally on matters of tocial reform. He supported in the main Mr. Gladstone's mani- festo. He was strongly in favour of the amending of the Land Laws, and the revising of the mode of procedure in the Lower House. In answer to a question, he spoke in favour df an Affirmation Bill. Me. SHAW LEFEVRE ON LAND REFORM.—Mr. Shaw Lefeyre„ M.P., speaking at Maidstone, on Saturday evening, said that Parliament had passed a great democratic measure of franchise reform and meet expect democratic results. There must be a reform of local government in rural die. tricta, because at present there was practically no real local authority in villages and small agricultural districts. These bodies ought to have authority to grant allotments of land to their agricultural labourers, and to look after their in- terests in other ways. 1.,0RD lienats AT OLDHAM. -- At a meeting in connec- tion with the Oldham Conservative Working-urea's League, on Saturday, Lord Harris supported a resolution .expressing eatisfaction with the ability brought to bear in the settle- ment of the difficult foreign complications left by Mr. Gladstone's too late and vacillating Ministry, acknowledg- ing the claim of the Government as the working-man's friend in the appointment of a Royal Commissionto inquire into the present unparalleled depression in trade, and believing that by the supremacy of Conservative prin- miples only can England regain and rqaintain her position as a nation. THE GENERAL FLECTION.—The undergraduates' cases at Oxford ended, says a London correspondent, as was antici- pated, but the notice of appeal even in this important in- stance has not revived anywhere apprehensions of a post- ponement of the election. It is now the best opinion that' Parliament will be dissolved by proclamation in the usual way on Tuesday, the 17th November, and that the writs for the elections will be issued the same evening. That is also customary. If this be correct, the borough elections would generally take place about the 24th and'2sthlsTovem- ber. In 1880 the dissolution was proclaimed on March 24, and the elections in Manchester and Salford followed on the Ist April. THE FREE LAND LEAGUE—Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P. (President of the Free Land League, gave an address at nlast Grinstead, on Saturday night. He said he looked upon the allotment system as most valuable, in that it must be a great step in the way to small or peasant proprietor- ship. The people of the country were divorced from the soil, and that separation had now passed into estrangement. That was due to the land laws. He wanted to see nine- tenths of the soil in the south of England cultivated by occupying owners. He hoped the time had come when the enfranchised men of England would labour to free the soil from all that hindered and obstructed the largest use Of it by the people. RETIREMENT 05' MR. F. H. O'DONNELL. Mr. F. H. O'Donnell, who has sat for Dungarvan sincel.B3o, an- Ounces that the condition of his health prevents him from seeking re-election. Mr. O'Donnell was elected as a Hones Haler, but he long ago broke away from allegiance to Mr. Parnell. In taking leave of Parliamentary life, he has a fling at the Parnellites. He condemns them for having crushed all independent action and reduced popular organ- ' iaation to the mere procuration of money and auto- cratic power. Parnellism, he save, has carefully and deliberately discouraged and thwarted every branch of political action which lay outside the capacity of five or six individuals. LORD DUNRAVEN AT STOCKFORT.—Lord Dunraven, ad- dressing a Conservative meeting on Monday evening, at Stockport, contended that the depression of trade from which this country was suffering was due to a foolish per. severance in a fiscal policy which, while it might have suited us admirably some years ago, when our condition and that of foreign nations was different, did not suit us now. He characterised the methods advocated by Mr. Chamberlain for the creation of a class of yeomen as con- stituting the worst form of Protection, aria expressed the belief that Lord Salisbury and a Coneervative Government only could extricate this country from the troubles which menaced it in the East. NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATIOIL—Tbe annual meeting of the National Liberal Federation Was held at Bradford on Thursday. Mr. W. Kendrick, who presided, in moving the adoption of the report, spoke confidently of Liberal pros- pects at the next election. The report, in commending the passage of the Franchise Bills, said the House orLords had received a respite, not a pardon. Mr. 5. Kitson was elected president, and resolutions were adopted in favour of the I reform of the laws of primogeniture, entail, and settlement :1 Idemanding security of tenure and compensation for improve- ments for -tenants; urging compulsory registration of titles ; the enfranchisement of leaseholders:; the allotment of land to labourers by local authorities-; in favour of free education, local government, and disestablishment. Mn. CHAMBERLAIN AND DISEsTABLISHMENT TN SCOTLAND. —Mr. Chamberlain has been questioned by Mr. A. Taylor- Innes, who moved a resolution in favour of Disestablish- ment at the recent Liberal Confunence in Glasgow, as to whether, in his opinion, it would be premature to submit is resolution on the subject in the next Parliament. Mr. Chamberlain's reply is that he would not consider such a resolution premature, and that he looks 'forward to the question being in that way brought under the notice of Par- liament and the country. Though it may be impossible to deal finally with the Scottish Establishment in the next Parliament, that is a very different thing to taking the opinion of the Scotch members and of the House of Com- mons. To do this is merely to prepare for the struggle of which the preliminaries are now being brought into view. Lome ROSEBERY AT Handeez.-Lord Rosebery, addressing a meeting of the Surrey Liberals at Reigate, on Monday evening, said, in spite of the reproaches which it had brought upon his head, he still clung firmly te the handle of the Liberal umbrella. Referring to the recent events in 'Roumelca, he said the main achievement of Lord Beacons- field's Administration, which was to divide Bulgaria into two parts, had faded away like snow before the sun, and the establishment of a united Bulgaria had realised the best hopes for liberty in the East, and the best security against Eussian aggression in that quarter. For the last five years the Tories had lived on a• diet of anathsma and abuse, which was very good as a condiment, but made a very bad etaple. In addition to questions in Mr. Gladstone's mani- fest% he wanted to include in the Liberal programme that of reform in reference to excessive hours of labour amongst some of the working population. This was a most press- ing reform, and if nothing could be done in this direction he should have much to answer for. MR. JESSE COLLINGS ON ENCLOSURE ACTS.—Mr. Jesse Collings. M.P., addressed a large meeting of Liberals in the Albert Hall, Leeds, on Monday evening, in support of the candidature of Mr. Lawrence Gene, Q.O , for East Leeds. The hon. geetlemen spoke principally on the question of land reform. There was a time when almost every cottager in the country had land to till, but there had been between three and four thousand Enclosure Acts in this country. From 1800 to 1845 there were two thousand Enclosure Acts, and from 1760 to 1845 there were nearly seven millions of acres of land enclosed. This was nearly a third of the ground and a fourth of the cultivated land is England. He had received a letter that morning calling his attention to a speech of Mr. Guy Dewnay's, who accused him (the speaker) of having brought his figures no further down titan 1845 because in that year a Conservative Government had decided to allow no more Enclosure Acts to be passed. He granted that the conduct of the landowners had been so atrocious that they themselves were ashamed of it. But

from 1845 to 1867 there were 450000 acres enclosed, and of those only 2,119 acres were set aside for what Mr. Guy Dawnay called the labouring poor and for recreation. What did they cell that in plain lammage ? ("Robbery.") Well. let them call it robbery. (Cheers.) Surely the rights of the poor deserved special reverence, and he thought that if the new electors were what he took them to be it would be looked into. (Cheers.)

fists M. H. BE ACE AT SALISATRY.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer (Sir M. Beach) spoke at a meeting at Salis- bury on Wednesday evening. He said the Conservative Government came into office with the goodwill of the coun- try, and they did not believe that the country had yet seen any reason to regret the event. On the subject of the re- volt in Eastern Ronmelia, he said the aim of the Govern- I ment wtuld be—though it was not a matter in which the 1 country was especially concerned beyond any other of the signatory Powers—to confine the area of any possible dis- turbances, and to arrive at such a solution as might be best consistent with justice and with the maintenance of Euro- pean peace. Ho asserted that misrepresentation had been made lathe contrast drawn as to the state of Ireland under the late Government and at ;.he present moment. No effort, however, would be wanting on the part of the Government to deal with the existing lawlessness with a fi-in hand. The law must be upheld, and combinations against it must b suppressed. In reference to Mr. Gladstone's manifesto, hc• declared that it.was misleading as to past facts, while ete" promises as to the future were vague... He exhorted th, people not to give the ez-Premier a political cheque to be

endorsed to whom he pleased for purposes at present un- known, and said that Liberal candidates should be asked to say " Yes " or " No " to two questions, viz.," Will you or will you not disestablish and disendow the Church ?" and Wia you or will you not maintain the hereditary princi- ple in the House of Lords ?" Mn CHAMBERLAIN AT BRADrORD.—Mr. Chamberlain addressed a great Liberal meeting at Bradford, on Thursday night, in connection with the annual conference of the National Liberal Federation. He twitted tbe Government with having adopted the Liberal programme, and said the best specific agaisst obstruction was to put the Tory-hi:li party ou the Treasury Bench, where they would be 'care- fully watched by a Liberal majority." He referred to the Eastern difficulty, which he said was a bitter humility for Lord Salisbury, and regretted Parliament was not sitting, 80 that the policy of the Government might be ascertained, for ' Ministers who had spoken since the disturbances broke out bad failed ,to give any tatisfoctory explanation of their views or the course they intended to adopt. Peace with • honour bad become a byeword, and we should be glad to secure peace at any price. He next spoke of the many measures which had been passed to alleviate the condition of the working classes, and said there was much more to be done. He was satisfied the newly-enfranchised eleetors would nrr. allow the rnitery and wretchedness which pre- vailed in their midst longer to exist without an attempt to apply a remedy. He looked to the questions of the land and free education for a great deal, and believed people could Tress these subjects at the general election. England ' could,xot be merry England with the men who tilled the soil divorced from it. Ma. BRADIAIME AND MR. GLanstem's MAN/FESTO.— Mr. Bradlaugh has published a statement respecting Mr. Gladstone's manifesto. He expresses regret that Mr. Glad- stone has not written a word with reference to the 'great constitutional struggle" which commenced in 1880, and goes on to say—•"l disagree with hiaa that paramount in- terest' compelled the military intervention in 1882, though I admit it was the legical consequence of the pledges given bv the Conservative Government. I regret that as Prime Minister, Mr. Gladstone did not firmly resist the Jingo ten- dencies of members of his own party, and of his own Cabi- net, as well as of the Tory party, and with him now T ask, as I have always asked, for our entire withdrawalfrom Egyptian territory at the earliest moment.'" Mr. Bradlaugh refers to our excessive expenditure, and then writes :—" A few points of the programme of the Land Law Reform League are covered by Mr. Gladstone's letter. I understand him to advocate the abolition of primogeniture and entail, te propose to facilitate the transfer of land, and to revise its taxation. All this we Radicels can support ;1 it is in the right direction, and though it is not enough, the securing this will be no hindrance to further reform. On reform ia the House of Lords, Mr. Gladstone says justly enough that' knowledge and virtue alone have an intrinsic right to govern.' It is, therefore, most unfortunate that he should add that he hopes 'that iu the reconstruction of the House of Peers' when it arrives, a reasonable share of power may be allowed, under wise conditions, to birth.' Heredi- tary claim to legislate is absurd in view of the new reform bills, and birth in a peer's family has not yet proved art in- fallible guarantee of either knowledge or virtue. It is, however, matter of encouragement to Radical reformers that the reform of the House of Lords is now sufficiently within the realm of practical politics to figure in the special ency- clical of the head of the Liberal party."
SIR WM. HARCOURT ON FREE TRADE AND TEIE

LAND QUEeTION. Ott Monday evening Sir William Harcourt addressed a meeting of the electors of Dorsetshire at Blandford. He said that in coining down be had been naturally animas to keow what wdre the manners and political habits of Dorset. shire. He came upon a paragraph which threw a good deal of light upon the question. The newspaper said :—" Politi- cal picnics have begun again. In order to allure the new democracy of Dorsetshire te Sherbourne Park on the 3rd of next month, on which day a grand Conservative demonstra- tion is announced, a programme is to be gone through that would satisfy the most fastidious music hall patron." (Laughter.) It then proceeds to describe that this great political discussion was to be accompanied by sensitionel globe rolling, performances upon the high wire, juggling, hat spinning, clowning, eccentric performers, burlesque ac- tors, horizontal bar performances, roundabouts, dancing, and shooting galleries, and that it was to finish up with the grandest display of fireworks ever seen in the Weet of Eng- land. and a glorious illumination of the !ruins. (Great laughter.) Well, it struck him that this was the most sin- gular method of conducting a great political discussion he ever heard of. (Hear, hear.) But in the midst of the globe rolling and the hat spinning was to appear the respec- table form of Lord Iddesleigh ; at what stage, whether he is to be the great transparency in the midst of the fireworks which are to illuminate the ruins was not particularly spe- cified. The noble lord was a fair and courteous opponent, and he was sere he would make an excellent speech, but whether the speech would leave the men of Dorsetshire much wiser than it found them was more than he could pre- tend to say. If he were to venture upon a criticism of Lord Iclleeleigh's style—and an old writer says "The style is the man "—he should say it was a little vague and somewhat indistinct. Now, the Liberal party had no ruins to illumi- nate. They had the light of their own principles, which was sufficient to illuminate the English constitution which they had built. (Cheers.) The Tory party were now trying to say that they had given the suffrage to the counties. They had done that just as much as King John was the author of Magna Charta, and if there had been a Tory majority in the base during the past few sessions, did they believe for a moment that the extended franchise in the counties would have been granted ? (Cries of " No.") He saw in a Dorset paper that day that a challenge had been given to him to deal with the question of Free Freda and Fair Trade. He was quite willing to do so, but he would ask them to give a similar challenge to Lord Iddes- leigh when be appeared before them because Lord Iddes- leigh was the chairman of the Royal Commission. He be- lieved the noble lord had some difficulty about his recruits, the same sort of difficulty that Falstaff had with his re- cruits when he marched them through Coventry. (A laugh.) Lord Iddesleigh was an experienced man. He had held many offices which had made him acquainted with, or ought to have made him acquainted with the true state of the finances of the' country. Why, then, did he want a Commission to tell him about Free Trade and Fair Trade ? After his forty years of public service was It not the busi- ness of a responsible Minister to know and see for himself what the state of affairs was and what were the remedies which ought to be applied to the case? What he wanted to know was, if the Commission were really a genuine affair, or whether it was a piece of hocus-pocus to help people to conclusions which they did not think it safe to avow. What did the Tory party complain of? That every- thing was too cheap. They said food was too cheap. (No.) It was getting cheaper, thank God, bat the Tory party did not thank God for it—(cheers)—and they were appeal- ing against the bounties of Providence to a Royal Com- mission to see if they could not find out some means to stay this plague of abundance. Again, wool was cheaper, and, consequently, clothes were cheaper. Wood and metals were cheaper, and they were therefore able to build better houses,:but those gentlemen thought rents were too low, that the profits in capital were too low, in fact, that everything was too low except wages—for they said that if they were allowed to raise peic-s the people would get higher wages. Since Free Trade the population of the country had nearly doubled, but the land had not increased, and how could we suppose the people of this country could have lived if they lied not received support from elsewhere? What do we get from abroad ?-47f0,000 live cattle, more than 1,000,000 sheep, more than 6.000,000 head of dead meat, 2.500 cwts. of butter, and 2,000,000 cheeses were imported; and yet the consumption of the live cattle of the country had not diminished. All this was in addition to what was produced at home. (Cheers.) If then they paid less for their bread, for their meat, for their bacon and their butter, they were able to buy more of other things, and the consequence was that they were able to get 213,000,0001b5. of tea and 24,000,000ewt5. of sugar, and did they want a change in that respect? ("No.") Free Trade bad shown this, that there bad been a gradual in- crew° in the wealth of the country ever since, whatever might be said to the contrary. Then, with regard to the condition of the people, surely there had been a great im- provement since the repeal of the Corn Laws, as was shown by the Poor Law returns and the returns of crime. He desired now to say a few words about the land. His opinion about the land was that those who inhabited and tilled the soil ought to have a different interest in it from that which they now possessed, and that involved a can- siderable change in what Lord Beaconsfield called the hier- archy of the land, but it involved no change inconsistent with the rates of property. It required, however, a great political force, and that force depended upon where the centre of gravity lay, and the centre of gravity had been changed by the enfranchisement of the agricultural labourers. After the Reform Bill of 1832 the middle•class had the power, and much was done for the farmer, and those who had the power always would have their interests attends to. Now, without injustice to anyone, the agri- cultural labour would be looked after, and it was quite time they were. He did not consider that the labourer ought to rely solely on the weekly wage, but he ought to have an interest in the soil upon which he lived. He asked them not to sell their birthright for a mess of pottage, but to see that they had what was their legitimate due, notwithstand- ing all that was said about socialism and plunder In con- clusion, he said he regarded the government of Ireland as dangerous, and feared it was getting as bad as ever. Lord Salisbury had seen the Berlin Treaty go to smash. In fact, it had received such a fall as bad not occurred since the days of Hampty-Dumpty. A conference was suggested to give the agreements with Turkey Christian burial; but if there was to be a European scramble for territory, he hoped we should have nothing to do with it.
