PEASANT PROPRIETARY.
BY JAQUES.

Of all the many schemes to amend our land system which have been propounded, none have been so much obtruded upon the public notice as that of a peasant proprietary. The economic benefits of the system and the social virtues of the peasant proprietor have been favourite themes of that school of ecemotnists which is regarded in this country as the orthodox school, but some of whose tenets have, much to the advantage of the people, been little regarded of late, and it is likely, will be less regarded in the future. So powerful ropagandic agency as the Cobden Club has also striven to popularise this scheme, and at the present time it is ad vocated by a section of politicians whose influence is in- creasing every day, and patronised by a combination of aristocratic landowners. Yet is spite of these conspiring forces it cannot be said that the peasant proprietary scheme has taken a Crone hold of the public mind or aroused much enthusiasm. The agricultural labourer in whose behalf it is proposed to make a lavish use of the public purse is said to be a good deal enatnoured of the scheme, but in the great industrial centres of the country this solution of the (sad problem, if not regarded with absolute hostility, is certainly not espoused with any degree of heartiness. It may ba confidently anticipated that, no matter what Government is In power when measures of land reform are placed before Parliament, the legislation on the subject will be fashioned by the Liberal party. There are now, no doubt, not a few Conservatives who advocate moderate land reform, and at the ether end of the scale there is a kind of guerilla force which fights for changes more drastic than any that have yet been admitted into the Liberal programme. But, it is certain, that the views of these latter will not be embodied into practical legislation for some time to come, while the Conservative who advocates land reform has really aban- doned the cardinal article of his faith, which is to conserve, and turned Liberal for the occasion. It may perhaps not be incorrect to say that the Conservatives, who have in the first instance opposed all change and then fallen into the ranks of the progressists, do not so much occupy the posi- tion of useful auxiliaries with ate influencing voice, as they occupy a position somewhat analogous to that of those cap- tives who, conquered and humiliated, marched in the triumphal processions of ancient Rome not of their own free will, but under the compulsion of a power greater than their own. They are land reformers because if they persisted in resisting reform they would., poatically, cease to exist. It may be taken for granted, then, that if we wish to forecast at all events the earlier stages of the coming land reform we I mnst first ascertain as far as possible the feeling and bent of I the Liberal party. When this is done nothing is more ob- vious than that there is, as yet, but little popular force be- hind the peasant proprietary scheme. The preference which many, who justly claim to speak on behalf of large numbers of working-men, express for other solutions of the land problem is significant, and even at the conference of dele- gates, representative of all shades of Liberalism, held at Warrington on the day of Mr. Chamberlain's visit the dis- approval of the forcible breaking up of land into small holdings was emphatic and unanimous. It is evident that there is great diversity of opinion as to the best method of land reform. Upon the points included in Mr. Gladstone's programme there is something like complete harmony, but as soon as the more drastic measures are discussed discord sets in. Yet it is certain that few Liberals and no Radicals believe that the land question will be settled by the abolition of primogeni- ture and the cheapening of transfer. The differences are not so much as to the need of further reform, but as to the nature of that reform. These differences will, without doubt, be soon subetantially harmonised through the me- dium of a free and full discussion, and as the peasant pro- prietary scheme is sure to have, probably to a greater degree than any other szheme, the advantage of powerful and eloquent advocacy, it behoves everyone who may be able to influence, if merely to the extent of a single vote, the land legislation of the future, to consider whether that scheme is the likeliest to work out the desired result. It may, there- fore, not be out of place to point out what are likely to be i the effects of the scheme if adopted. When a person selects an instrument of any kind it is advisable, if he wishes to make a wise choice, to keep clearly in mind the kind of work that instrument is destined to perform. This remark applies with particular force to the selecting of the instrument of land reform. It is essential to a wise choice that, in the first instance, the evils it is intended to remove should be clearly apprehended, and then to ask of etch of the schemes of land reform : Is this scheme the likeliest that could be devised to remove those evils?" The scheme which most conforms to the require- ments of this question would, undoubtedly, be the best , scheme of land reform. Now what are the evils connected I with our present lend system ? Do not those which are most grievously and widely felt spring from the fact that land, which, from the very nature of things, is the closest of monopolies, is in the hands of but a portion of the people who inhabit it? When landowners draw almost fabulous some in the shape dt ground rents from the inhabitants of cities and towns; when royalty owners exact the lion's I share of the wealth that is annually created by poorly-paid miners; and when the owners of agricultural land pocket larger rents because by the labour and capital of other people a two has been built or a railway or some other improve- ment has been made in the neighbourhood of that land, what is it but the exercise of the power of monopolists to reap where they had never sown? In short the greatest, and probably the root evil of the land system is that of the " unearned increment," that is to say the enormous increase in the annual value of land which landlords ap- propriate, but which they have done nothing to create. The "unearned increment" has been a favourite theme of land reformers, and it has always been held that a land re- form to be at all adequate must ensure that this " incre- ment " is taken from those who do not earii it and turned over to those who do. Yet this is the end which of all others will not be accomplished by the creation of a peasant proprietary. It is true enough that by that means the "unearned increment" will be taken from those who at present enjoy it, but only to turn it over to others who, if anything, have less right to it. By parcelling out an estate into fifty or sixty allotments, and then putting them in the possession of an equal number of "peasants," you do not abolish the unearned increment or even give it to those who have created it; you simply divide it amongst a larger number of people. Let us take a local illustration which will very clearly impress this fact upon the mind. The Manchester Ship Canal, we will assume, is an accom- plished tact, and that prior to its being completed it thorough peasant proprietary scheme had been adopted by Parliament, and the land on both Bides of the canal had been allotted to peasant owners. The changes brought about by the canal, let us also assume, fulfilled the most sanguine expectations; industries sprung up at certain points along its banks and population accumulated. It is evident that the annual value of the peasant properties at these points would increase ten, twenty, and even a hundred fold. The fortunate peasants who owned these properties would perhaps sell them for large sums of money, or thsy might adopt that method which is very well known in most , of the industrial centres of Lancashire, of leasing out their ; land on the terms of a sabstantial yearly ground-rent and a reversionary right to both the land and the houses that are built upon it, and then our happy peasant might retire and live at his ease upon a very handsome income. But would he be living on his own earnings or the fruits of his own earnings? Not at all. This income would consist as largely of "unearned increment" as that of any patrician in the land. And were a peasant proprietary created all over the kingdom the same process would go on wherever a town increased in wealth and population, and wherever a public improvement such as a canal or a railway was made. It is evident, therefore, that a peasant proprietary is not the instrunnt which will perform the work of taking the increment in the value of land from those who have not earned it and distributina it amongst those who have earned it. The most that can be said of this scheme is that it will considerably enlarge the number of those who will en- joy that increment. But this being admitted, it must , never be forgotten that though peasant proprietors be ' multiplied to the greatest possible extent they will still, of necessity, form but a small proportion of the population of an industrial and merchantile country like England. Were the Englishmen of to-day living, like their early Saxon ancestors, in village communities and drawing all their sustenance direct from the land, a scheme like that of peasant proprietary might do very well. But when the bulk of the people live in cities and towns and are engaged in manufacture and commerce to divide the land amongst the agricultural popula- tion would be but to perpetuate an injustice in a somewhat mitigated form. A minority of the nation would still be in a position to exact unearned wealth from a majority who created that wealth. A remedy of that kind would. justly be considered very imperfect, and weuld only be tolerated if a better could not be found. But in the case I of the lend na One can pretend that there are no methods by which the unearned increment could be appropriated to the use of those who create it, that is to say, the community. It might, therefore, one would think, be taken for granted that nobody who keeps in mind all that is necessary to a just and complete land reform will choose a peasant proprietary scheme as the best instrument to perform it. Besides not being adapted for accomplishing the work of land reform, there is one inherent defect in a peasant pro- prietary scheme which almost compels one to think that it wmld intensify the evils it is intended to abolish. It should neveabe forgotten in dealing with an economic question like that of the land, that the people of a country live upon the produce of their labour, and that consequently the greater the amount of that produce the better off ought the people to he. It is true we hear a great deal just now about over- production, but at the same time we hear occasionally .of people starving to death; and a large number of others.liv- iog lives of abject misery because of the want of the things " over-produced." It is clear enough from this that the suffering arises not from over-production, but from the us- fair distribution of the things produced. It ought. to be the endeavour of statesmen to, in the first place, f:acilitato the production of wealth, that is to say, food, clothing, ana in fact everything that minister to human necessity and comfort ; and, next, to further, as far as somal arrange- ments can further, the fair and natural distribution of wealth. As we have already seen, a peasant proprietary scheme is very little better adapted for securing a fair dis- tribution of the wealth produced than the present system of landholding. In addition to that, it is almost certain that it will be less favourable to the production of wealth than the present system. To realise this we need only find out the answer to'the simple question : Why do farms become larger and larger ? Is it not the obvious answer to this question to say that farms grow larger for the same reason that cotton mills and ironworks grow larger, that is to say,

I because labour is infinitely more productive when combined I It is, no doubt, possible to abolish by legislative enactment the huge cotton mills of Lancashire, and relegate spinning L and weaving to isolated workers, as in the days prior to the inventions of Hargreaves, Arkwright, and Crompton ; and the iron industry might b. left In the hands of the village blacksmith. Sup- port for proposals of this kind could be found in the spe- cious argument that as these industries are carried on at present the capitalists receive too large and the workmen to small a share of the wealth created. But though the truth of this argumest might be admitted the utter foolish- ness of the proposal it was intended to support would 113 seen by everybody. It would be seen that it meant the throwing aside of that greatest of allindustria devices, the division of labour, and the repudiation to a great extent of those aids to labour which science and invention have placed udder the control of the modern workman. It would also be seen that the adoption of such a proposal would so reduce the produce of labour that tkough the share of the capitalist would undoubtedly be vastly lessened, that of the workman would as surely be lessened in proportion. Yet in its. way the peasantry proprietary scheme is a proposal of the same nature as the one here mentioned Those engaged in the agricultural industry are just as much actuated be self- interest as other people, and the explanation of their hav- ing thrown land into big farms is that experience has taught them that the industry can be carried on most profi- tably in that way. Implements are used by the large far- mer which the "peasant proprietor "would never dream of, and consequently the quantity of 'produce of big farms in proportion to the labour expended is very much greater. It is true that under the present land system im- provements in agricultural implements as improvement in almost every other direction, operate chiefly to augment the landlord's revenue without much benefitting either the farmer or the labourer. But the remedy for this is not the bringing about of a state of things which would very largely preclude the use of improvements, and thus leave work to be done by hurnats drudgery, which might with incompar- able ease be.performed by mechanical appliances. A "reform" of this description would, surely, be of a very retrograde na- ture, and more suggestive of the ignorance of the time when labour-saving contrivances were regarded as inimical to hu- man welfare than of the enlightenment ef the latter part of the ninteenth century.

Sir John Lubbock at Birmingham, on Thursday, unveiled a marble statute of the late Sir Josiah Mason, which has been placed in the square between the Science College and the Town Hall.

The representatives of IG6 tawns have already accepted invitations to be present at the Jubilee Banquet of Munici- pal Corporations, on October 9th, in London, at which Earl Granville, the Home Secretary, and others are also exi- pected. Six children of James M'Fadyean, clerk, of Glasgow, were poisoned on Thursday by eating sweets purchased at a grocer's shop, but under medical care they are recovering. The police have seized all the cnafections in the shop and those left by the children for analysis. MURDER OF A LION TAMER.—A labourer named Thos. Hewington. residing at Spitalfields, was on Wednesday com- mitted fur trial at the Wership•street Police Court, London, charged with the wilful murder of Alexander Hugh Munroe a negro lion tamer, by stabbing him with a knife. THE WELSH MURDER.—At Bettws•y-Coed, on Wednes- daw, three men, named Edward Jones, blacksmith, Bethes- da; George Hutchinson, coach guard; and Robert Roberts, coachman, Bangor, were charged with the wilful murder of Morris Jones, coach proprietor, Pwllheli. A further remand was granted. _ _ .

INSPECTION AT ALDERSHOT.—The Duke of Cambridge arrived at Aldershot on Saturday for the autumn inspection of the forces. The troops, numbering 6,000 men, with 1,447 horses and 44 guns, under General Anderson, were reviewed in the Long Valley, and after executing a series of military mevernents marched past. A large number of spectators were present. GREAT FIRES IN AMERICA.—EXtCR2iVe fires at Dakota have been wasting thousands of acres of wheat lands. On many large farms all the buildings have been destroyed. The fires have raged during two weeks for hundreds of miles along the Northern Pacific Railway, from Brainard west- ward beyond Bismarck. Nearly all, however, have been got under control. MADAGASCAR.—U.M.S. Bacchante, which is now due at Mauritius, in under orders to pay a visit to Tematave. This will be welcome news to British subjects in Madagascar, who have not seen the British flag for a long time. It is believed at P.mtananarivo that the Italian Consul is en- deavouring to promote a settlement of the difficulty between France and Madagascar. A VIOLENT TEMPER.—WhiIe some boys were playing in a street at Canterbury on Saturday, one of them, named Edward Dawkins, was pushed into the doorway of a butcher's shop, where he fell. The proprietor, George Wilkinson, in a fit of exasperation, threw a cleaver at the boy, who was struck on the head, and a severe gash inflic- ted. The lad had to be conveyed to the hospital.

A SAD DEATIL—An elderly man, named Thomas Severn, met with his death on Saturday, at Wednesbury, under dis- tressing circumstances. For some time he had been ill, and, after partaking of breakfast, he went to walk by Ell- wells Pools. When walking by the edge of the water he was seized with a tit and fell in, and before he could be extricated was drowned. The deceased lay in three feet of water.

THE BRADFORD TRAMWAY ACCIDENT.—The coroner's inquiry Into the cause of the recent steam tramway disaster at Bradford was resumed on Wednesday. Very little additional evidence was given. The Coroner, in summing up, laid stress upon the fact that John timpleby bad not made proper connections on the engine before getting up steam. The jury found a verdict of manslaughter against Umpleby. Music HALLS AT LEICESTER.—At Leicestrr Brewster Sessions, on Monday, the magistrates declined to renew music and singing licenses to any house except recottnised music halls, the experiment tried last year under the local Act not beiug satisfactory. It was stated that .£2 000 had been spent in structural alterations on one house. The prin- cipal attendants were young people of both sexes from 15 to 20 years of age. WORNME!..7'S TRIBUTE TO MR. GLADSTONE. A move- ment has b.rot statted hi London with the object of raising "workmen's tribute " (by means of subscriptions on the penny basis) for presentation to Mr. Gladstone, "as a token from the working classes of their appreclation of his un- rivalled genius, and of grateful thanks for his life•long de- votion to the permanent interests of the great ins sa of his toiling fellow-countrymen." THE IMPUDENT TICEET•OF-LEAVE Max.—At Glasgow, on Thursday, the convict Stewart Samson, who returned his ticket-of-leave to the Home Secretary with the request that he should light his pipe with it, has been sent to penal ser- vitude until the expiration of his term of seven years, in April next. On inquiry at Dundee, it was found that Stewart had no cause of complaint against the Prison Aid Society, or the Provost of the town. •

DECREASE OF CRIME —The number of sentences of penal servitude in England and Wales was last year lower than in any previous year on record, being only 1,349. In the five years ending 1859 there was an annual average of 2,589 such sentences, the average in the five years ending 1884 was only 1,427, though population had increasad by considerably more than one-third. The decrease is the number of women convicts is greater than that of ths men.

DESPERATE PoecntsG A FFRAY.—A desperate poaching agray took place at Lyme Park, near Macclesfield, at three o'clock on Thursday morning. A large gang, including some most notorious poachers, had netted about three hun- dred rabbits and hares, and were making off with them when they were stnoped by a large force of watchers and keepers. A most desperate encounter followed. Sticks and stones were used by the neachers, eight of whom were captured. EXTRAORDINARY AFFILIATION CASE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, John Fitzpatrick, of Earlee• town, appeared to answer the fourth summons to (Mow cause why he should not contribute to the support of the illegiti- mate child of Ellen Ball, of Earlestown, of which he was alleged to be the father. The complainant .7as represented by Mr. Richardson, of Bolton, and Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, defended.—Tne magistrates decided to adjourn the case for the production of witnesses, after some discussion as to whether the case should be heard.

A DIABOLICAL ACT OF REVENGE.—A shocking occurrence took place at Ynynetel, near Pontypridd, on Seturday. A man named Lewis called at the house of a collier farmer, and finding the latter not at home was invited inside to wait. While doing so Lewis suddenly produced a revolver, with which he fired at the servant and Evans' children, hitting the termer and one of the girls. The servant ran out of the house pursued by Lewis, who hit her severely on the head with a poker. The injured ones lie in a critical condition. Lewis, who it appears hod been in Evans' employ, but had been discharged for idleness, delivered himself up to the Aberdare police laterie the day. A LONG FIRM BROKEN UP.—At the Central Criminal Court, on Saturday, Emma Isitt, George Isitt, Samuel Cramer, Robery Sidney, Robert Muroford, Mary Ann Dun- dee, Thumas Williams, and Rebert Grey were indicted for conspiring to obtain goods by false pretences. The prison- ers appeared to have adopted the plan of taking furnished houses at the West End and letting them out to lodgers; after this they ordered large quantities of goods, which they obtained. The female prisoners were sentenced to six months' imprisonment each; George Lehi. Cramer, and Grey to 18 months each; Sidney and Williams to 20 months each ; and Mumford to 15 months. TILE CASE OF ELIZA AII3asTBOND.--At the Bow-street Police Court on Saturday the bearing of the charges against Mr. W. T. Stead, Rebecca Jarrett, Mr. Jacques, Madame Mourez, Mr. Bratnwell Booth, and Mrs. Coombe, of abduct- ing the girl Eliza Armstrong, was concluded. Mr. Stead attempted to read a long statement which he had prepared explaining the motives which influenced him and going into various matters which Mr. Vaughan declined to admit, as, be said, he was only concerned with questions of fact and law, and not of motive. Mr. Stead was allowed to read ex- tracts, in which be described the course of the pr.,cedure be had adopted in obtaining evidence in support of the revela- tions in the Pall Aral Gazette, and asked that if his agents had unwittingly transgressed the law the sole punish-. ment might fall on him. Mr. Vaughan, in giving his deci- sion, commented on the /falsehoods which Jarrett had ade mittedly told in order to get the girl in her power. Th ere- was no doubt from the statement which the defendant Stead had made, with some self-glorification, that he had brought himself within the statute; and there was no doubt that Bramwell Booth, Jacques, and Mrs. Coombe had taken. part in the abduction; but he acquitted Booth and Mrs. Coombe en the charge of indecent-assault. The defendant Stead had in his very able paper endeavoured to show that Vaughan) confessed tbat if thisan m d nuortai v wasnnt i praiseworthy. a ibs env iteihr et h(ysi. r might haveetlr b:e surroundings, that a undlionfgtsy, that was no justification for taking her away from her par- ents. There might, however, have been motive existing in his mind to obtain material for the nauseating and deplorable article which had appeared in the Pall ~11a11 Gazette on the 6th of July, and which bad certainly given great pain and sorrow to many good people, and had greatly lowered the I English people in the etlitnation of foreign nations. But I the law of this country could not be broken for the gratifici- i tion of any motive whatever. He could not see any differ- , ence between this Case and that of any relieious enthusiast ! who went into a family and took away a child because the parents were not of the same religious belief as himself. Such a taking away could not be justified, and it would be ! most perilous to the liberty of the people of this country ,it such an infraction of the law were to be permitted. If I such a motive as that were held to be within the law there would be an end to the freedom and security and independ- ence of every family in this country. On the principle of law and on the facts of the case, it was his dety to commit , the defendants for trial for the varieue ffe against them, except only upon the charge° ofniCnedse cent chargedag et sault against Mrs. Coombe and Mr. Bramwell Booth. instead of school fees. The Legislature might, as Alr. CHAMBERLAIN points out, easily supply the money from imperial sources which is now, in many cases, painfully ob- tained from parents, and the Schools, except as to lessened friction, could go on just as before. The truth is the poor are too much already at the mercy of the machine; and it i§ to get rid of its crushing effects that freedom in education is proposed. Mr. CARLETON juggles with words, and, as many a Tory has done before him, he would have the working classes believe that those who would strike off their fetters are bringing "chins and slavery." But he will not suc- ceed; those who wear the shoe know where it pinches. What is it that the machine does to-day? It brings heart-ache every Monday Morning to thousands of poor parents who are hard put to it" in supplying their Children with school-pence when they feel that the money is needed rather for food and clothing. It forces the poorest of the poor to appear before Boards of Guardians or School Attendance Committees to submit the poverty they would hide to inquisitorial dissection. It compels some to accept orders for payment of school fees which they can- not take without the feeling that they are being pauperised. It searches out widows who may be left struggling with large families, and fines them for the irregular attendance of their offspring, caused by a small and irregular supply of funds. It does all this week in and week out the year round, making education hateful to those Who should welcome it as a blessing; and it is because it. does this that statesmen like Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, who have hearts as well as heads, have determined that "the machine" shall have less play—that it shall cease to grind the faces of the poor. Hence the proposal for Free Education. Raising another issue, Mr. CARLETON says Free Education "would give a fatal blow to denominational teaching ;' but he does not offer a particle of evidence in support of his assertion. This sort of dogmatism may do for the pulpit, but it will not do for the press. If he would convince the public, he must give 'a reason for the faith that is in him. It seems to us that the Queen's shilling will prove Just as useful if derived from income tax, as it is found now, received as it is from the hands of the children who take it week by week to the schools. Assuming that the scholars of the school with which Mr. CARLETON iS Con- nected pay a certain sum, say I2S, per head per year as the average, we should like to know how the school would cease to be a de- nominational school if the 25 per head were paid by the Government, or even by the ratepayers. With a view to the General , Election, it is the way, we know, of those who have been in the habit of shouting "No Popery" to tell Roman Catholics that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S "proposal would give a fatal blow to denominational teaching" But they do not prove their case; for they cannot prove it. The inference is the other way ; it will be an aid to the sects, and there are some who will object to the scheme on that account. No one knows better than the Catholic priest that Catholic schools suffer because there is a large proportion of Catholic .children who are irregular in attendance resulting from the poverty of their parents. Their schools feel this in two ways; they feel it in the lessened amount derived from school fees ; and in the smaller grant consequent upon inferior attendance. Free Education would, therefore, be the boon of boons to them ; they have more to gain by it, individ- ually and collectively, than any other section of the community. In saying this we scout the idea that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S proposal "would mean universal School Boards." This is a false weight thrown in the scale by the 'reverend gentleman—with the idea of making the other scale kick the beam. Free Education could be given by means of uni- versal School Boards, but it is not the scheme which was propounded at Warrington by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. Mr. CARLETON'S tirade on this head goes, therefore, for nothing. He either cannot or will not understand the issue ; but we will take care that our readers do not go astray in a similar way, We shall return to this important subject of Free Education; and, if Mr. CARLETON likes, we will discuss the matter with him on a public platform.

THE condition of Ireland does not seem to improve any under the benign rule of the „., L ories, notwithstanding the blessings that We to flow from the Maamtrassna alliance. Lord SALISBURY as never tired, when in Opposition, of abusing the late Government for their lack of firmness in dealing with Irish affairs, and he sought to convey the impres- sion that if the chance were given him he would soon mend matters. Well, the chance has come; it has come, too, it should be stated, in the way favourable to him—that is by an understanding with the PARNELLITEs, and et there is no improvement visible. On the contrary, Ireland is in a very disturbed condition. That once familiar line in the news- papers—" The State of Ireland," had happily disappeared whilst the Liberals were in office, but now that Lord SALISBURY is Prime Minister it again stares us in the face. The Conservatives in Ireland are alarrned, and well they may be; they find that they have jumped out of the frying pan into the fire; and if report speaks truly they are inunda- ting the Government with letters of com- plaint. Even the. CHANCELLOR of the Ex- CHEQUER—the leader of the Tory party in the House of Commons—is compelled to admit that "it is a grave fact that the system known as boycotting is rife in many parts of Ireland; and has been increasing during the last few weeks." He speaks under official restraint, and is certainly not interested in exaggeration. Some Conservatives who are more at liberty are speaking more freely. Mr. C. E. LEWIS for instance, the Conserva- tive member for Londonderry, is sufficiently outspoken. He says the present condition of affairs is fearful; and expresses his fear that "defeat, disgrace, and dishonour will overtake the present Ministry for their Irish policy." He adds : Many Conservatives are asking what is their duty at the general election, and, holding their breath, ask, Will it not be better that we should have a large Liberal majority than a Conservative contin- gent, only capable of being turned into a majority by the aid of Mr. Parnell, Mr. 'Healy, and Mr. Red- mond? Ido not know what other people may do or say, This I know, that not one of my three borough and five county votes will be given to any Government candidate unless the Ministry make a most explicit and satisfactory announcement as to their policy to attempt to defeat Mr. Parnell and all his works. I believe that hundreds and thousands of other Conservatives will do the same. This is plain speaking, at any rate, and if We have more of it the present Government Will be compelled to declare themselves. They have sown the wind in following the advice of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, and they are now reaping the whirlwind.

THE Socialists of London have won all along the line in their fight with the authori- ties on the question of street meetings. If Mr. SAUNDERS, the Stipendiary Magistrate who has fined so many people for obstruction, is right in his view of the law, there were 30,000 law breakers in Dod-street on Sunday last—a rare harvest for the police, if they had dared to reap it. But they did not dare; they were challenged, but they did not accept the challenge—they kept out of the way. It was thought a fine thing, in the first instance,' to "run in" the poor fellows, ostensibly on the plea of obstruction, but really because they preached doctrines that were distasteful to the authorities, There can be no question that some of the Socialists hold views that are visionary and absurd ; but if people are to be locked up who talk nonsense we shall have half of the House of Commons in gaol, and three-fourths of the House of Lords, to say nothing of the millions, "mostly fools," as CARLYLE has it, of ordinary citizens. The Englishman is a constitutional grumbler; he has the right to grumble; and it was wrong of the authorities to seek to rob him of his right. Meetings, whether in street or in public halls, are the safety valves of society; they are the means of letting off the surplus steam when the pressure gets high. It is a mistake to attempt to sit on a valve, as the London police have been taught previously. A Tory Government experimented in this direction in 1866, and the result was that the railings of Hyde Park were torn down, and the people had their way. A Tory Govern- ment is again in office when the attempt has been made to interfere with freedom of speech, and the people have again had their way. We are not bringing a charge against the present Government ; we are simply stat- ing a fact. It may be that the Police Au thorities jumped to the conclusion that they would be patted on the back if they put down the Socialists, who are for the most part Democrats of a revolutionary type; and we dare say they would have been, if they had succeeded. But they failed ; British blood was roused at the sight of injustice; and then it was—not before—that the Govern- ment stepped in and put the curb on the police. Sir RICHARD CROSS was wise in time, for it would have gone hard with the Home Office, if not with the PRIME MINISTER, if blood had been shed in the metropolis on Sunday last. The days of Peterloo are passed, and we are glad that it is so.

ME. JOHN HowE, a grocer in an extensive way of business, who has shops in Earles- town, Golborne, Wigan, and Tyldesley, was recently brought 'before the Newton magis- trates for " selling an article as butter which was not of the nature and quality demanded by the purchaser." The certificate of Dr CAMPBELL BROWN, the county analyst, was against the defendant; but he protested that the article he sold as butter was butter, and induced the Bench to adjourn the case in order that a sample might be sent to Somerset House for analysis. This was done, with the result that the authorities in London pro- nounced the sample sent to them to be genuine butter. There was nothing for it, therefore, but to dismiss the case when it came before the magistrates again on Satur- day last; and the Bench went the length— rightly, as it seems to us—of allowing Mr. HOWE something in the way of costs. Dr. BROWN should be more careful ; it is not the first time he has been at fault, for we learn that, quite recently, there was a collapse of a charge against a publican at Morecambe who was summoned for selling adulterated spirits. The case, after being before the public for several weeks, broke down at the last moment through the County Analyst finding that he was in error. Mistakes of this kind are serious matters for tradesmen. It is easier to get a bad name than to get rid of one; and it is not therefore sufficient that costs are allowed in case of the failure of a prosecution. If County Analysts were made to suffer in some way for their errors, cases of fair-dealing tradesmen being dragged into a Police Court would be ,few and far between. It is by no means reassuring to find, from the last report of the Commissioners of Inland Revenue, that in 23 cases out of 31 they were "unable to find evidence of the charges alleged." Such wholesale blundering is dis- creditable; it brings the law into contempt.

THE JURY Liars—The jury lists for the townships in the Runcorn Petty Sessional Division were submitted to and approved by the Runcorn magistrates on Monday. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT ST. MICHAEL'S, DITTON.—The annual harvest thanksgiving service at St. Michael's Church, Ditton. took place on Friday, when a sermon was preached by the Rev. H. Southward, of St. Catherine's College, Cam- bridge. The services were continued on Sunday. The in- terior of the edifice had been beautifully decorated with the fruits of the earth. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.—SerMong in aid of tills church were preached in the edifice on Sunday by the Rey. J. W. Chisholm, of Liverpool. There were good congregations at both morning and evening service. On Monday evening Mr. Chisholm delivered a lecture entitled " Playing at Soldiers," in which he dealt with the want of earnestness and strength of purpose of too many members of our religious and temperance organisations. Mr. F. J. Norman occupied the chair in the absence of his father, who was unable to fulfil hie engagement through ill

h- ea. lth'. FUNERAL AT RIINCORN.—The funeral of Mr. Richard Orme, who died very suddenly on Thursday last week, under circumstances reported in the Examiner, took place on Saturday. The procession from the ;deceased's residence in Wellington-street to the Parish Church was taken part in by members of the Star of Freedom lodge of 1.0. of Odd. fellows, and 38 employes of the firm of Messrs Brundrit and Co., in whose employ the deceased had been for a period of 40 years. The coffin, covered with beautiful wreaths, was borne on the sheulders of eight of the workmen. Members of the family, and several relatives of the deceased were also present, and there were many signs of mourning and regret. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. T. M. Arrnson. Each vocalist succeeded in obtaining the honour of a recall, and criticism therefore would only be invidious. LAWLESS BnornEns are now offering special value in 2s Tea, and cannot be beat-5, Old Market- place, Warrington.—Advt.

IMERSEY SALT AND BRINE COMPANY, RUNCORN.—The erection of works for the manufacture of salt by this coin- pany was commenced this week on the site they have pur- chased at Weston Point. Mr. Richard Beckett, of Hartford, is the contractor, and the buildings are expected to be com- pleted in 12 months, when employment will be given to about 150 men. HARVEST IiESTIVAL AT ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WIDNES. —St. Paul's Church was crowded on Thursday evening on the occasion of the first annual harvest thanksgiving ser- vice. The interior of the edifice had been tastefully decor- ated with flowers, itic. The Rev. H. B. Blogg, of Frodshem, occupied the pulpit. The choir rendered specially selected hymns and anthems, under the directions of Mr. I. B. Imi- son. The collections made in aid of the building fund realised .£l2 2s. Runconer Irma NATIONAL LEAGUE.—The usual weekly meeting was held on Tuesday, when Mr. Edward Hill was appointed president in place of Mr. Quinn, who was unable to attend. It was resolved to send money to the general secretary for 22 cords of membership. Mr. John Talton gave an interesting lecture entitled " One year of Crom- well's life in Ireland." The President read a speech de- livered at New York by Father Bourke on "The manners and habits of the Irish people." RUNCORN BOWLING Cum —The members of the bowling club which has its head quarters at the house of Mr. George Haves, Bridge Hotel, brought a successful season to a close on 'Tuesday night, when about 35 persons sat down to an excellent knife and fork tea provided by the host. The subsequent proceedings were of a convivial and highly en- joyable character. Songs were given by Messrs. Lambert, Blench, Shaw, and the host, Mr. Ravenscroft ably officiating at the piano. The secretary, Mr. Robert Hughes, presented a favourable report of the past season's doings. POLICE INSPECTION AT RUNCORN.—The Hon. Captain C. E. Legge Government Inspector of Constabulary of the Northern Division, made his annual inspection of the police in the Runcorn Division -on Monday. There were on pa- rade Supt. Leah, Inspector Roache, 3 sergeants, and 23 conetables, all attired in full dress. The Inspector expressed himself well pleased at the marked improvement of the drill of the men, and having exanrined their accoutrements. he proceeded through the offices and cells, and concluded his inspection by a thorough search of the books. Everything was found to his satisfaction. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT WlDNES.—ThanksgivinH services for the ingathering of the harvest were held at the Simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel en Sunday, when ser- mons were preached by Mr. Luckless, of St. Helens. In the afternoon Mr. S. Owens delivered an address to parents and scholars. On Monday evening a fruit banquet took place under the presidency of Mr. Rollason. Addresses were de- livered by Messrs. Ryder, Whitley, and Marshall. During the evening fruit was distributed, and the choir rendered the proceedings very agreeable by the singing of ceoice selec- tions of sacred music, under the leadership of Mr. Rees. Master Rollason was at the harmonium. The edifice had been tastefully decorated by Mod imes Rollason, Owens, Wiles, Crossley, Pinches, Adams, Jones, and Webster ; and on the motion of the Rev. J. Calvert, seconded by Mr. Owens, they were heartily thanked for their services. A similar compliment was paid to the chairman, the speakers. and the donors of fruit, flowers, and cereals. THE PAYMENT OF JURYMEN AT WIDNES.— it the con- clusion of an inquest at Widnes, on Tuesday evening, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, referred to the fact that the motion made by Mr. Fitzpatrick at a previous in- quest as to the payment of jtryneen, and his (Mr. Hus- band's) observations on that occasion had been commented upon in leading articles in the London papers. He was glad to notice that the writer' of the article in the Globe upheld-his views. Since his (the speaker's) remarks had been made public they had net with considerable opposi- tion from persons who would ba called upon to pay the rate. But be thought these people did not properly understand the question. His plan was that a voluntary rate of a far. thin in the £ should be levied upon all persona assessed up to £lOO, and that those assessed above that sum should not be charged beyond that limit. 'By that means any per- son or firm 'would not pay more than 2s id in any one year, and he was satisfied that the amount collected in one year would last for about half a dozen years, the scales of pay- ment being, say, as follow : Coroner's jurymen 2s 6d per inquest, jurymen attending sessions or assizee in I iverpool 5s or 7s 63 per day for their services. RUN'CORN BOARD OF CrITARDIANS.—The useal fortnightly meeting of this body was held on Tuesday afternoon, at Dutton Workhouse, the chair being occupied by Lieutenant- Colonel Ashton. There were also present the Revs. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner, J. J. Bryant, and Messrs. Weir, Norman, Aaron, Mclntyre, W. Wilkinson, J. Smith, H. Percival, J. G. Hamilton, J. W. Baguley, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. 11. Lirraker (deputy clerk.)—A letter was received from Mr • Peter Wright, late relieving officer for Runcorn, thanking the Board for the superannuation granted him.—The Revs. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, and Messrs. W. Weir, Norman, and Mclntyre, were appoin- ted a committee to look through the tenders. The follow- hog tenders were accepted :—Coffins, Mr. John Barrow, Halton coals, Mr. John Spender, Runcorn ; bacon, Mr. James Nichols, Runcorn; beef and mutton, Mr. William Gill, Warrington; drugs and oils, Mr. J. Speakman, Run- corn ; carting, Mr. William Grounds, Aston ; wheat and straw, Mr. Thomas Bennett, Keckwick • shoes, Mr. James McQuinn, Runcorn ; clothing, Mr. D. W. Jones, Runcorn ; drapery, Mr. Thomas Wright, Halton ; groceries, Mr. Jack- son and Mr. Collier, Runcorn.—This Was ill the business. VIOLENCE AT WIDNES: DESERVED PUNISHMENT.—Be- fore Mr. J. Brock and Mr. H. S. Hall, at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, James Daniels, a rough-looking man, was charged with assaulting Emma Jones. The prosecutris said she WAS the wife of James Jones. and resided at 23, Albert-road, Whines. On the evening of the 26th September, about eight o'clock, she ha just passed Peelhouse-lane, on her way home, when the prisoner came across the road to her and asked where Smithson-street was. She replied that she did not know, and he then asked her to direct him to another street. She again replied that she did not know it, whereupon the prisoner seized hold of her, dragged her across the road, threw her to the ground, and fell upon her. She screamed loudly, and to prevent her doing so he placed his hand upon her mouth. A man came past at this time, and witness managed to release herself from the grasp of her assailant and ran home. The pri- soner was a perfect stranger to her.—Mr. Lewin (deputy magistretes' clerk) said it was very fortunate that that man arrived on the scene.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and said he had had some drink.—Superintendent Barker stated the prisoner was fined 5s and costs on the 2nd September for being drunk.—Mr. Brock said itiwas a most abominable thing that a person could not go along the highway with- out being assaulted in this fashion, and the Bench would make an example of the prisoner by sending him to gaol for two months with hard labour. I RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHOIIITY.—A meeting of this body was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton presiding. There were also pre- sent the Revs. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner, and J. J. Bryant, and Messrs. Edward Aaron, Thomas Hewitt, J. A. Arrowson, William Wilkinson, John Mclntyre, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and Farrington (nuisance inspector).—The Clerk read a letter received from the Local Government Board sanctioning the reap- pointment of Mr. James Farrington as inspector of nuisances for the district of the Authdrity, at a yearly salary of £l4O. —A letter from the Local Government Board, read by the Clerk, requested that the Board might be informed of the present position of the question of the sewerage of the township of Weston. The clerk was instructed to deal with the matter. Mr. Aaron remarked that he* had, in accordance with a proposition made, inspected the sewer on the Authority's behalf. He found that men were working at the foundations for the erection of buildings thereon. He proposed that instructions be given to take proceedings against the Mersey Brine and Salt Company for commencing building operations on the public sewer of the Authority at Weston Point—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the proposition, which was carried.—Mr. Farrington, inspec- tor of nuisances, reported that the public pump at Moore had been put in rder: There had been a slight defect in the outfall of a sewer at Weston Point, which would be im- proved at a small cost ; it was agreed that the improve- ment be made.—A tender had been submitted for the im- provement of a sewer and inlet at Etelsby, but the matter was adjourned for specifications to be prepared.—A. tender for the construction of manholes at Stockton Heath was received, but was not considered satisfactory—This was all the business. FATAL SWING BOAT ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—ATIOthee swing boat accident, making about the sixth this year. oc- curred on Widnes Market Ground on Saturday night. Law- rence Bonon, labourer, 19 years of age, who was employed at the Widnes Foundry, was swinging in one of Mr. Sil- cock's boats in a standing position, although he had been Ordered to sit down when he fell out. His head came in contact with the ground, and he sustained a severe frac- ture of the skull, and seriously injured his spinal cord. He was conveyed to his sister's house in Midwood-streat, where he was attended by Dr. McCambridge. He never rallied, however, and died on Monday morning. On Tuesday even- ing Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest upon the body at the Police Cond. After evidence had been taken herring out the above accounts, the Deputy Coroner said he had held several inquests of a similar char- acter to that in which they were now engaged, and he bad come to the conclusion that the Legislature ought to take some action in order to stop these accidents. If people would persist in standing up in swing boats a netting ought to be provided so as to prevent the boat going higher than a certain altitude. The local authority had power to take away the license of swing boat owners if they allowed the persons who patronised their boats to stand up in them, and he thought the Local Board ought to make that power opera- tive.—Mr. Sheppard, the market inspector, said he warned every boatowner that used the market ground that if he Allowed persons to stand up his license would be forfeited. The matter was of such an Impartant character that he pro- mised the coroner to bring it before the Market Committee. —The Deputy Coroner cautioned Silcock, the owner of the boat, and Hickey, his manager, that if they neglected to tell persons standing up to sit down, and an accident oc- curred, they would land themselves in a very awkward position.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." PROPOSED VISIT OF Mn. HERBERT GLADSTONE M.P., TO RuNconer.—The Runcorn Liberal Associa-. tion have arranged for a great political demonstra- tion in support of Mr. Brunner's candidature, on the 20th of the present month. Mr. 11. Gladstone, M.P., son of the ex-premier, has consented to be present and deliver an address, and several other members of Parliament and Parliamentary candi- dates will also attend. •

div.head: TTTE FXAMIN 11 SATURDAY. OCTOBER 3, 1885.
div.p: TTTE FXAMIN 11 SATURDAY. OCTOBER 3, 1885.

THEFT OF k DRESS AT RONCORET.—On Thursday, at Ran- I corn Police Court, Jane Evans, alias Jane Ellen Price. was charged with latcany as a bailee. Rose Pearle, domestic at the Cornwall and Devonshire Inn, entrusted the prisoner with some material for the purpose of making a dress, and the prisoner pawned it. ' She was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. hIINCORK PARISH CHGRCH HARVEST FESTIVAL. The annual thanksgiving service in connection with Runcorn Parish Church took place on Thursday evening, when the Right Revd. Dr. Stubbs, Bishop of Chester, preached from Isdah 40c, 10 v. The building had been beautifully adorned by the ladies of the congregation. The service was full choral. The church was so crowded that accommoda- tion bad to be provided in the aisles. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—MT. G. H. Danbv, on behalf of the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not sending their children regularly to school : —Pat Mystall, Adam Green, Thomas Moore, Thomas Tur- ner, Richard Williams, John Corrighan, John Keating, Joseph Peacock, John Martin John Keenaghan, Wm. Lee, Elizabeth Sparkes, John Feder), and Wm. Fallon. The cases were proved by the attendance officers, Messrs. Davies, Joynson, and Rowe, and the usual penalty of 68 was im- posed. ROBBING A lIALEBAN% ORCIIARD.—At Widnes Petty Sessione, on Wednesday, John Roberts, Thomas Smith, and Thomas Houghton, boys, were charged with stealing apples from the orchard of Mr. George R. Jackson, Halebank.— '1 he boys were caught in the act by James Welsby, a labourer.—Mr. Jackson said his garden had been frequently robbed (hiring the past summer.—Roberts and Houghton were fined Is and costs, Si 64, or seven diva' hard labour; apd Smith, who did not appear, was fined 2s 6d and cos s, or ten days' hard labour. A WIDNES UOTISEHREPER AND THE BOlLER.—Margaret McCann, a married woman, was charged at Widnes Petty 'Sessions, on Wednesday, with having on the 24th Septem• bar stolen an iron boiler, worth 5s 64. and a fire bar, the property of Mrs. Eliza Davies, of Page Villa, Appleton. The case was proved by Mr. Charley Davies, builder and con- tractor, and John Lee, rag gatherer, Warrington. The pri- soner was the tenant of Mrs. Davies at 14, Elizabeth-street, and on the date in question she sold the boiler and bar to the rag gatherer.—The prisoner said the boiler was in her own yard and no good, and she did not think there was any harm in selling it. She did not steal it.—Mr. Brock said the Bench did not think there was any felonious intent, and a fine of 5s was imposed. THE WORST CHARACTER IN WIDNES. —John Hannon, who did not appear, was summoned to Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Wednesday to answer a charge of assaulting Mr. Henry Turner' landlord of the Wellington lintel. On the I.9th ult, the defendant purchased a pint of beer in the hotel, and whilst carrying it from one part of the bar to another he upset the liquor. He asked Mr. Turner to give him a glass of hoer, hat as it was then eleven o'clock the landlord refused, and had to send for a policeman to eject the defendant. Before the arrival of the policeman the de- fendant struck the landlord on the nose and ran away.— Superintendent Barker said the defendant was one of the worst characters in Widnes, and had been 24 times before the magistrates. Fines did this man no good.—a. sentence of a month', hard labour was passed. A MONTH'S IMPRISONMENT FOR STEALING A FORE.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, James McGee, a labourer living in Lacey-street, was brought up on remand charged with stealing a fork value 6d, the property of Mrs. Unsworth, Victoria-road Dining Rootns.—On Saturday night the prisoner had three pennyworth of potato pie at the rooms, and on his departure the fork was missed. Early next morning P.C. Laing apprehended the prisoner and found the fork in his coat pocket —The prisoner said he was in drink, and did not know how the fork got :nto his pocket. —Superintendent Barker said cases of this character were very common. Men went into this refreshment house and purchased about two pennyworth of pie, and then purloined articles of greater value. It was very hard upon the pro- prietorese —The prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. ISLE OF MAN STEAMERS. The Fleetwood ser- vice of the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company has this week been discontinued, but we understand that there will be daily service from Liverpool, Sun- days excepted, throughout the winter. MAJOR LYONS, it is announced, will contest the Widnes Division in the Conservative interest. It is not supposed that the Conservatives have much hope of winning, but they think it advisable to keep the Liberals employed during the General Election. FREEMASONS.—The annual meeting of the West Lancashire Provincial Grand Lodge of Freemasons was held in Liverpool yesterday, under the presi- dency of the Earl of Lathom. There was a large gathering of brethren. It was reported that the Province now contained 82 lodges, with 4,608 sub- scribing members—a number higher by 1,100 than any other province under the Grand Lodge of Eng- land. The financial stahment was of a satisfactory character. SIXPENNY TELEGRAMS.—The sixpenny telegram service came into operation on Thursday, and, as was to be expected, the result was a large accession of business in London and the chief centres of population throughout the country. The new terms are twelve words for sixpence (including address), and a halfpenny for each succeeding word. At the Warrington telegraph office the in- crease of business was about 25 per cent., the aver- , age being taken on the work done the previous Thursday. To meet the increased local business two duplex instruments had been provided, and we understand that some addition has been made to the staff. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—On Wednesday evening the final meeting of the committee having in hand the arrangements of the late Ship Canal demonstration at Eccles was held at the Cross Keys Hotel, Mr. James Andrew presiding, for the pur- pose of receiving the report and balance sheet, which showed that the expenditure had been £139 18s 11d, and that there was a small balance in hand of is 11d. Mr. J. T. Lewis intimated his intention of giving another ox on the occasion of the festivi- ties in connection with the opening of the Ship Canal. Mr. Alderman Bailey said it was proposed to hold a demonstration at Salford, and to confer the freedom of the borough on Mr. Daniel Adamson. It was stated that the late demonstration at Eccles had been the means of influencing people to take

up shares. CARDINAL MANNING ON MODERN BABYLON.--A London- correspondent says:—" I mentioned three weeks ago that Cardinal Manning had undertaken to write for the North American itevietz an article upon the revelations in the Pall Mall Gazette. The article appears in the current month's issue, and is, on the whole, strongly in favour of Mr. Stead. To my mind, his eminence puts the whole case in a sentence when he writes, Many of those who profoundly sympathise with the motives which induced the Pall Mall Gazette to take up the ques- tion might have desired its modes and expressions to have been revised and chastened, but the sub- stance of the action is intrinscally just and merci- ful.' A subscription has been opened to indemnify Mr. Stead against any pecuniary loss owing to his prosecution.' THANKSGIVING SEAR:VICES AT PENKETH.—The Penketh Wesleyan Chapel presented a very pretty and effective appearance on the occasion of the an- nual thanksgiving harvest services. The pulpit and altar had been profusely. adorned with grapes, apples, vegetables, corn, interspersed with choice flowers, consisting of rows of ivy leaves intermixed with dahlias, forget-me-nots, &c. The decorations have been done by the Misses Garnett and Moses, and reflect great credit on them. The sermons were preached by the Rev. J. H. Jones, in the morning from the 100th Psalm, and in the evening from 10th chapter of St. Mark, 17-22 verses. Contributions for the decorations had been received from Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., Miss Davies, E. Cross, H. Hughes, &c. There were large congregations morning and evening, and collections were inade on behalf of the

circuit funds. GARDEN PARTY AT KNOWSLEY.—The Earl and Countess of Derby on Saturday gave a grand gar- den party at Knowsley Hall. The principal fami- lies of Liverpool and the neighbourhood were in- vited, and the most ample arrangements were made by the Earl and Countess and Lord Lionel Cecil for the entertainment of their guests. Although cold, the day was bright and fine, and a stroll among the charming grounds proved *a source of pleasure to many. The company began to arrive about three o'clock, and were received in the grand saloon of the hall by the Earl and Countess of Derby. After presentation the guests walked about the grounds. During the afternoon refreshments were served in the grand dining hall, a magnificent apartment, the walls of which are adorned with some splendid pic- tures, among them being portraits of distinguished members of the house of Stanley. The Liverpool Police Band, under the leadership of Mr. F. R. Beardhall, bandmaster, were stationed in the lawn in front of the hall, and during the afternoon per- formed a selection of music. The band of the Sea- man's Orphanage was present, and also played a selection of music. There are at present staying at the hall as the guests of Lord and Lady Derby : Lord Winmarleigh and the Misses Wilson-Patten, Mr. Herbert, Canon Hornby, Lady Margaret Cecil, and Lord Lionel Cecil. Amongst those who were present on Saturday were the Earl and Countess of Sefton, Lady , Latham, the Ladies Wilbraham, Bol- ton Rev. J. 8., .Banner Mr. and Mrs. Edward, Bright Mr. and Mrs. A. IL, Barnacle Rev. J. and Mrs., Cros- field Mr. and Mrs. W., McCorquodale Mr. and Mrs., Gamble Colonel, Mrs., and Miss, Gaskell Mr. Hol- brook and Miss, Gamble Mr. and Mrs. J. C., Harri- son Mr. and Mrs.. 'Pimmis Mr. and Miss Sutton, Timmis Mr. and Mrs. Sutton, Macnaghten Rev. H. rAC% CHAMBERIAIN AND THE IRISH QUESTION. - ."-MT! John Perguson, of Lenzie, has received the following letter :—" ilighbury Moor, Birmingham, September 21st, 1885. Dear sir,—l have only to acknowledge briefly your letter of the 15th inst. as regards the Irish question. You will do me the justice to acknowledge that in writing to you some time ago, and before any idea had got abroad of Mr. Parnell's recent manifesto, I stated that I was con- scientiously opposed to a separate Parliament for Ireland, believing as I did and do that it would be absolutely ruinous to the best interests of Ireland, as well as dangerous to the security of England. I hope you will carefully consider the terms in which I made my statement at Warrington, and that you will see that they are full of sympathy for Irish grievances and respect for Irish leaders; but I can- not alter my conviction upon the main point.—l , am, yours truly, J. CHAMBEIILAIN." 1

div.head: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.

A court for the revision of the lists of voters in the Ron- corn Polling District, which includes Clifton, Halton Nor- ton, Stockham, and Weston, was held at Runcorn Sessions House on Tuesday. The revising barrister was Mr. David Archer Vaughan Colt-Williams. The Liberals were repre- sented by Mr. W. Handley and Mr. O. Leak, and the Tories by Mr. C. J. Hughes and Mr. J. W. Lightburn. The Run- corn list, which contained the names of 3.500 voters, had been prepared with such accuracy by the Runcorn over- seers that the two parties agreed to take them as they stood without objection, and the only matters of interest were the lodger claims, 25 in number, which were decided upon their merits. Several of the claimants paid 15s per week for board and lodging, occupied a bedroom exclusively, and a sitting room with other members of the family. In all these cases the Revising Barrister allowed the claims. During the proceedings the Revising Barrister said his work had been materially facilitated by the efficient manner in which the lists bad been prepared. -7- Mr. Hughes re- marked that they had been prepared in an ad- mirable manner and had saved both parties con- siderable trouble. The revision, which was expected to continue three days, was concluded at half past seven on the evening of the first day. Mr. Hughes, on behalf of the , party he represented, expressed his thanks to Mr. Wil- liams for the kindness and courtesy he had displayed dur- ing the revision, and for the valuable assistance he had ren- dered to the parties.—Mr. Handley said it had been a great pleasure to follow the Revising Barrister to the varieus courts in his circuit, and he was sure no one could have conducted the proceedings in a more impartial manner.— Mr. Leak also bore testimony to Mr. Williams' impartiality. —The Revising Barrister thanked the gentlemen for their utterams, and added that be had received very valuable assistance at all the places on his circuit from Mr. Handley, Mr. Hughee, and Mr. Watson. A revising barrister had to depend a great deal upon party agents, and the gentlemen named bad given him great assistance, and the work had been rendered easier than it otherwise would have been. The court then rose.
