CONGREGATIONAL JUBILEE AT RUNCORN. The Congregationalists of Runcorn have this week cele- brated the jubilee of the opening of Bethesda Chapel, High- street, by a series of interesting services and meetings. The establishment of the independent cause in Runcorn, how- ever, dates further back than 50 "ears. In the unpreten- tious manner which characterised the birth of many a flourishing church in existence in the present day, a few earnest believers in the principles of Congresaionalism I commenced a Sunday school in a house in M. teey-street, in! the year 1829, but not many months had nessed before a large-hearted townsman, Mr. William Pennington, built a school in Mason-street. Wall larger scope came greater re- sults, and it, 1830. again through the generosity of Mr. Pe- nnington, a chapel was attached to the school. After the lapse of two years the denomination felt equal to the sup- port of a minister, and on January let, 1832, the Rev. W. Robinsots, father of Dr. Robinson, of Runcorn, entered upon his pastorate. To him belongs the honour of being the first minister. It was not till June 27, 1832, that the congrega- tion formally and solemnly conetituted themselves a church " According to the views held lay the Independent Com- munion of -Protestant Dissenter:," the names of those who unjted in "church fellowship ' teeing : elev. William I Robinson (pastor), Ricuard Lever, Mrs Handley, Mrs Hodg- son, Joseph Miller, Thomas Handley, MlB3 Hodgson, John Handley, James Sutton, John Sutton, William Evans, and Charles Holland. Most of those whose names are tome re- corded have been laid in their last resting place, and their lives and influence are a revered memory of the past. Mrs Handley, we believe, is the only survives, and her name still finds an honoured place in the list of the members of the church. The progress of the denomination was rapid. The efforts of the humbler workers were seconded by the richer brethren, who were gifted with a generous spirit that lightened the burdens of fioancial problems in an eminent degree. In 1835 Bethesda Cnapll was erected in High-street at the expense of Mr. John Tomkinson, of Liverpool, and the church was removed from St. Luke's Chapel to the new and more handsome structure on the 29th September of that year. Additional interest was lent to the ceremony of that day by the ordina- tion of the Rev. W. Robinson, and the proceedings were of a joyful and inspiring character. The reverend gentlemen who took part were Dr. Raffles, of Liverpool ; J. Widows, of Liverpool ; G. B Kidd, of Maccleetield ' - John Wilson, of Northwich ; John Ely, of Leeds ; and Kelly. Rogers, and Potter. Of those who were members at that celebration there are now only alive Mrs. Eleanor Handley, Mr. Samuel Constantine and Mr. Samuel W 489. Mr. Thomas Ingles- field, admitted to the fellowship in 1838, and Mr. Thomas Speakman, admitted 1842, are still in existence in the town. During the last hialf century the following pastors have occupied the pslpit at Betuesda for varying periods of time :—William Robinson, Samuel Hillyerd, Richard Bever- ley Blakehurst, Andrew Thomas, John T. Jeseon, W. H. Mann, Ronson, Thomas Davies, S. Yates, and the Pre_ sent respected and able minister, J. D. Thomas. The clouds of adversity have occasionally overshadowed the congregation, but the church has still within itself a hearty vigorous life, and occupies a prominent place amongst the other Dissenting denominations in the towu. The jubilee celebration commenced on Sunday, when the , Rev. Thomas Davies, of Barking, a former pastor, preached both morning and evening. At each service his eloquent sermons were listened to by large congregations. Hymns specially selected for the occasion were rung, and the choir, strengthened by the addition of several voices, greatly added to the interest of the musical portion of the service by sing- ing several anthems, under the leadership of Mr. W. Hand. ley. In the morning " I was glad " and " 0 love the Lord " were rendered, and in the evening " 0 Lord my God" and "As the hart pantetb." Mr. Ravenscroft was at the organ. On Tuesday, the day of jubilee, a good con- , gregatiche assembled in the chapel to hears sermon from the Hey. J. Cruinnese Rogers, 8.A., of London. The rev, gen- tleman took his text St. Luke mix., 3rd verse : "And he sought te see Jesus who be was; and could not for the press, because be was little of stature." In the coarse of his discourse, which was directed against the prejudices and bigotry of religions sects, and the hindrances our human moral and spiritual littleness placed in the way of a clear and full perception of Christ, of His work, and of His Gospel, said some people seemed to think that their intellects were not to be etnployed about religion, and to have written over the door of their intellects " Religion has no place here." He found men whose religion was all gush, all sentiment. They seemed to have arrived at the convic- tion that teason had nothing to do with religion. There could be no greater mistake. It was an injury to themselves, to the truth, and to the cause of God. They were dwarfed in their own religious conceptions from the fact that they disi not think out the thoughts connected with the truths of God's word. They simply took the creed they found generally accepted—did not examine it or prove it, and never thought of growing. It was high time we got rid of this idea that ignorance was the mother of religion. Ignorance was the mother of superstition ; not of religion and not of faith. God did not mean man to bring to Him imperfect and mildewed service, bat the service of our whole nature. All the parts of our wonderful nature were to be senctified to God, and if really sanctified then he said the more a man knew, the larger his acquaintance with men and with things —all that brought to bear upon the Gospel the clearer would be his understanding and clearer his acceptance of the Gospel of Christ and God. At the conclusion of the service tea was provided in the schoolroom, where about 400 persons assembled and par- took of the repast. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Misses M. Chadwick, Gregory, Chadwick, Riley, A. Chadwick, M. Ainsworth, E. Ainsworth. Edith Riley, Widders, M. Con, Booth, Bessie Speakman, M. Littler, N. Handley', F. Handley, Edith Littler, Lydiate, Beck, M. Beck, Ireland, and Mrs. Evans. The room was tastefully and appropriately decorated for the occasion, with banners, flags, and greenery. At half-past six an adjournment was made to the chapel, where a meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Righy, of Overton. On the platform were the Revs. J. G. Rogers, S. B. Handley (Stafford), S. Yates (Spalding) a former pestor of the church, E. Williams (St. John's Presbyterian Chinch), W. Yause (United Methodist Free Church), and tbe Rev. J. D. Thomas, pastor. After devotional exercises, the Rev. J. G. Rogers, who was com- pelled to leave by an early train, addressed the large audience present. Fifty years was a period of considerable importance in the history of 'a civil community and in the history of a church. Fifty years had ruined Runcorn so far as natural beauty was concerned, and in one sermon he had described it as a land of barrenness and of desolation, where not a green blade of grass was to be seer, and where not a single flower bloomed. (Laughter.) He hoped the spiritual progress of the town was more in accordance with the material advancement than the natural aspects of the place. He referred to the marvellous changes which had taken place in the country during the last half century throsgh the introduction of railways, electricity, cheap newspapers, ikc. He was most deeply interested in the attitude which Nonconformists were likely to assume in relation to the subjects now pressing on for decision by our Legislature. They were subj,cts which concerned the very life of the nation and the life of the Church of Christ in the nation; for the question which was raised at the present moment was not one merely of the supremacy of any class. So far as political power was concerned that question was settled. It was settled beyond the possibility of reversal that the power in this country should be with the ejitire people and not with any one class. (Appplause.) The nest election would be for the first time an appeal to the entire people of England to decide what kind of legislation they wanted. The question which naturally started up fleet was " what more can be done to make the condition of the humbler classes in this country happier than they had hitherto been?" England had hitherto been a paradise for rich men. What oueht to be tried now was how far it could be, made a place for the whole population of the Kingdom. (ad lowerAnpplanse.s)ectTiohnosoetptrheseetnntidrdeplerecsleansst_edhomwaiwnolytydbtehemyadwdhloe had won their rights before, act now when thequestion wasone which did not so much affect them as a class as it affected the working people and the poor of the country. For him- self he frankly admitted that if he were to think only of his own personal prepossessions and feelings, he should say the•e was a question which to him stood paramount to all others. That was the injustice and ignominy of the Estab- lished Church, and he was so conscious of the injury it was doing to the cause of spirituel religion in various ways that if be only followed personal predilections he should say " Let 119 before we do anything else insist upon complete religious equality." (Applause.) But he saw the tearful surging evils that were growing up in the country—the overcrowding in our cities and towns—and the moral vice and wickedness which were the results of that overcrowd- ing. When he thought of the multitude of people in this country who were living in a condition in which we might to feel they were a disgrace to christianity and a scandal to our civilization—(hear, hear)—and if anything could be done by means of legislation to facilitate the ele- vation, the education, and the improvement of those people, then he thought they should be prepared to make some sacrifices in order to do it. The idols of political economy might well be burnt when this question of the elevation of the people was at stake. (Applause.) It was on that account that he looked forward with interest and anxiety to the approachicg election. They as Nonconformists had, du. ring the past fifty years, stood forth in the van of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) They had been plentiful in their service, and they bad received but scanty reward. (Hear, bear.) They did not ask for reward. They were still faith- ful, he trusted, to the principles, and he hoped that haying been champions of progress in every department during the half century that had passed, they would pursue the same course of advancement and progress in the century that had to come. (Loud applause) On the motion of the Rev. J. D. Thomas, seconded by the Rev. S. B. Handley, Mr. Rogers was cordially thanked for his sermon and address. The Chairman, in a brief address alluded to the influence of the Christian Church upon the lives of men, and in the forming of high and noble characters. The Rev. S. B. Handley delivered an address, in which

PROPOSAL TO FORM AN ARC sellOOL. Mr. Moss drew attention to the fact that Free Library Committee were empowered to receive grants from the com- mittee of the Council on Education towards the erec,ion and maintenance of science and art school& This proviei tri, he took it, was intended to enable local authorities acting under the Free Libraries Acts, to do for science and art education what school boards had done for elementary education. As they were aware, the first step in art was taught in elemen- tary schools. and there were scores of your* people in the town who held the certificate of the Science and Art De- partment showing that they had passed the first grade in drawing. But at this point their progress was stopped be- cause there were no means in the town by which they might attain the higher branches of art. No matter what their abilities or talents may be they could not get any fur- ther. Some of them might possess all the talents of a Ru- ben, a Gainsborough, or a Millais, but however that might be there were no facilities for them to progress. There had been science classes carried on in a spasmodic manner, and it was very unlikely that one would be held during the en- suing year, so that it was probable there might he no science teaching whatever in the town. Ile had shown, he thought, that there was room for further means to be pro- vided in science and in art, and he need scarcely argue that science and art ought to be encouraged in the town. The expenses attending science ancrart classes seemed to divide themselves into three heads—there was accommodation, ap- paratus, and teaching. He proposed that the Free Library Committee should provide the accommodation and appara- tus. The teaching would not be any expense to them, inas- much as the teachers of both science and art were willing to undertake classes for what they could make in fees and Government grant. There was a room in that building over the reading room which would answer the purpose admir- ably, and he thought the Commissioners would permit them the use of it. The cost for apparatus and furniture would not exceed £5 or £6. He proposed that appl ca- tion be made to the Science and Art Depat- ment asking for permission to commence science and Art classes in connection with the Free Library, and also that application be made to the Commissioners for the use of the room, the rental to be stated. Mr. Moss pointed out that application must be made before the let October or the classes could not commence for another year. He had brought the matter before them in a somee hat crude form, but he felt sure they would sympathise with it and help him out as well as they could.—Mr. Shaw pointed out that the room alluded to by Mr. Moss had not been appropriated in order to keep the bedroom of the caretaker private, and all the publ,io departments of the town now being located in that building it might be necessary to have a man on the premises to keep order and do various things, and the room mentioned might be required as a bedroom. He suggested that the School Board should use the Commissioners board room for their meetings, and that the the room now used by that body as a boardroom could he converted into a com- mittee-room, and used at nights for the purposes of ecience and art classes. If that could not be done, there was land which belonged to the town, and a proper building might be erected thereon. The object Mr. Moss had in view de- served it. (Hear, hear.) The town was not heavily rated, notwithstanding the complaints that were made ; it was not burdened with any great debts ; but of course the rates pressed rather heavily at the present time because trade was not as good as it ought to be. He did not altogether follow Mr. Moss about the very light expense. In Widnes the Science and Art School entailed an expense of about £lOO to £l5O a year. But the circumstances on the two sides of the river were very different. He knew people in Widnes able to give whe felt it not only a pleasure, but a duty to assist in carrying on the work, and he thought they in Run- corn would find the manufacturers willing to help because they knew that if they could educate their young they would have better men in their offices, in their laboratories, and in their workshops, and that, therefore' they would he benefitted by the outlay. He (Mr. Shaw) would be glad indeed to contribute towards the support of scierce and art classes in Runcorn, and he felt quite sure that others in the town would do the same. .He did not think they would have any difficulty in get- ting about £lOO a year towards this noble object. He advised them whatever they did to do it well" The Chairman said he bad every sympathy with Mr. Moss's proposition as far as it affected the establishment of science and art education in the town; but he could not support it out of the library rate, as their expenditure was already heavy. They were told by Sir James ?icon and other gentlemen who had had great experience in public libraries that it was out of the question to open a reading room as well as a library. In the face of that experience and advice they had opened a reading room, and it had been a great success. This, however, had something to do with the library, but they could not keep pace with the literature of the day and the current literature, because it was too ex- pensive for them, and they had to wait in most cases until the books were second-hand or a cheap edition was published. He thought it would be almost folly to cripple the library, which was used by the whole of the town, in order to assist perhaps Some 20 or 30 individuals taking an interest in either drawing or science. If Mr.laloss was inclined to go on with the matter, any five gentlemen who would sign the neces- sary forms would have no difficulty in starting science and art classes at once. He expressed his willingness to become one of the five necessary.--Mr. Moss said be had made some calculations as to the cost. He had had Mr. Knight, an artist from Nantwich, there, who was a gentleman of con- siderable abilities, and who possessed the requisite certifi-

cates, and he would have been perfectly willing to take the he gave some interesting reminiscences of the pastors of classes on the terms he had mentioned. The science teachers the Church, having made the acquaintance of all but one, would be on the same footing. Mr. Annett would have and of the members of the Church, whose memories were come there and used his own apparatus, so that there would still cherished. He made special mention of the late Mr. have been little or no expense except the rooms, which be John Brookes, his character and work in the Church. Ta- was informed was unappropriated. (Mr. Shaw: That is so.) ing A retrospect of the last half century in the history of If there were difficulties in the way this year he supposed Bethesda Church. they had many reasons for thanking God he must rest content with having ventilated the matter andl and for taking courage. Mr. Handley spoke upon the rela- hoped that in future any farther effort would have a prae- (ion of Congregationalism to other Christian communities, tical result,—Mr. Shaw promised to subscribe if Mr. Moss and the relation of Congregationalists to one another. The would form classes in the way suggested by Mr. Lake.— I New Testament was the ecclesiastical polity of the Con. After some further discussion the subject dropped. g regationalists, and their motto was " Live and let live." (Applause.) The Rev. S. Yates spoke of his ministry at Runcorn, and the mode of thought that then ruled the congregation. ,No portion of his life was more real, more joyful, more ; beneficial to him than his life at Runcorn. (Applause.) The Rev. E. Williams expressed his pleasure at being present, and made reference to his pleasant connection with several of the members of the congregation and the min- isters present. He proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the ladies for preparing the tea and presiding at the tables, and to the gentlemen who had decorated the school- room The Rev. Sr. Vause eeconded the motion. It gave him great pleasure to take part in the jubilee. The Rev. J. D. Thomas proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Rigby for presiding, and to their good friends, Mr. Yates and Mr. Handley, for their presence and addresses. Alluding to his pastorate at Bethesda, he said while he had experienced some troubles and some annoyances, he had found their the truest friends, and some of the hest workers in connection with the cause of Christ that be had ever known, and he only hopsd that all the unpleasant feelings would be forgotten, and that that jubilee would be as it ought to be, a new beginning for evaryone of them ; that they would all try unitedly, with one heart, and with their faith fixed in our Lord Jesus Christ, to make a brighter history for this church, and make its influence more power- ful in the town, than it had been in the past. (Hear, hear.) Taking all things together, they had a brighter prospect before them at the present time than at any period since he had been in their midst. (Applause.) Mr. W. Handley seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The proceedings concluded with a hymn. A collection was made at each service in aid of the funds, and nearly £2O was realised. On Wednesday evening about 350 of the children attend- ing the Sunlav school were given an excellent tea. Sub- sequently a short service was conducted by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, and an address was given by the Rev. S. Yates. The rest of the evening was spent in various games, and the young people thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

div.head: CONCERT AT WIDNES.
div.p: CONCERT AT WIDNES.

In aid of the Welsh Presbyterian Chapel, Milton-street, Widnes, a concert of more than usual excellence took place in the Drill Hall on Monday evening. The building was crowded in every part, and upwards of £2O will be added to the fund for liquidating the debt of £llO that now burdens the congregation worshipping at the chapel. In a short opening speech, Mr. E. Carey, who presided, gave a few facts regarding the denomination. The chapel was built in 1866 at a cost of £BOO, and would accommodate 200 per- sons. The services were conducted entirely in Welsh, and the attendance averaged 170 to 180, occupying about nine- tenths of the sittings' a proportion that very few denomina- Hens could equal. There were 120 scholars in regular attendance at the school. On behalf of the citizens of Widnes present that night, and on his own behalf, he wished the Welsh Presbyterian friends all possible success and prosperity in their undertaking. (Applause.)—llle quality of the ehtertainnsent may be gathered from the fact that the principals were Madame Laura Smart, soprano, • Liverpool ; Miss Annie Williams, contralto, of Liverpool; Mr. Ben Davies, recrntly leading tenor of Mr. Carl Rosa's Opera Company ; and Mr. Joseph Cantor. Mr, Ben Nevin vais the chief attraction, and, as he was in fine voice, the audience had a treat rarely experienctel in Widnes. His contributions were "The Message," "Once Again," and "Good Night Beloved," and be was associated with Madame Laura Smart in the duet "Oh that we two were Maytag." On each appearance he was enthusiastically en- cored, and in response he favoured the company with a song in the Welsh tongue, and that charming song from the "Bohemian Girl"—" When other lips and other hearts." Miss Annie Williams sang with pathos the "Better Lend," arid she was recalled. By desire she also gave "Jeanette and Jeanot " with taste and feeling. Madame Laura Smart gave a cepital interpretation of Bis- hop's fine song "Bid me discourse," and she was heartily encored, when she sang "He'd nothing else to do." She also contributed Ganzy's charming song "Sing a rreet bird" with expressive power. Always a favourite with Widnes audiences, Mr. Cantor delighted the audience with his fine rendering of" Shipwrecked" and several hurnouroua songs, and he was recalled three times. Mr. James Stirk, a skil- ful local cornet player, performed " Weber's last waltz " in la manner which earned him a deserved encore to which he responded. The performances of t'-e Birkenhead Quartette Party were much enjoyed, their voices harmoeising with sweet effect. The programme was opened and closed by the Widnes soap Works Brass Band, who p'ayed "Moses in Egypt" and" Ntbucodonosor " in their usual unimpeach- able style. .Mr. W. Jennett conducted. Miss Maggie E. Evans, an Eisteddfod celebrity, was an efficient accompan- ist, and added to the pleasure of those present by her able execution of the pianoforte solo "The storm at sea." Mr. John Davies, the organiser of the coucert, must be compli- mented upon the result of his effort.

CONGREGATION ALls'd AT WIDNES. To defray the cost of the proposed repairing, painting, and general renovation of Walton Congregational Chapel, Widnes, and also to form the nucleus of a fund for erecting Sanday schools, a bazaar was opened in Malin's Temper- ance Hall. on Thursday, by Mr. R. Pilkingt,n, J.P , of St. Helens. Stalls laden with an artistically xli,pleyed assort- ment of fancy and useful articies wets conveiiiently arran- ged timed the room, which wee also tastefully decorated, the effect hoing bright and pleasant. Stall No I was in charge of Mrs Harrison, Mrs (.1. Rae, Mrs Wilkinson, Miss G. Warne; No. 2 was presided over by Mrs Lewis, Mrs Chapman, Miss T.avis, and Miss E. Warne; Sunday school stall, Miss Knight, Miss Wiftierne, M i,S Edwards, and Miss Thomas; refreshment stall, Mrs Licaigkinson, Miss Barer, Miss McCritne, Mrs. Creonze Warner. There was a good company present at the opening ceremony, when in addition to Mr. Pilkiagton there were on the platform the Revs. R. G. Hughes, pastor, R. Yeatnian (Baptist), G. Jones (Welsh Wesleyan), and C. Bradbury (Presley Cross Con- gregational), Messrs. H. S. Hall, J.P. and John Brock, lE—The Rev. R. G. Hughes, in opening the proceedings, said it was a very difficult matter for any minister to carry out successfully the work in connection with a church with- out proper accommodation for Sunday school scholars. At present they bad unfortunately to conduct the Sunday school in the church, and this method was detrimental to true and complete success. A few of the ladies of the congregation, wives of working- men, for they had no wealthy men in connection with the church, had been zeal,insly labouring for the bazaar for months past, and the splendid results could now be seen. They hoped to raise £3OO. (Applause.)— Mr. U. S. Hall sal I. in spite of the fact that he was a churchman and the son of a parson, he thanked God from the bottom of his heart that they had Independents amongst them, for he believed they had done great and glorious work not only In religion but for the Liberal cause as well. (Applause.) Independency had a great and noble future before it, because they represented to a certain extent freedom in religion, and their foundation was the Good Old Book, and that was a thing they could not over- estimate. He believed Independency meant light and i liberty in religion and progress n civil matters. e must progress At the same time he would not underrate the efforts of the various Christian churches. If people were good Churchmen, good Baptists, good Methodists, and good Catholics, let them alone. (Hear, hear.) It appeared to him that the great thing wanted amongst the Indepen- dents of Widnes was !inity. There ought to lee Indepen- dency enough in IN idnes to•fill two or three churches. (Hear, bear.) He was surprised they had not made more headway. He expresed his pleasure at being present, and said his best word to them was unity. (Applause.)—Mr. J. Brock made a few remarks. He cordially sympathised with them in the eff.irt they were making to raise the sum of money mentioned by Mr. Hughes. He saw no reason why they should not get all they required. As a rule the most money was not obtained from the rich men, but from those who systematically acknowledged their dependance upon , God for all they received and desired to give back to Hint some of that which after all was only His own. lie could not foLow Mr. Hull in all be bad said. He was incliLed ta think there were Creeds in the world that a man we, Much better rid of. Although at one period of his life he had attended the Independent Ministry, from the choice of those near and dear to him, who had been brought up under the Congregational Ministry, he was not a Congregatioualist, but he cordially endorsed what Mr. Hall had said, that this country was tremendously indebted to the Dissenters. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. R. Pilkitton then declared thg bazaar open in a brief speech, in which he expressed his tOeasure at be- ing enabled to assist in the effort they we.re making. In Widnes money spent in building a school was well spent.— The fair saleswomen then commenced their task.

PADGATR WEpLEYAN gIITUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The eighth session opened with a soiree on Thursday. Mr. Frederick Wright genially offi- ciated as master of ceremonies, and the following programme was executed to the evident enjoyment of the audience, being varied by intervals for con- versation : Pianoforte solo, "Puns de Corail," Miss Helen Bennett; song, "Come Lasses and Lads," Mr. E. Booth; reading, "A Legend of Navarre," Mr. Charles Plinston ; " Spinning Song," Miss Tates ; recitation, "William Tell's Address to his Native Hills," Mr. Alfred Perris; song, "The Children's Home," Miss Turner; reading, "The Suicide," Mr. Arthur Bennett; song, " The Last 7ifilestone," Misg Edith Wrightson ; reading, "The Diver," Mr, Theo- dore C. London; song, " A Penny for your Thoughts:: Miss Tates ; dialogue, "Over the Garden Wall,' Messrs. W. J. Bennett, J. E. Richardson, and Walter Bennett; and song, "Jack's yarn,„ Mr. E. Booth. Miss Tates, Mr. E. Booth, and Mr. Alfred Perris were each encored, and the dialogue, which was of a highly amusing character, was the source of much laughter. A session which has commenced. so auspiciously can hardly fail to be successful.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Alderman Davies (in the chair), Coun- cillor Greening, and Mr. John Fairclough. DRUNIEENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness :—William Stokes, in Roserjard, on Sat- urday evening, fined 203 and costs; John TOole, in But- termarket-street, on Sunday morning, fined 55, including costs; William Litherland, junr., in Buttermarket-street, on the previous evening, fined 103 and coats; Daniel Crosby, in Market-place, discharged with a caution ; William Yates, in the Market Hall, tined lOs and costs; George Marsh, in Rvland-street, on the 19th inst, fined 5s and costs; . Richard Griffiths, in Ryland-street, on the 19th tilt, fined 58 and costs; Peter Kelly, in Winwick-read, on the 19th tilt, fined 51 and costs; Charles Stewart, in Horsemarket-st., on the 23rd ult, tioed 5s and costs ; James Jordan, in Mar- ket-place, on the 19th tilt, fined 53 and costs ; Mary Burns, in Old-road, Latchford, on the 20th ult. fined 5e and costs ; Mary Coyne, in Scotland-road, on the 22nd nit, sent to pri- son for a month. BREACH OF THE PEACH —Margaret Riley, charged with committing a breach of the peace in Buttermarket-street on the 21st ult, was discharged. Funtons DRIVING.—Arthur Millward was charged with furiously driving a horse in Bridge-street on the 23rd nit. Mr. A. Browne defended. A fine of 103 and costs was imposed. OnsnancrioNs.—For creating obstructions by allowing vehicles to stand an unreasonable length of time in the street the following persons were fined :—.John Liddle, 28 6d and costs; Joseph Caldwell, 5s and costs ; Frederick Sil- cock, fined in the costs. ASSAULTS. Peter Fleming and Arthur Stokes, young met), were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rose- yard, on Saturday evening, and with assaniting P.C. Neill and P.C. Chantler at the same time and place. The as- sault was a severe one, and both prisbners were sent to gaol for a month. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES —The following persons were summoned for neglecting to send their children to school, Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, prose- cuting :—Thomas Harrison. coal beaver, Warburton, boy ordered to be sent to the ship " Clio" for five years; John Platt, labourer, fined ss; William Burton, forgeman, Bew- sey-road, fined se; John Ryan, stonemason, Lord Nelson- street, fined 53 ; Robert Greenway, coal heaver, Silver-street, fined 2s 61 ; Ann Hart, labourer, Silver-square, child ordered to be sent to the Workhouse ; Peter Molyneaux and Peter Cane, cases adjourned. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough and Major Litton. . _

DRUNKENNESS AND BRUTALITY.— Michael Dyer and Richard Rigby, young men, and strangers in the town, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- street on the previous evening, and with assaulting a young man named William Moran. The two were drunk and as Moran was passing one of them pushed him against the wall. He remonstrated and was then struck, knocked down, and kicked by the prisoners.—P.C. Monoghan witnessed the aaaauit,which he said was quite unprovoked.—The Bench sent prisoners to gaol for a month. THURSDAY,—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. DRUNKENNESS. Henry Stringer, for being drunk in Mersey-street On the previt)4; evening, was fined 25 ed and costs. Famar.—Before Captain Reynolds, Mr • Garnettl and Pr, Gornall, DESERTERS.—John Souter and Arthur McDonald were charged with being deserters from Her Majesty's South Staffordshire Regiment, stationed at Manchester, and were remanded to Walton. MASTER AND SERVANTS.—EdMVaId Mills. fustian cutter, was summoned by Sarah Webb and Mary Ann Webb, who claimed L 1 as compensation by reason of their not having been supplied regularly with work, as provided in the in- dentures.—Defendant admitted that the gins bad not been regularly supplied with work, but alleged that when there was work they would not come.—The magistrates thought it advisable to cancel the indentures.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY—Before Mr. J. Brock. MrscguArruous.—Christopher Farrell was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for sleeping on the works of the Widnes Alkali Co.--Elixabeth Travis and Thomas Moran were bound over to keep the peace for riotous conduct. —A fine of 5s and costs was imposed upon each of the following per. sons for drunkenness :—James Kelly, Martin Brown, John Gregory, John Brady, Michael McHale, and Patrick Spell- man.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Bock and Mr. F. H. Gossage. DRITNXENNESS.—Sarah Ann Taylor, Robert Evans, and Thomas Walsh were each fined for this offence. MISCELLANEOUS.—Robert Crow and William Williams, who did not appear, were each tined 53 and costs for riding bicycles on the footpath at Halewood.--For throwing stones in Warrington-road Thomas Miller, a boy, was fined 2s 6d and costs.--Esther Beasley was summoned for as. saulting Maria Hoseman. It was alleged that on the 20th ult. whilst the complainant was shaking a rug near the back gate of her house the defendant threw a quantity of ashes upon her from a basket. The defendant threatened to "do 'worse" if she caught complainant there again.—After hearing the evidence the Bench dismissed the case.

div.head: RUNCORN PET I Y SESSIONS. MONDas.—Before Mr. James Handley and Mr. A. Thomas
div.p: RUNCORN PET I Y SESSIONS. MONDas.—Before Mr. James Handley and Mr. A. Thomas

(chairman). WARLIKE WITH WHISKEY.—Charles Taylor was sum- moned for assaulting Joseph Barker. On Saturday night, the 19th inst, Barker was standing at (be door of his house in Cooper-street, when the defendant came up and said " You are listening again and taking all in. are you," and invited him to come out if he were a man. Barker was about to shut the door when the defendant struck him on the face.— The defendant pleaded guilty. Hs had had, some whiskey, and was not used io it. A THREAT.—Joseph Leathwood was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £l.O and two sureties in a, or 14 days' hard labour, for threat- ening Martha Worthington, a woman with whom he had cohabited in Wilson's-row.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TCESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall, W. Long, J. Mar. eon, R. Piet point, C. Broadbent, and W. C. Jones. DRCNE IN CHARGE OF A CART.—Richard Holcroft was charged with haying been drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Appleton and was fined 5s and costs. AN UNLICENSED Doo.—James Highfield, a lad, was charged with having kept a dog at Stretton without a li- cense on the 16th August. The ease was dismissed. SANITARY OFFENCE AT STRETTON.—Robert Fairhurst was charged, that be being the owner of certain new cot- tages at Strettou, he permitted the same to be occupied be- fore he obtained a certificate from the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary Authority that there they were provided with a supply of water for domestic purposes. Mr. P. Davies, of Warrington, represented the defendant, and said that his client was really not the owner of the premises, but only the builder. He did not, however, object on that account, but he explained that the people who had taken the cottages Persisted in going into them before the certificate was ob- tained. There was about 50 yards from the houses a pump with a sufficient water supply for the whole of Stratton. and ,Mr. Fairhurst obtained the certificate a few days after the people went into the house. Inspector Farrington, who prosecuted, not pass for a heavy penality.—The defen- dant was ordered to pay costa. A Row IN A Pm3rac•HorsE.--Barry Roach, an elderly man, was charged with having threatened Charles William Philips, the landlord of the Ring.o'-Bells, Daresburv. Mr. P. Davies defended. Prosecutor said that OD Sonday.the 30th August, there was a row in his house, and when he inter- fered between two men who were fighting, the defendant threatened to smash his face with a pewter pot. He was putting defendant out, when the latter gave a about, which was the signal for those in the taproom to upset and break the glasses, atc., in the room. Benjamin Whittaker and John McGrath were charged with haying done malicious damage by breaking' glasses, Sm., on the day in question. Mr. Davies again defended. Ihe prosecutor was not able to say he had personally seen either of the defendants com- mit damage, and as he had rio witnesses who could speak to that effect these charges were also dismissed. Assnuty.—Williana Spann was bound over in £lO to keep the peace for six months for an assault on the 25th ult. at Preaton-o'-tia'rHill.—John White, summoned for an assault OIL Albert ann. was bound over in a like P amount.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), and Messrs. Brown, Appleton, Greening; Darbvshire, Ratmiffe, Jolley, William Houghton, Broadbent, Grange, Ba!harry, Bonnet!, John Houghton, Kilshall, Gibson, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk). SCHOOL COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee contained a resolution that a special meeting of the committee be called to con- sider the appointment of a medical officer for the Padgate Schools. Th superintendent reported that the children con- tinued healthy and cheerful.—ln the course of some conver- sation as to the proposed structural alteration to the schools, the CHAIRMAN said the spouting was so constructed that the water instead pf running to the down spouts ran the other way—(laughter)—and the spouts were so put up that this defect could not be rectified without cutting the spouts off and lifting the slates. He moved that the whole matter be referred to the committee, and that a medical officer for the schools be advertised for.—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE did not think it was necessary to appoint a medical officer for the schools, inasmuch as the schools are situated in a district for which they already had a paid medical officer to visit the pauper cases. He thought it would fairly come within that officer's duties to perform the medical services of the schools for nothing, but if the officer was insufficiently paid because of the increase in his duties, let :hem increase his salary instead of having a special appointment for the schools.—The CHAIRMAN said they were under a legal obli- gation to have a distinct medical officer for the schools.— Mr. APPLETON said be agreed with Mr. Dar- byshire's suggestion.—The CHAIRMAN: But we are under a legal obligation.,— Mr. APPLETON said he would second Mr. Derbyshire's proposal.—The CHAIRMAN: But there is no proposal ; I cannot receive a proposition if it is not legal —The CLERK said the same question had arisen before with regard to the appointment of medical officer for the Workhouse, and the Local Government Board Insisted that the appointments be distinct —Mr. DARBY- SHIRE contended that there was a difference between the Schools and the Workhouse, and he suggested that informa- tion be got as to the nature of similar appointments at Chesterfield and Birmingham.—ln reply to Mr. Bonnell, Mr. DARBYSEIIRE said he had not spoken to Dr. Joseph or any other doctor about the matter.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that Dr. Joseph had only been asked to temporarily take charge of the schools.—Tne CLERK thought that he might safely say that in no institution of the kind were medical officers appointed in the way suggested by Mr. Derbyshire. —Mr. Derbyshire's proposal not being seconded, some dis- cussion took place as to the salary that should be paid to the medical officer of Padgate Schools. It was stated that Dr. Spinks, the late officer, had been paid £35 a year.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE proposed that the salary in future be £lO, as, bethought, there was not much to do.—At the request of Mr. Greening, the CLERK read a long list of the duties of the medical officer of the Schools.—Mr. DONNELL did not think they would get anyone to render for £lo.—Mr. Der- byshire's proposal was not seconded. Mr. El REENING moved, and Mr. JOLLEY seconded, that the salary be £25 a year.—Mr. DONNELL moved as an amendment, and Mr. APPLETON seconded, that it be £2o.—On being put to the vote the amendment was carried by 10 to s.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE then moved ass further amendrnent,that. the question be postponed while the clerk 'ascertained what was paid to other medical officers under similar circumstances—This was seconded by Mr. APPLETON, but negatived, only four voting in its favour.—Mr Bonnell's proposition was then agreed to.

THE HOUSE COMMITTEE. In the minutes of this committee it was recommended that Mr. S. M. Webster supply the medicines for the coming year. Mr. Scotson's sample of whiskey was approved and his contract was recommended. The committee also recom- mended that the following regulations be strictly observed, namely, that the porter see that all persons coming to the Workhouse (except infectious cases and those who are un- able to walk) come through the front door; that each nurse report in writing to the master or matron all admis- sions to the hospital with particulars thereof directly after they receive the case, and see all the meals properly served to the patients, and the outside doors in the hospital locked after supper ; that all officials of the Workhouse during their temporary absence from their department leave their keys in the place appointed for them.—Mr. Ilnown moved, and Mr. APPLETON seconded the adoption of these minutes. —The CHAIRMAN supposed that the last resolution arose out of what they had seen in the newspapers.— Mr. BROWN said that was so. The minutes were then passed.

Mr. Bleakly wrote in reply that he was at present at Brighton, but upon his return, if they still wished it, he would be pleased to come before them and render an explanation as far as he could. div.head: ESTIMATES.
div.p: THE ESTIMATES.

The CLERK, in .s;l27mlt'tin—g----ti;e half-yearly esti- mates of expenditure, read the following statement, viz.:— The estimate of contributions required for the half year ending at Lady Day, 1886, with particulars of common charges, are submitted to your Board for approval. The present rateable value of the Union is £310,450, compared to £309,911 at the corresponding period of last year. In several successive years preceding 1869, substantial addi- tions were made to rateable value with the effect of easing the burdens of local taxation, when weightier duties and new responsibilities devolved by the action of the Legisla- ture, and by the growth of ordinary Union work, upon Beards of Guardians. It is within my experience that in a single year a leap of £20,000 was made in the rateable value of your Union. In the first four years of the last decade the average annual increase exceeded £lO,OOO. In the six years the average fell below £5,000, so diminishing in a downward course as to yield but £539 to the past year only £209, which increase is due to the second half of the year. The average of the six years was also due to a con- siderable extent to the action of your Assessment Com- mittee in subjecting certain railway properties to revision, with the result of material augmentation of value for rating purposes. For the present then, rateable value may be viewed to be at a standstill, or as moving only at a pace hardly to be reckoned progressive. Boards of Guardians provide for their expenditure by two systems. "Common charges" are apportioned against parishes according to the rateable value, and included in such charges are costs of maintenance, out-relief, lunatics, medical relief, non-resident poor. vaccination, registration, salaries, superannuation ratisms of officers, establishment charges, and other miscellaneous expenses. " Separate charges" are made against the parishes in respect of county rates, school fees for non-pauper children, School Attend- ance Committee expenses, 9alaries of collectors of rates, &C. According as these respective expenditures rise or fall, without the aid of increased rateable value, will calls upon the parishes by the Union also fluctuate. Increase of population necessarily affects certain expendi- tures as those for registration, vaccination, &c., otherwise the sums for common charges will not materially vary ex- cept at periods of increasing or diminishing pauperism. For the now expiring summer half year a sum of £2,300 was provided for maintenance, that is to say, for provisions —necessaries, clothing, outfits, and drugs for the indoor poor,and the cost of burials of persons dying at the Work- house. It is calculated that that sum has been exceeded, and as the present estimate is for the winter half of the year, £2,400 is fixed upon as against £2,176 es 5d the amount of the actual cost of maintenance in the correspond- ing half of last year. The actual monies expended for out- relief in the winter half of last year was £1,833 17s 7d. In the first quarter of the present summer half year the sum so disbursed was £924 2e 84, and the multiple thereof be- ing £l,BlB 5s 41, .C 2,000 is deemed necessary for the ensu- ing winter half-year. A small increase to provide for the cost of lunatics is also desirable. The actual cost in the corresponding half of last year was £1,103 Sc lid, in the first quarter of the present half-year £566 is Id. The pre- sent estimate is for £1,125, being £75 in excess of the estimates last adopted. The county rates estimated on the actual receipts at the corresponding half of last year were £1,847, now similarly meaeured, the sum is £2,121. Having regard- to the balance estimated to remain at the end of the present half-year in favour of parishes, an actual increase of £366 in the calls over the last contribution is advised. It is anticipated that the sum called for will carry yos over the half year, and that fair balances in favour of parishes will remain at its close. There is no reason to suppose that ample provision is not made for ordinary out- lay, Poor law unions are liable however to have a spring made upon them ill such matters as county rates, and there is no remedy available to them in regard to the liability. Your Board have fairly and reasonably given to the subject of county rates your attention and consideration, and par- ticularly so with reference to a bridge at Penwertham. When a bridge connecting the two counties of Lancaster and Chester, at a paint acrola the Mersey , within your union, known as the 11,xton and Warburton Bridge, the Act was obtained and the bridge built at private cost, and it is at Present not easy to see why Rixton and the rest of your union are to be taxed ':r new bridge at Penwortliam. Whether the old verse reading "Out of his bounty he built this bridge at the expense of the county "is ap- plicable or not, the outcome of the proceedings you have entered upon cannot fail to be instructive arid useful. —lt was agreed, on the motion of Mr. DARBYSHIRE,. seconded by Mr. Boemaxr. to have this statement printed for the use of the members. A CORIGUSEPISILE.

The Local Government Board forwarded to the Gruirdians a copy of the following letter, NY:3la had been received by them, viz.:—Gentlemen of the Local Board. Gentlemen,— I write to inform you that I went to the Warrington Union

to ask the Guardians if they wood allow me a trifle to help me a little while. I was out of work; I only wanted a little, and they would not order for the house, and I told them I tvould not go in, for if they would look after ray husband sooner. I told the relieving officer he was coming to Warrington, and if he had been looked after then I should not had asked much relief; and the people that drink day after day can get relief, but one that does try to get a honest living there Is nothing but an order far the house, but if there is one that is (?) homeless and has no Ana to speak for them and can't go dressed op like ladies they are nothing thought of in Warrington. It is not the poor that gets what is paid in the rates, it is them that does not need it that gets it, and I think it very hard that I have a husband and they will not look after him they want me to do that for them. You must excuse my (illegible). So I have no more to say now, so no more at present.—(Sign-d) MARY MEEKS, at Mary Flynn's, Berry-yard, Tanner's-lane, Warrington.—(Laughter.)—The , Clan/max thought they need not take any notice of that letter.—The CLERK said the facts of the case were that they . offered £3 reward for the apprehension of this woman's bus- • band, and the Relief Committee had dealt with the case OR its merits. The Locll Government Board did not ask for any remarks.—The CHAIRMAN: I do not think the letter ; calls for any remarks.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON: It is not worth while.—The matter then dropped.

RUNCORN V, MANCHESTER GYHNASIUM.—This match was decided at Runcorn, on Saturday, the home team scoring the substantial victory of three goals, five tries, two minor points, to the Gymnasium nil. The visitors started the ball, and it was soon seen that the home players had the game in their own hands, Lindland scoring the first try soon after the start, V/ Hughes failing at the place kick. Play being resumed, Speakman and Sutcliffe put in some work; the latter ran well to Broady, who checked him, and boon after an exchange between Broady and H. Hughes get the ball in the Gynasiums' quarter, and a little later Wright scored the second try, W. Hughes again failing ,to increase its value. The ball again being put into play, Speakman and Broady made a good exchange, and a minute later Mc- Cracken succeeded in pushing Wainwright touch-in-goal before the latter could ground his charge, but the visitors could not keep the home team from their 25, for Wright got up to the line. Lewis, being quick on the ball, grounded it over, from which be kicked a goal. In reply to the kick- off from the centre, W. Hughes ran strongly to the centre, when Broady soon after got hold of the ball, and came through, obtaining a capital try. Lewis took the place, but failed to increase its value, and half-time was given a little later on, the game standing—Runcorn one goal, three tries, to nil. After changing over, the ball was started by W. Hughes, and the visitors failing to get it out of their half, Galley looked like scoring, being only held under the post. Whitehouse here relieved for a moment, when Broady, Wainwright, and Holland made strong efforts, the latter getting in under the bar. Leavis'a kick at goal failing, play was again resumed. An- drews, Sutcliffe, and Whitehouse pat in some good work, but Wright and Cox coming through with the ball, Cox crossed the line before he PAS checked, Woods kicking a gaol from the place. Play was again located in the visitors' half, where Siatcliffe bad plenty of work in stopping Wain- wright, whom he tackled safely on several occasions. and following an effort by Speakman, Broady again scored, Woods failing to increase its value. Starting off again, the visitors made an effort to score, playing well against so heavy a defeat, but the play did not remain long out of the Gymnaeittms' half, for Galley got over, grounding the ball, Lewis being successful in placing the ball over the bar. A minor point was soon after conceded to Runcorn, after which time was called. The home team played a good loose game, the passing tactics being improved considerably to the game played last week. With more cohesion the Run- corn team would show better results. The visitors played well, considering they were so heavily overmatched. The teams were :—Runcorn : Full back, Woods ; three-quarter backs, Broady, Speakman, and Wainwright; half backs, H. Hughes (captain) and Andrews; forwards, Wright, Clarke, Hoftland, Lightburn, Lewis, W. Hughes, Dean, Cox, and Galley. Manchester Gymnasium : Full back, Whitehouse ; three-quarter backs, 'H. W. Sutcliffe, Taylor, and Blinkhorn ; half backs, Hall and J. Crawford ; for- wards, Froggatt, McCracken, Stroud, Chadwick, Gadd, Wilkinson. Li. Sutcliffe, Orme, and Stephenson....

WARRINGTON T. WALTON.—The first match of the season I of these clubs was played on Saturday, in splendid weather, I on the Walton ground. The Walton captain, Mr. Bulcock, I won the toss, and elected to play down hill. Turner set the ball rolling for Warrington at 3-40 ; it was well re- turned, and the first scrimmage was formed in the visitera' half. It was soon apparent that Warrington were the stronger in the scrimmages. Warren got the ball and made a short run, passing to Jolley, who relieved by a kick and transferred play to the home half, where scrimmaging , was the order of the day. Warren was again to the fore, with a pass to Massey, who missed. When play was taken to neutral ground, with a combined dribble, Warrington for- wards took the oval to Walton 25 yards flag, but Fair- clough nicely saved. From a pack Gilbert passed to , Barnes, who essayed one of his formidable drops, but failed, resulting in a touchdown. Hancock dropped out ; Gilbert was next prominent with a run, and then passed to Warren, who soon cried hold. Shortly after Warren passed I to Barnes, who threw across to Jolley, and he in turn passed , to Gilbert, but being pressed he parted. Dillon being well up took the ball across the line but was called back, the ball being ruled thrown forward. Soon after Fairclough nicely interrupted a pass from Warren, and ran the ball to the visitors 25 flag, but was brought down by Buxton, when a splendid bit of play by Massey transferred hostili- ties to the home 25 flag. After a series of scrimmages, Gilbert dribbling well forced Walton to touchdown. After" the kick out, Barnes getting 'hold put in one of his splendid ! dodgy runs and parted to Hayes, when a splendid piece of passing among the Warrington forwards took place, which thoroughly nonplussed Walton, and enabled Dillon to again cross the line. Fairfield Turner took the place, but did not add the major point, being a difficult position. After the drop out Massey was next on the go, but was pushed into touch by Fairclough, from a line up Walton rushing the ball along took play into Warrington territory, and from a scrimmage Butcher passed to Legge at centre, who made a poor attempt to drop a goal, which resulted in a dead ball. Turner brought the ball out, and Ashton drib- bling beautifully compelled Walton again to touchdown. Half time was soon afterwards called, with the game in Warrington favour, Warrington 1 try, 3 minors, Walton 1 minor. Restarting, Massey returned from a loose scrim- mage, Warren kicked up and dashing through his oppon- ents in fair style crossed the Walton line, but was tacked by Butcher, and a maul resulted in Butcher pushing War- ren in.touch in goal. Warren claimed a try, having touched the ball down, but was over-ruled. After some give and take play, Gilbert made an excellent pass to Barnes, who, with one of his deadly drops, landed a splendid goal. From the kick off Buxton returned, and Warring- ton taking the ball alone compelled Maswelt to save. Shortly afterwards time was called, Warrington winning a pleasantly-contested game by 1 goal, 1 try, and 4 minor points, to Walton 2 minor points. All the Warrington backs played well, especially Warren, who played a grand half- back game. Forward, Ashton, Dillon, D ,vies, and Turner played a capital game. For Walton Butcher and Fairclough played best behind the scrimmages, and Forward, Bulcock, Drown, and Baker played a good and hard game. Referee, F. T. Parry. Warrington team: J. Buxton, full-back; J. T. Massey, T. Barnes, J. Jolley, three-quarter-backs : C. Gilbert, J. E. Warren (captain), half-backs; F. Turner, H, As.hton, T. Davies, E. Dillon. W. Povey, W. Heyes, Turner, W. Speakman, and J. Jones, forwards. Walton team : Maxwell, fall-back ; Lonsdale, Legge, and Fairclough, three-quarter-backs; Butcher and Brooks, half-backs • Bul- cock (captain), Stiraker, Brown, Idencock, Baker, Morrie, Horton, and Fowler, forwards.

Sr. PAUL'S F.C. v. LONGFORD EXCELSIORS F.C.—The first match of the former club was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter. The whole team showed up well. The match ended in an easy win for St. Paul's by one goal, two tries, six minor points to nil. Loughlin, Webster, and Lawrinson got the tries, and Allford kicked the goal. War- burton and Forster were the best for the losing side. Sy. HELENS V. A SPULL.—This match was played on Saturday at St. Helens. The Inn was started by Bothwick for the home team, and before five minutes had elapsed the visitors were forced to save, but this was followed by more substantial points, as Birchall dropped a goal, and Brammil secured a try, but the goal kick failed. On the change of ends Sr. Helens quickly scored two tries, and Pilkington dropped a second goal. Lawson added a try to the visitors side a few minutes before time, and Siddon added a fourth for Aspull, who won by 2 goals, 4 tries, and 8 minor points, to St. Helens 3 tries and 1 minor point.

RUNCORN OLD BOYS vMoss BANK. WHITE STAR, WIDNES.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and after a hotly-contested game ended in a draw in favour of the Old Boys by one gsal, four minor points, to one goal, two minor points. The goal for the Star was gained by Dennett, that for the Boys being obtained by Dutton, from which Brockley kicked a neat goal. The play of Hewitt, Crompton, Jones, and Brockley was very good for the Boys, as was that of Dennett and Warning for the Star. Teams :—Old Boys: Shaw, back; Booth, Crompton and Brockley, three-quarter backs ; Jones and Whitfield:hal f backs ; Leach, Dutton, Bate, Ellis, Shaw, Hinde, Prince, Lunt, and Hewitt, forwards. White Star : Myers, back; Hartnett, Boyle, and Merty, three-quarter backs ; Machone and Bennett, half backs: MacManus, Lowe, Bee, Gormley, Eastwood, Hewitt, and Wernisg, forwards. SANKEY V. STAR OF HOPE (WIDNES).—These teams met for the first time on Saturday, on the ground of the former. A start was effected about 3.30, Harding kicking off against the wind. Immediately after the kick off. Jones gained possession and put in a nice run, but was then " brought to grief "by Jefferson. A " scrimmage" was formed, after which the visitors' forwards ran the ball into home territory, forcing Barton to touchdown. The ball being re-started, Harding picked up, and alters, nice dodgy run succeeded in placing the ball over the goal line. The same player was entrusted with the place, but failed to im- prove on the score. Nothing further was recorded in the first half, but in the second half the home team had far the best of the game, keeping the visitors penned in their terri- tory the whole of the time. At the close the home team were declared the winners by I try (Hardin), 3 minor points, to 1 minor point for the visitors. All the home team played well together, while Jones for the visitors put in scrne good runs. _

WABRINCITON ("A') v. WALTON (2ND.) This match was played at Warrington on Saturday in beautiful weather, the game being witnessed by a goodly number of spectators. The visitors arrived rather late, and being short-handed, substitutes had to be procured to raise their team to its full strength. Walton winning the toss elected to play with the wind and sun in their favour. Whittle kicked off, and the forwards following up well prevented a return, the first scrimmage taking place inside the visitors' twenty-five. Belshaw, Whittle, and Webster soon made themselves conspicuous, especially Whittle who passed in grand style. A good rush by the forwards took the ball close to the visitors' goal line, when Savage, kicking up smartly, scored the first try, amidst the cheers of the spec- tators, but Hewitt failed to improve. Appleton made a good run, and on being collared, kicked into touch. Belshaw and Webster showed good form about this time, gaining a lot of ground, but this was chiefly owing to the passing of Whit- tle. Foster got over the goal line, but the try was not allowed. Another good pass by Whittle to Belshaw en- abled him to take the ball well up the field, and when collared, passed to Webster, Nivens compelling the try but the kick was again a failure. Shortly after a maul took place between two of the Warringtonians and one of the Walton forwards, the former being victorious, the result being a splendid goal kicked by Appleton. Some time after, Webster, who had the ball passed to him by Whittle, ob- tained a try, but Appleton this time failed to improve. In a few minutes time was called, bringing to an end a very enjoyable game. Teams :—Waltori : Walsh, full-back ; Boardman, Acton Barlow, threeequarter backs; Brown, Whitehead, half-backs ; Pickering, Corban, Leatherhar- row, Potter' Helsby, Summers, Pritchard, and Adkinson, forwards. Warrington : Hewitt, back ; Belshaw, Apple- 'ton, Webster, three-quarter backs; Whittle, Lightfoot, half- ., g backs ; Brimelow, Bashford, Molyneaux, Foster, Burgess, Robinson, Littlewood, Nevins, and Savage. forwards. WAREtINGTON v. MANCHESTER —Mr. T. R. Sutton, of the Sporting Chronicle, having kindly volunteered to bring a strong scratch team from Manchester to oppose Warring- ton, the offer was at once accepted, and the arrangement was made for Thursday afternoon to give those an oppor- tunity of witnessing a really first-class gains who cannot, through business, see the club's ordinary matches. At 4-15 a fair number of spectators was assembled; the weather, though fine, being windy. When the Manchester team came on the field, and names gone over. it was seen that Warrington were opposing the strongest individual team that has ever appeared in Warrington. The Manchester capt Ain, A. Teggin (internationalist), won the toss, and chose to play wile the wind in his favour. Warrington kicked off, and after a very pleasant but stubbornly con- tested two thirty-fives. Warrington were • declared the winners by one try, against five minors scored by Man- chester. There was loufl applauston the field when Barnes, with a grand ran, scored the winnine point for Warring- ton. Buxton played a safe game at full back, Jolley and Barnes played a good game at three-quarters ; the half backs played their nstial dashing and saving game; for- wards Turner. Asbta, and Davies played a splendid game. For Manchester, Coop, Slevin, Jordan, and Dean 4 played .a grand back game; and Teggin. Moss, andiMilier were the pick of the forwards. Warrington Team :—J. Buxton; fall back; J. T. Massey, T. Barnes, and J. Jolley, three-quarter backs; J. E. Warren (captain) and E. Gilbert, half backs : Fairfield Turner, H. Ashton,. W. Povey, W Hayes, T.

FARLESTOWN ROVERS V. BILLING.—These teams played at Ear lestown on Saturday, and, in a very one-sided game, the home team won by ten goals to none. Sr. HELENS ST. MARK'S (2ND) V. SHERDLEY ROVERS.— This match was played on Saturday last, on the ground of the latter, and a pleasant game resulted in an easy victory for the visitors by eight goals to nil. _

. NICOL-LANE 2ND V. NEWTON ST. PETER'S IST.—On the ground of the latter, after a very hard game, the Stars won by four goals to three. , Johnson, Goulding, and S. Win• stanly were the goal kickers for the winners. The Stars are hardly up to their old form yet or they would have secured a far mare easy victory than they did on Saturday. EAIILESTOWN (A TEAM) V. ST. HELENS AMATEURS. These teams met for the first time on the ground of the first-named, the Mesues, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon. The home team was weakened by the absence of Siddeley. Ferguson, and W. Line who were filling vacancies in the first team at Davenham. The match was evenly contested. Within a few minutes of the call of time no points had been scored, but the leather was then forced through the Earlestown uprights. No other goal was registered, and the Amateurs thus won by one goal to none. EARLESTOWN v. DAVENITAM.—The Liverpool and District Cup-holders journeyed to Davenham with a weak team on Saturday, and met with their first defeat during the present season. They were without the services of Whalley, Rich, and Dusbury, whose places were filled by Ferguson, Sidde- ley, and Line. There was a good turnout of spectators. During the first half Davenhane had the advantage of a slight breeze, and scared four goals to their opponents' none. On the change of ends Earlestown soon scored their only foal. The home team, however, managed to add two other goals, and thus won a victory by six goals to one, Teams— Davenham: Fellows, goal; Goulding and Riley. backs; D. Dalton, W. H. Dalton, and Vernon' half-backs; Stringer, Robinson, Haddock, T. Holland, and H. Holland, forwards. Earlestown: Appleton. goal; R. Green and J. Green, backs; Siddeley, Lane, and Bowker, half-backs; Dagnall, Sims, Ogden, Ellison, and Ferguson, forwards. Referee, Mr. G. Plant (Northwich Victoria F.C.)

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Saturday last is generally looked upon as the opening day of tbe Rugby clubs, but few really first-class matches were down for decision, as the principal organisations are not thoroughly in harness yet. In a few days the game will be in full swing. The only match of much importance in the district was between Broughton and Bradford, the cracks of their respective shires, but Broughton was defeated by two goals scored by Bradford, one dropped from play by Robert- ,haw. It was hard lines for Broughton, who scored two tries; and had their forwards shown more combination the result would perhaps have been different. Manchester have not opened their season yet, though , they have had two pract:ce matches, and by the time they play their first match—on October 10th—their men should be in good form. Liverpool do not don the war paint before next Saturday. I notice their list of fixtures is not a very strong one. Wigan opposed Swinton on the ground of the latter, and were defeated by two tries VI one. What' long faces the Wiganers must have pulled when Anderton failed to add the major point. Warriogton opened their season well by defeating Walton on their own ground, and when they meet Broughton to- day I hopb ttley will give a good account of themselves. I. am give* to understand that Broughton will meet them at the station with a four-in-hand Widnee should .ihave. opened., their season by. plaving Litherland at"Widnes, evirything wail' ready and there was a fine concourse of spectators on the ground, but they were doomed to disappointment, Litherland not turning up. It was rather too bad.

Runcorn defeated, rather easily, Manchester Gymnasium, but it was only what could have been expected, as it was only an easy fixture for them. Aspull journeyed to St. Helens, when scoring was the order of the day. At call of time the men from the colliery district were the vktors by two goals, four tries, to St. Helens three tries. Newton-le-Willows met Audenshaw at Newton, and the home team won a good game by one goal, three tries, to one goal scored by their opponents. Batley met Manningharn and won by two tries to nil. The Moss Side Football club have ceased to exist. The experiment of lower charges for admission was made at the opening match of the season on the ground of the holders of the National and Lancashire Challenge Cups, and though the reduction from 6d and is to 3d and 6d, with similar charges for admission to the stands, was not generally known, there was an improvement in the atten- nance. The first annual general meeting of this union was held at Liverpool on Saturday. There was a crowded attendance of delegate. Mr. C. A. Cronsbaw occupied the chair. The honorary secretary intimated that the Earl of Lathom, Lord Winmarleigh, Lord Claud J. Htmilten. rair B. A. Cross, Sir A. B. Walker, Colonel Ireland Blackburne, the Mayor of Liverpool, the Mayor of Wigan, and the Mayor of South- port bad kindly consented to become patrons. The honor- ary treasurer then read the balance sheet, which showed that £43 12e 8d stood to the credit of the union. The rules of the union were passed. It was proposed the challenge tro- phy take the form of a shield; bet the amendment, that it be a cup, was carried by a large majority. The meeting then proceeded to the passing of the cup rules. The follow- ing officers were elected for the ensuing season:—President, the Right Hon. the Earl of Lathom •, vice-presidents, Mr. C. A. Cronshaw (Wigan) and Mr. A. T. Kemble (Liverpool); honorary treasurer, Mr. C. C. Hall ; honorary secretary, Mr. F. T. Parry. The following clubs were elected to send delegates to act on the committee :—Wigan, Warrington, Widnes, Runcorn, Aspull, Vulcan, Bootle Wavertree, Wal- ton, Southport Olympic, Old Boys, and St Helens. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought a very agreeable meeting to a close.

THE ALLEGED ADULTERATED BUTTER. THE COUNTY ANALYST AT FAULT. . . . _

i Before Colonel IldeCorquodale, Mr. B. Houghton, Mr. T. J. Gillespie, add other magistrates, at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, John Howe. grocer, Go'borne, Bides- town, Wigan and Tyldesley, was summoned for an offence tinder the Adulteration Acts by selling an article as butter which was not of the nature and quality demanded by the purehaser. The defendant was represented by Mr. Walker, of Manchester, and when the case was called that gentleman said the case had been formerly before the court, but was ! adjourned for a sample of the butter to be sent to the ' authorities at Somerset House, London for analysis, as the analysis of the county analyst was Objected to. He (Mr. Walker) had received a letter from the Superintendent of Police, from whick be understood that the result of the in- quiry had been favourable to his client, as the sample was I genuine. Under those circumstances he applied for the de- li fendant's costs. He did not know if there was anyone there , to represent the Coney Analyst, but the analyst had either done his work negligently and brought a stigma upon , Mr. Howe and entailed expense upon him, or confused the I sample of butter and returned a sample which did not belong to them. But whatever the explanation was, it was quite clear that Mr. Howe was entirely exonerated from any I offence under the statute. It had not come as a surprise to , them that the butter was perfectly pure, but he did not wish ' to be understood to say that the County Analyst had any motive in making a false certificate. Probably a mistake , had been made, and it was a mistake for which his client , should not suffer.—After some Conversation, Superintendent Weir said he did not know whom the magistrates could I make responsible for the costs. He did not see that they ' could make Dr. Campbell Brown responsible, and they ' could not make him (Superintendent Weir) responsible.— Mr. Walker : Surely it is not urged upon the Bench that irre- sponsible persons bring prosecutions haphazard in the cunty If Dr. Campbell Brown had not made a mistaKe we should , not have been brought here.—The magistrates consulted about the matter, and in formally dismissing the summons lexpressed their pleasure that the butter was found to be I pure. It .was satisfactory to the Bench to know that, and they were quite willing to allow reasonable expenses.

Goop TEMPLMIY.—At the weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars, on Monday evening, Bro. Grgorge Clarke, P.W.C.T., presided, and there was a large attendance. After three candidates had been initiated, the evening's programme was "Auction night," and a considerable number of assorted articles given by various members were disposed of to the highest bidder. The proceeds were devoted to tie lodge funds. The duties of " auctioneer " were carried out by Bro. George Clarke. Tun DRUNKEN WOUAN.—In our last issue we stated that Emma Millington, wife of Thomas Millington, Collins' Green,fell into the canal near the Vulcan while in an intoxicated condition. She was summoned to appear for drunkenness at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, but her husbind appeared on her behalf.—ln reply to the Bench he stated that his wife was ill in bed. fie believed his wife was drunk on the date mentioned in the summons. It was the first time and be supposed it would be the last.—The Bench observed that it was a painful case, and inflicted a fine of 5s and costs.

Licarrsiwo Sussiog.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday Mr. Longton applied for a renewal and transfer of the off-license at present held by Joseph Broom, 306, Liverpool-road, Sankey. The application was made on behalf of John Wood, who had baught the license, but the gistrates at the anneal licensing session declined to grant the transfer en the ground that due notice had not been given to the police authorities. The applicant was now selling under a temporary authority.—Superintendent Jack- son said he had no objection to the transfer or renewal, and tte application was granted.

DICUID'S DINNEIZ—On Saturday the members of the Royal Oak Lodge, 918, Order of Druids, held their annual dinner at the Prince of Wales Hotel, E irlestown. Dinner over, the usual meeting took place, Mr. A. Schol. field, P.N.G.A., presiding; Mr. G. Williams, V.G.A , oc- cupying the vice-chair. Mr. J. Nash, secretary, responded to the toast of The Lodge," and remarked that its finan- cial position was sound and in every way strong, whilst the number of members was upwards of 80. He pointed out the advantages of such a society, and recommended all young men to join some society of the kind. its then pro- ceeded to present the host, Mr. R. Havdock, Riston-with-Glazebrook, Woolston, Poulton-with- ' Fearn head, Ho ugh ton-with-Arbury, Gol borne, Great Sankey. and Warrington. APPOINIMENT OP MR. IL J. DURMAN. - Many church people will be pleased to hear that Mr. Henry J. Darman, the late organist and choirmaster at St. John's Church, Earlestown, has secured a similar appointment at St. John's Parish Church, Liverpool. Mr. Darman ' was formerly organist and choirmaster at the last- named place of worship-a post he held for nearly six years-and in 1879 he accepted an appointment at St. John the Baptist's Church, Earlestowc. His services were highly appreciated in every respect and on every hand, until the unfortunate dispute of 18 months ago alienated from him the sympathies of the vicar, the Rev. T. R. Matthews and the latter ultimately discharged him. With Mr. 'Dar- man's dismissal nearly the whole congregation left the church. For the last twelve months Mr. Darman has bad no special' appointment, though he has officiated as choir- master in connection with the services in the Co.operative Hall, under the auspices of the Earlestown Gospel Mission. A vacancy having occurred at St. John's Church, Liverpool, Mr. Darman communicated with the vicar, the Rev. T. Whalley, and last week the latter gentleman wrote to Mr. Darman stating that he was very pleased to re-appoint him organist and choirmaster-the appointment to date from the let October. Mr. Darman, who some time ago was pre- sented with a handsome testimonial and other tokens of re- spect by the former congregation of St. John's Church, Earlestown leaves Earlestown with the well wishes of a large number of the inhabitants.
