div.head: DEPRESSION IN TRADE.-SHORT TIRE AT THE VULCAN.
div.p: DEPRESSION IN TRADE.-SHORT TIRE AT THE VULCAN.

The announcement that the workmen employed at the Vulcan Ironfoundry are being placed on short time will cause a sad feeling throughout the neighbourhood. This depression will be more severely felt following so closely as it does upon the partial stoppage of the Sankey &roar Works. A few weeks ago we announced that several hands were discharged from the Vulcan Foundry owing to the absence of any new orders, but it was not expected that the general body of workmen would suffer from the depres- sion. However, on Thursday morning a notice was posted on the board in the foundry yard stating that on and after that date there would be no more work in the foundry on Saturdays until further notice. This official announcement created considerable surprise among the large body of workmen.

div.head: FOOTPATH PROSECUTION. SUMMONSES DISMISSED.
div.p: THE FOOTPATH PROSECUTION. SUMMONSES DISMISSED.

The much-talked-of prosecution arising out of the al- leged obstruction .of a public footpath across the Mains, between Earlestown and Newton, took place at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, when there was a crowded court-room. t. keen interest was manifested in the case at its commencement, but its extreme length—a few minutes short of seven hours—drove many persons from the room. Since then its details have formed a topic of conversation throughout the district. As the majority of the local ma- gistrates are members of the Newton Improvement Commis- missioners, by whom the proceedings were instituted, they were prevented by law from adjudicating upon the case, mid consequently Captain Withingten and Mr. John Crosfleld, two county magistrates from Warrington, uninfluenced by local feeling, attended for deciding the case upon its merits. fhe prosecution was conducted by Mr. J. E. Worsley, soli- citor, Warrington, law clerk to the Commissioners, while the defendants, W. J. Legh. M.P., Lyme Hall, Cheshire, lord of the manor, the Earlestown Football Club (per James • Duxbury, secretary), and Margaret Clarke, tenant of the land, were represented by Mr. W. R. Ellis, of Wigan. The Clerk intimated that the information in the three cases—against Mr. Legh, Mr. Duxbury, and Margaret , Clarke—had been laid by Mr. Richard Brierley, clerk to the , Commissioners, and the offences alleged against them was ' that of erecting certain timber upon a public footpath there, being the Queen's highway, crossing land known as the Mains, and allowing the same to remain thereon after they were required to remove the same by the Surveyor of High- ways for the said parish. Mr. Worsley, in stating the case, said he appeared to stir- port an application by Mr. Richard Brierley, as the duly- constituted and authorised surveyor of the district under a section of the Highways Act, which afforded a convenient way of bringing a case of that kind before a tribunal such as that court. The facts were very short. There was an ancient footway leading across certain fields in Newton, and going from thence on to land celled the Mains, and this ancient footpath had been open and used by the public for a long time—a time immemorial—the evidence which be would bring before them coming down from a very early period up to the present. No one so far as they had beer, able to as- certain had been interrupted in using it, and it in fact formed part of a footpath at present very much used, and was the main road between Newton and Earlestown. He be- lieved some years ago, about 1870 or thereaboute-there was a notice board put up in the Mains near the fence stating that trespassers would be prosecuted. That board was not put on the footpath, and whether it meant that trespassers in the direction of the board or the adjoining land, or whether it was an intimation that it was to stop the road, he (Mr. Worsley) conld.not say. • All he could say was that not- withstanding the board they had evidence to prove that its effect was practically useless, and the road continued to be used. A right to the road had been established, the road was then a footway and a highway, any attempt to step it would then have been useless, and the land had con- tinued to be used until a short time ago, when the road was stopped up. Mr. Legh allowed the Earleetown Football Club to have the use of a part of the land, and they placed a wooden fence to enclose land for the purpose of playing football, and that fence at two points etc:lased the footpath. They had also fenced in a field be- longing to the farm through which the footpath approached the Mains the footpath being thereby obstructed and people were unable to pass along it. Some correspondence ensued between Mr. Brierley, who was the eomplainant on behalf of the Newton C immiss;onere, the custodians of the high- ways in the district, with the view of having the footpath re-opened, or with the view of having some arrangement made whereby the public could pass along the footpath, or they were quite willing to arrange the matter in any ami- cable manner so long as public rights were not interfered with. But those negotiations not being fruitful in re- sult, Mr. Brierley served notices upon the three defendants in pursuance of the section of the Highway Act, calling upon them to forthwith remove the obstructions, or it would be lawful for him to apply to the magistrates for an order to remove the obstruction or nuisance. These notices having been disregarded, the application was now made to the magistrates for an order directing Mr. Brierley to remove the obstruction. That was the application before their wor- ships, but going to the root of the matter the question would rest upon whether or not it was a highway, because if it was a highway they wanted the obstruction removing. and if it was not they did not want it removing. He alluded to the Act and a recent decision of Justice Blackburn, ac- cording to which no individual officer could himself decide whether a footpath was a highway or cot; and that was the reason why that case was brought before the Bench. He alluded to the evidence he proposed to call, and concluded by asking the Bench, if they were satisfied that the road was a highway belonging to the public, for an order to enable the surveyor to remove the timber from the road. and thus open it for the public use: . .

The Chairman (Captain Withington) asked how many witnesses it was proposed to call, and said he did net think it would be necessary to call eight or ten witnesses when the same facts as to right of way might be proved by two or three.—Mr. Worsli.y replied that that was so, and asked the Bench to state when they felt that he had given suffi- cient proof on that point. Richard Brierley was then called. Ile said he was the clerk and surveyor to the Newton Improvement Commis- sioners—a post he had occupied since 1865. He was ac- quainted with the road hi question, and produced a plan of it. The plan showed Tanhouse Farm, through which the footpath passed. to the railway arch in the Mesnes. He also produced the ordnance survey map.—Mr. Ellis objected to this map,. urging that it was not evidence. There was no statute which made it evidence, and it was on the level of other piano. was important to that case to know what waar the state of things as far back as possible. I Keep your temper, it is more valuable to you than to any- body else. "Should auld acquaintance be forgot P"—Not if they have money. Left to her own reflections—A good-looking lass in a room full of looking-glasses. A polite way of dunning a delinquent debtor is to send him a bunch of forget-me-nots. Is there a word in the English language which contains all the vowels P—Unquestionably. What man most invariably have his glass before he can do his work satisfactorily ?—A glazier. Life's experience as described by an unsuccessful man— Fortune feeds soup to most men with a fork. There are only 128,000 hairs on the average human head, and no wonder that some husbands complain over losing a handful.
ton being notified that she was divorced from her hus- band, a Chicago lady said to a friend that she "felt quite unmanned.'

"Do they Miss me at borne ?" "Why do you ask me such a silly question? Don't you know, dear, it's always plain Jane at home ?" The heading of an editorial in the New York Sun was intended to read "The Revised Bible," but the types made it "The Ruined Bible." An Irishman contentedly laid his bead upon a large stone jar for a pillow, and replied to one who inquired if it was not rather hard, "Not at all, my jewel, for I have stuffed it with hay." BOBBY'S EXPLLEATION.—Mamma, dining out: It isn't polite, Bobby, to smack your lips when eating. You never do that at home.—Bobby: 'Cause we never have anything worth smacking over! "Well, my son' what did the minister preach about this morning ?" inquired a fond parent of his 9-year old son, on the latter's return from church. "He preached about an hour and a half, and I'm as hungry as a bear," was the reply; "is dinner ready ?" DOMESTIC CONFIDENCE.—Mrs. Briggs: Victor Hugo's family have refused to let his brain be examined.—Mr. Briggs: They were right. I shouldn't allow any one to ex- amine my brain.—Mrs. Briggs: I don't think you will ever , be troubled with any one asking you to do so, my dear. ' In summing up a case, Rufus Choate was so severe on the ' opposing lawyer that the latter jumped up and exclaimed, "I'd like to know if the learned counsel thinks lam a fool!" Choate reflected a moment, and then quietly said, "My friend wants to know if I think he is a fool. In response to that interrogatory, I can only say that I am not prepared to I deny it!" A Texas cattle-man married a refined young lady be- longing to the best society of Dallas. A friend, meeting him shortly after his marriage, congratulated him on his happy fortune. "It's all right; but I had to make sacri- fices," replied the newly-made husband, shaking his heal. "What sacrifices?" "I had to give up going to bed with my boots and spurs on when I. came home tired." A Scotch farmer was leading a calf by a halter across a bridge; but on approaching the rise of the bridge the creature refused to move farther. The farmer, seeing the rural postman coming towards him, said to him, "Mister Postman, wad ye jist gie a blew o' yer horn ahint the calf and mak' it come on ?" The postman gave a shrill blast, and with one bound the animal cleared the parapet of the bridge, and fell into the running stream beneath. The fumer first looked at the postman, and then exclaimed, "Man, you stupid ass, that was far owre big a blast for a calf !" . . .

—::What sort of a watch is this?" asked a gentleman, picking up a curious old timepiece in a shop in the neigh- bourhood of Wardour-street. "That," replied the dealer, 1" is a real curiosity. It is a watch that belonged to Alex- ander the Great when he died on the barren island of St. Helena." "The deuce it is! Why, man alive, in the days of Alexander the Great there were no such things as watches !" "That's just what makes it such a rdrity." "And Alexander the Great didn't die in St. Helena." "He didn't —eh? Well, that makes it a still greater curiosity !"—and, taking up the rare relic, the dealer locked it up in his bur- glar-proof safe. ANSWERING STRAIGIIT.—Fond pipe, proudly displaying the accomplishments of his six-yedr old boy to the visiting clergyman: "Now, Tommy,, tell the gentleman what yon would like to be when you grow up to be a great big man." Tommy, pointing to the visitor: "I'd like to be a minister like him." Visiting clergyman, greatly gratified: "Oh, my young friend, you would like to be a clergyman like me, would you? Tell me, why would you like to be a clergy- man like me." Tommy promptly: "Cause I heard pa say yesterday that you had the easiest job of any man he knew —nothing to do but talk an hour every Sunday, live free on the members of the congregation, and be worshipped like a little tin god on wheels by all the women in the parish." Tableau! FORGOT THE TEL-rm.—lt was at a local restaurant. He had ordered a beefsteak. He waited. The waiter did not wait. He came and went and came and went, but the beef- steak did not arrive. The guest called the meteoric indi- vidual. " Have the cows coins home yet ?" he asked. The waiter gave a feeble in:Ole—waiters are very hard to reach with sarcasm. "It'll be here in a minute, sir, all right." The Mock kept going on the same. He stopped him again. " Tell the cook I'll take that part of it that is done. lam not in a hurry, but my wife will never believe this as an excuse for my staying out all night." At length the beef- steak was brought. He began on it. It was like leather. Once again he gently called the waiter. "I say, are you sure you have forgotten nothing ?" "No, sir; I've brought you everything—a knife, a fork, two spoons, a plate— no, sir." "Don't you provide a net of teeth with the beef- steak ?" _ .

The late General Grant was called the "American Sphinx" and " Ulysses the Silent," and was popularly, supposed to move about with sealed lips. When travelling through New England during the summer after the close of the civil war, It was soon seen that stories of his reticence had preceded him. The trip was the first of those grand ovations with which he was always greeted by the people through whose communities he travelled. The train stopped for a few minutes at a small town in Maine, and the people, as usual, took the opportunity of extending a greeting and delivering their words of welcome. As the general stood in the door- way of the last car, a tall gaunt-looking woman elbowed her way through the crowd till she got near the platform. Here she stopped and put on a pair of spectacles with glasses in them that looked about as big as the lenses in large telescopes, and, taking a good look at the general, said, gasping for breath as she spoke, "Well, I've come down h'yere a-runnin' right on the clean jump, nigh onto tew mile, just to git a look at the man that lets the women do all the talkin'."

This story cornea from the "Peak Countree." The great cavern at Castleton attracts large numbers of tourists every year, and now and then notabilities visit the place. A visitor somewhat shabbily dressed presented himself before the guide, an official employed by the Duke of Devonshire, and asked what it would cost to see the sights. "Seven shillings," was the man's reply. "It seems a lot of money," said the inquirer. But the guide, with a glance at the man's garments, deigned no answer. The visitor, however, resolved to go in. Emerging into the light of day again, he entered his name in the visitors' book, and said, "There's seven shillings for your master and something for yourself." The something was a sovereign. The guide, staggered by the magnitude of the gratuity, hastily scanned the visitors' book, and found the signature of a well-known millionaire duke. He looked the surprise he felt. "You didn't expect that, did you ?" drolly asked the Duke. "No, your Grace, I did not," said the guide, honestly. "And you thought, now, I was scarcely good for the seven shillings?" persisted the Duke. The thought, from the guide's frank admission, certainly had crossed his mind. "Well," said his Grace, " never in future judge a man by the coat he wears."

CHAMBERLAIN AND THE BANKRUPTCY ACT.—Mr. Chamberlain was recently written to by a rentlemAn at Bournemouth, who sent the right hon. gentleman some local bankruptcy statistics reflecting adversely upon the new Act. Mr. Chamberlain replied that ft was imposs ble to form a judgment on individual cases without a know- ledge of all the circumstances. No legislation could secure to the creditors in all cases 20s in the pound ; but the re- sults of the Act has far exceeded the most sanguine expec- tations of its promoters. THE LONDON SOCIALISTS AND THE POLICE.--II is esti- mated that about 30,000 people marched on Sunday morn- ing from Stepney Ureen to Dod-street, and subsequently to the West India Dock gate, as a protest against the interfer- ence of the authorities with the meetings held at those places by Socialist lecturers on previous Sundays. No at- tempt was made by the police to interfere with the holding of meetings. A communication had been received from the Chief Commissioner r f Police intimating that the police had nothing to do with the views of the Socialists, hut only to see that they caused no obstruction of traffic. On the motion of Dr. Aveling, a resolution was adopted protesting against the arbitrary action of the police is endeavouring to suppress the right of open-air meeting, demanding equality of treatment for the exponents of all opinions. and urging that the police should be prosecuted for perjury in cartain g immediatelyi s ate and that John E. Williams, now in magistrate, cases, that the attention Of the Home Secretary should be called to the conduct of Mr. Sparuinsodne,rssh, tohuu e released. ELECTRIC HOUSE BELLS

CIiIIACH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—The opening meeting of the season took place on Monday even- ing, at the Houghton-street schools. which were crowded. The Vicar, the Rev. H. A. Macnaghtee, occupied the chair. The Vicar, after making a few remarks on the advantages of temperance, introduced ladies and gentlemen, who kindly contributed to the enjoyment of the evening by a programme of songs. readingsAc ,for which credit is largely due to Mr. Halsall, the indefatigable secretary. CONCERT AT THE NBP7 ASSEMBLY HALL.—The first of a series of miscellaneous concerts took place in this hall on Tuesday evening. arid was of a specially attractive charac- ter. The hall. which is the largest and best adapted in the town, was well filled, and high appreciation was shown by almost every item being encored. The following was the programme :—Overture (piano) Miss Quick; song "The waves are bearing us home," Madame Wiseman; song "The sailor's grave," by Mr. Sydney; followed by "The better land," Miss Nora Powell, who on being recalled gave "Somebody." Miss Kate Parry sang "To the woods," and Mr. Richardson for his " Wolf " was recalled and gave " The diver." Miss A. Gorse " Lullaby," encored ' • a glee "Lovely night" by a chorus of thirty voices, the chorus also sung " Where art thou beam of light." Miss Powell then gave a song in Welsh " A tear on my mother's grave," for which she was doubly recalled, and gave "The three young maids of Leigh," and another in Welsh, "The mother and babe"; duet, by Messrs. Richardson and Syd- ney, who also gave " Larboard watch." Miss Gorse sang "The minstrel boy," and Madame Wiseman " Tell him I love him so," and repeated the last verse. Mr. J. T. Syd- ney for his "Anchor's weighed," anewered a recall by " Kathleen." Miss Parry sang " Strangers yet " and "In the gloaming"; Mr. Richardson sang" Ihe skipper" and "The village blacksmith"; Miss Dora Powell '4 When the heart is young" (recalled) and the glee "Oh I. the flowery month of June," and the national anthem brought a very successful entertainment to a close. Mr. W. Berry ably acted as conductor, and Miss Quick as accom- panist. PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday at the Work- house, Whiston, near Prescot. Mr. J. Leatherbarrow pre- sided, and amongst those present, was Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P. (ex-officio). The master of the house (Mr. Hale) re- ported that there were 406 inmates, against 401 last week and 418 in the corresponding week of last year; vagrants relieved 49, corresponding week last year 72. The Rev. J. K. Sylvester, vicar of Roby, had sent a present of fruit for the sick inmates; and Mr. Richard Lord, of Huyton, had sent them a parcel of books. A vote of thanks was tendered to both gentlemen.—A letter was read from the Local Gov- ernment Board (who had agreed to the expenditure of a sum not exceeding £lO each in respect of sending two children to Canada), asking if they had arranged for any responsible person to take charge of them other than the steward and stewardess of the vessel. —The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) stated that the brother of the children was in the service of the Canadian Government at I Ottawa, and he had promised to meet them. The subject then dropped.—Mr. Sadler (Widnes) moved that Mr. Wm. Cooper, surgeon, be re-appointed medical officer of the Wid- nes Lower District, at a salary of £7O per annum.—The Rev. Father Finegan (Widnes) seconded the motion, which was carried.—Mr. Hartley stated that he had received an official intimation that Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., of Widnes, intended, at the Quarter Sessions, on the 3rd of November, to appeal against the present rating of their ex- tensive chemical works. That would make it necessary for him to shortly call a special Guardians' meeting for the purpose of obtaining their consent or refueal to fight such appeal.---A letter was read from sir. William Longton, of Eccleston Grange, intimating that in future the price of water supplied to the house would be reduced from 10d to , 9d per 1,000 gallons.—The L,ic al Government Board wrote sanctioning the contracts for vaccination entered into by ' the Board with Dr. Chisholm, of Woolton, and Dr. Casey, of Sutton.

MENT INQUIRY. Major-General A. de C. Scott, Royal Engineers, one of the inspectors of the Local Government Bo ird, held a public inquiry at the Prescot Union Workhouse, on Tuesday noon. in reference to an application by the Board of Guardians to borrow £BOO, the estimated cost of sinking a well on the Workhouse premises. There were present Councillor W. Longton, who at present supplies the Workhouse with water; Mr. E. T. Driffield, secretary to the Rainhill Gas and Water Company; Mr. H. W. Collins, solicitor; Mr. J. Leatherbarrow (chairman of the Board of Guardians), Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk), several Gus.rdiane, and Messrs. Mac- kenzie, Whitfield, dm. In asking the clerk to state the circumstances of the application, the Inspector remarked that an opinion had been pronounced to the effect that it was better for the Guardians to apply to the Liverpool Cor- poration in the first instance, then in the second niece to the St. Helens Corporation, and finally that they should negotiate with Mr. Longton, rather than sink a well of their own.—Mr. Hartley said the question arose in consequence of the attention of the Guardians being drawn to the danger arising in the event of a fire breaking out at the Workhouse. The attention of the Guardians wag drawn to the matter by means of a circular letter from the Local Government Board. The Guardians considered the letter and were anxious to make provision for a better supply of water to the work- house premises. They had been supplied for some years by Mr. Longton, but they attempted to negotiate with the St. Helene Corporation and also the Liverpool Corporation for a supply of water as suggested by Sir Robert Rawlinson. The Liverpool Corporation could not supply them at less than Od. per 1,000 gallons and the St. Helens Corporation abso- lutely refused to supply the water. Many of the Guardians were under the impression that they had a supply of water I on their own premises, which they might obtain by sinking! a well, and they called in Mr. Timmins, a man of experi- ence from Runcorn, who made a borehole and submitted an , estimate for what he would sink a well for. This amounted to .£7OO. The Guardians then instructed him (the clerk) by a, resolution to apply to the Local Government Board for their sanction to borrow the money. The Present Rate- , payers Association objected to this in the shape of a memo- , rial, and the Local Government Board asked for the observe. ' tions of the Guardians as to their ideas. XetttrO to the editor. THE ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRADE DEPRESSION. Sir,—l beg to enclose copy of a letter received from the Secretary to the "Royal Commission on the depression in trade and industry." If you will kindly give the same pub- licity in your valuable paper I think farmers' associations and farmers generally will be glad of the opportunity of placing facts regarding farming interests before the Royal Commission.-. 4 am, &c., HENRY T. STELFOX, Hon. Sec. Warrington Farmers' Club, Lymm, 30th September, 1885. [corr] The Treasury, 25th September, 1885. Sir,—ln reply to your letter of the 25th inst., I beg to in- form you that the Royal Commission on depression of trade will be ready toreceive and consider any representation which your committee may desire to make on subjects falling within the scope of this enquiry. No decision has yet been arrived at as to the order in which witnesses will be heard, or In what manner evidence will be taken, and I am therefore unable to give you any information on this point.—Very faithfully yours, GEO. H. MURRAY. ,TON.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The diffieuly in Eastern Europe is still dragging -on, and the general opinion continues to anticipate a peaceful conclusion. That there is nothing urgent in the case appears to be proved by the remarkably leisurely manner in which Her Majesty's Ministers advance to a Cabinet Council. It was reported that this was to have been held last Tuesday, and Lord Salisbury's return to Hatfield on Saturday night seemed to indicate preparation for the meeting. -Lord Randolph Churchill also began to move south- ward, but the Council was postponed for a week, and is now fixed for Tuesday next. One thing is unanimously agreed with respect to the settlement -of the question. Everyone, perforce including Lord Salisbury, admits that the handiwork of Lord Beaconsfield at the Berlin Conference, being undone, cannot be repaired. What is called the status gra ante cannot be brought about. But wherein the danger lies is in the possibility of an extension of the principle of nationalities, which may urge the Porte in desperation to take up arms. The Berlin Treaty settled a good deal besides the situation of Eastern Roumelia. It left Macedonia a Turkish province, and Old Servia was separated from the Xingdom marked out for the Serb. If Eastern Roumelia is permitted to flout the august decrees of the Berlin Treaty, why should Greece and Serie* remain quiescent? That is an inquiry the Greeks :and the Servians are plainly putting to themselves and Europe. Servia is arming. to the teeth; the Macedomans are prepared to rise and fling them- selves into the arms of Greece. In such case will Turkey remain quiescent, and will the Great Powers look on without protest? That is "The Eastern Question" at the moment, and is much more urgent than the condition of Eastern Roumelia, which is, in fact, practically settled. The home election campaign is going forward without, as yet, any signs of absorbing excitement on the part of the public. Mr. Gladstone's mani- festo has struck the keynote cif the battle cry, and it is not very exciting. Doubtless, as the fateful day draws nearer, the excitement will grow. It was understood in the House of Commons that Mr. O'Donnell had a brother in the Queen's service in India who was accustomed to rake up all kinds of little scandals and send them to the member for Dungarvon, who immediately asked a question upon the matter, or, not infrequently, attempted to raise a debate on going into Committee. But the distant ports of the earth did not absorb Mr. O'Don- nell's attention. 1 remember very well in the ses- sion of 1878 how he amazed a House prepared almost for anything by plunging into a discussion on the vaccination question. For nearly an hour he discussed lymph and cognate matters, as if he had spent his early years in a dispensary. It is to his credit that he never got on with Mr. Parnell. If a man is ready to brush Mr. Parnell's boots, hand him his hat and keep an eye on his carte, he may be as safe in his seat as Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Mr. Herring- ton, or the Redmond brothers. To that Mr. O'Donnell would never stoop. He even presumed openly to criticise Mr. Parnell's policy, and has for a long time been regarded as a lost man. It is charaee teristic of him that now he is going he turns and gives Mr. Parnell a vicious kick. A man of unques- tioned ability, hemight have been expected to make his mark in the House of Commons. So he did. But it was an unpleasant one, and, somehow or other, he came to achieve the reputation of being the most generally disliked man in the House. Sir Charles Dilke is to be married on Saturday, .and immediately after will re-appear on the politi- cal stage. His hoseymoon here will be short, but • after his speech at Halifax he proposes to go to the south of France where he has a charming house, and where he likes to live, the world forgetting, by the world forgot. -The house overlooks the Med- iterranean and is a veritable flower garden. Sir Charles Dilke is fond of flowers in quite another way than Mr. Chamberlain. I have heard the lat- ter say that he does not care for roses. In fact his -whole passion is concentrated upon the culture of orchids. Orchids are the most expensive and the most difficult flower to grow, and it is the pleasure of overcoming the difficulty rather than from any true love of flowers that Mr. Chamberlain grows or- chids. He certainly has achieved a remarkable triunaph in the field he elected-to work in. Ido not believe that anyone in England has such a collec- tion as he. His house in London is always supplied . with rare orchids, and his dinner-table display is unique. But Sir Charles Nike is content with flowers of less artificial growth, and his cottage at Cape Brun is a wilderness of color and perfume. He used to have indoors a great collection of Chinese pottery, and also some rare porcelain. I fancy the passion must have faded, for his house in Sloane- street does pot shine in this respect. This, as most people know, is Sir Charles Dilke's second marriage. His first wife was a charming woman, one of the lightest-hearted, merriest lathes I ever met. She took a strong interest in politics, and *vas thoroughly at one with her husband when he made his memorable speech in the House of Commons on the subject of the Civil List. Sir Charles was profoundly moved at her death, and for some time secluded himself from the world. Had she lived it is probable her • influence would have kept him more strictly to that wove in which he once worked with Mr. Auberon Herbert, now a philosophical Tory. Lady Dilke died at the birth of her only child. It affords some indication of her strength of mind that viewing the possibility of death she exacted from her husband a promise that she should not be buried in the or- dinary fashion. In obedience to this injunction, the bereaved husband carried the body to Germany, -where it was cremated. The publication of the list of persons who have benefited by pensions from the civil list is always a revelation. There is a sum of £1,200 a year set apart for the benefaction of persons who have done some conspicuous public service, or for their survi- ving relatives. The present year's allottment has been large.,4l"l swallowed up in connection with the Soudan, which swallowed up so Much else. The re- latices of Colonel Stewart received an appreciable proportion of the whole sum, whilst Mr. Pewee mother and lister each obtained a small annuity,

GREENALLISM V. DISSENT AT WAL'e. Sir,—Some few years ago Sir Gilbert Greenell had pre- mises built at Walton for the purpotes of a day school. The some premises are also used as the Church Sunday School of the village. It seems that there is just an odd Dissenter in the neighbourhood, who lives on the border of Walton, but within the township of Acton Grange. This man is. a Wesley,n, and his house is within a stone's throw of the school. For some time past one of this man's children, a girl of nine year of age, has been attending the day school in question, and more than one effort has been made to In- due her ti come regularly to the Sunday School also. Her father, being a Wesleyan, has for conscientious reasons pre- ferred to send ha children to the Wesleyan Sunday School at Moore. However, this difi not suit "the powers that be," and last Monday but one Lady Greenall herself informed this little girl that unless fihe would agree to come to the Sunday School she must not come any more to the day school. Dry school accommodation itS a scarce article in the neigh- bourhood, and as a ccnsequence of Lidy Greenoll's ultimo- ' turn this child has now to walk to a school fully a mile further away from her home than was previously the case. This is no bogus story—the name of the girl's father is Ver- non, and he has for many years past been employed at the signal box at Welton Junction. Incidents of this kind • speak in trumpet tones as to the real character of pure and . unadulterated Greenallism.—Yours,
A VOTER.

PUBLIC BATHS FOR EARLESTOWN. Sir,—ln your paper of a week ago I saw a paragraph in reference to a swimming bath for Earlestown. I and a good many more people would like to see such a healthy and necessary adjunct to cleanliness and civilisation in our midst, but as far as I can understand from inquiries I have made I believe the obstacle in the way is the price which would be charged for the water. People outside the district, and in fact, a large proportion of the people inside the town are not aware that we are dependent on the great London and North-Western Railway Company fer a proper supply of the indispensable water. The directors seem to be aware of this, and consequently they know how to apply their knowledge to their own advantage. To them it is a matter of so much per cent, on their dividends—the wants and convenience of the public are nothing for the shareholders and directors to consider. Those who have taken the ques- tion in hand and are bringing it in some tangible shape be- fore their fellow townsmen are deserving of every support and encouragement. I for one rejoice to see the start that has been made. It is not one moment too soon; but I trust the great railway company will not smother the baths by throwing " cold water" on its promoters. Surely they can give it a little support, and I hope our local Improvement Commissioners will assist in the steps being taken to secure that end. This wise body of men spend our money in unfortunate and exoensive litigation with the Warrington Beard of Guar• dians, and undertake the defence of bogus rights of the pub- lic concerning mythical footpaths. A great responsibility rests upon them in regard to the health and cleanliness of the district. We have`lately had scarlet fever and measles rife in our midst, and I would ask anyone who considers the question, is it likely that those diseases would have !Run half as bad as they were if we had had a good swim- ming bath in our midst ? Unhesitatingly I answer no. 'Chore are sins of omission as well as of commission, and if our Improvement Commissioners belie their name and become Non-improvement Commissioners by de- clining to support the movement for securing :public baths, they will have committed a sin against those who have placed them in power, and in Case of an outbreak of infec- tious disease, a great wrong, if not a crime, will be laid at their door. If they withhold their official support I hold they will be false to their duties, false to those who have entrusted them with the interests of the neighbourhood, and they will be acting contrary to the injunction with which we are all so familiar, "CLEANLINESS IS NEXT TO GODLINESS." Earlestown, 24th September, 1885.

div.p: • MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

_ Sir,—ln your last issue you favoured me by the inser- tion of my letter "A.8.C," Would you allow me to add that on a reconsideration of it, I am more convinced than ever that the objects of the Ship Canal would be greatly promoted by following out the proposal made, vic.:—That a Ship Canal Syndicate Company, Limited, should be 'formed and be registered under the Company's Act as a company without capital, its members' liability to be limi- ted to £5O, and the qualifications of its directors to be the holding of 100 and that of the members to ten registered shares in the Ship Canal Com- pany. I would suggest and propose that Mr, Adamson and

seven of the largest subscribers to the csnal fund should take it 111), and in concert with Mr. Pember, Q.C., form ar- ticles of association, and then invite all the gentlemen who have gone to London, and have given their evidence before each of the six Parliamentary Committees during the last three sessions of Parliament, to co-operate with them, and to register themselves as a company under this Act, or any other part of it, and also to invite the co-operation of all the other six thousand present subscribers for shares to be- come members of it, and also all future ones. I have little doubt in my mind, but that after Saturday's demonstration in Manchester, and the great public meeting to be held in the Free Trade Hall there on Monday next, the sth inst. when Mr.Pe mber, Q.C., will address the meeting, that this sekeme, or something better, would, if fairly intro- duced to the public, command increased support. The whole affair, If carefully examined, will be found extremely simple, and in practice be found very workable, especially as a body of gentlemen of the highest commercial character would have the conducting of it, besides which it is well known to be an undertaking which promises the most successful results of any that has hitherto been offered in the North of Eng- land. It has already secured the support not only of the most eminent financial authorities, but of great and influen- tial manufacturing and commercial bodies in the coun- ties of Lancashire, Cheshire, and Yorkshire, together with the wealthy and powerful Corporations of Manchester, Sal- ford, Warrington, and others, with their mighty manufac- turing population and vast industrial producing power, and it is believed by sound authorities " that it will soon pay eight per cent on their money, and more before bang." The industrial classes, comprising nearly all the co-operative as- sociations, a list of which appears, numbering 24 societies, in a petition to the Mayors of Manchester and Salford, in to-day's Manchester Guardian and other papers—all these, and very many other societies, are taking a wonderful amount of interest in this undertaking, and have in many instances subscribed largely to it. If the proposed Ship Canal Syndicate, Limited, were formed, and the deed or articles of association with all needful saving clauses were introduced, and sanctioned by Mr. Pember, Q.C., it would take rank as perhaps the most secure and powerful financial association existing, obtaining an amount of credit and influence hitherto unknown in these parts, and quite equal to that of the best banking establish- ments, and it would he enabled to treat with them on equal or the best financial terms. There would be nothing in the background about it, no fees, solativ.ms, promotion ex- penses, &c, but all would be plain and straightfor- ward. If the shares of the Manchester Ship Canal Company were wbat is called" placed " on the market, in London, Paris, America, &c.. &c., more than double the number re- quired would be applied for, and they would immediately be at a premium. But this sort of thing is not what the great body of the shareholders here approve of, and I think they agree with Mr. Adamson, that "there is no need for it," but that all the money wanted is to be found In these counties, and that "it will be speedily subscribed ;" also " that every man with a pound in his pocket will be enabled to take a share, and that the great body of the in- dustrial classes ought to have their fair share in the pros- perity of the Ship Canal." This. I thiek, would be se- cured to the shareholders by the propoeed syndicate, as it would protect the shares from adverse influence, provide a fair market for them, and also for those of any other com- panies that may be formed in connection with the Ship Canal if sanctioned and approved of by its directors.—l am, sir, yours, rfac., A.B.C.

CHRIST Council, Ciwrx.—The annual thanksgiv- ing services for the ingathering of the harvest were held on Sunday. The church having only recently been painted and decorated, the decorations for the festival this year were of a plain but artistic charac- ter. The Rector preached in the morning. The preacher in the afternoon was tche Rev. Herbert Monks, vicar of St. Peter's, Newton-le-Willows, who took for his text the 26th and three following verses of the 4th chapter of St. Mark. The choir rendered the musical part of the services in a creditable manner, under the conductorship of Mr. Ball, the organist and choirmaster, who presided at the organ with his usual ability. The collections, which were in aid of the church expenses, amounted to £l2. LuxuaLtsr AND SILKY HAIL—Mrs. S. A. It is rumoured that Russia proposes to dethroue Prioce

Alexander of B dgaria. _ A sum of VW has been subscrilsed towards Mr. Joseph Arch's election expenses fund. Mr. Ruskin has had a relapse, and the state of his health causes great anxiety to his friends. The principal of Old Bala Congregational College has re- ceived a letter from Mr. Samuel Morley, M.P., promising £1,500 towards the removal of the college to Bangor. A Lloyd's telegram states that .the German barque British Merchant, from Hull to Dantxic, with coal, is ashore in a bad position. Seven of the crew have been
drowned. The Rev. Owen King, curate of Llantarnam, has announced to his congregation that he has decided to quit the Established Church and seek admission to the Church

of Rome. A meeting of the Employers' Association is to be held at the Oldham Town Hall on Tuesday next, to consider the proposal of the operatives to accept an unconditional re- daction of 5 per cent. It has been notified from the offices of the Royal Arsenal that a reduction is about to be made in the wages of up- wards of a thousand men employed in the Government Laboratory Department at Woolwich. THE BRIGANTINE LATANTA pot into Queenstown on Fri- day for the purpose of landing Captain McDoughall and 13 men of the barque Sofala, of London, which she fell in with at noon on Thursday in a sinking condition about 95 miles S.S.W. of the Fastnet. THE EASTERN CRlsis.—Lord Salisbury arrived at the Foreign Office from Hatfield on Friday afternoon, and had a prolonged interview with Count Munster, the German ' Ambassador. Later in the afternoon M. Waddington, the I French Ambassador, called at the Foreign Office, and con- ferred with his lordship. LORD RANDOLPH CmoRcHILL having concluded his visit to Mr. Holmes. Attorney-General for Ireland, at Monkstown House, near Kingstown, is the guest of the Lord-Lieuten- ant at the Viceregal Lodge, Phcenix Park. To-day (Saturday) his lordship will leave Dublin for Howth, on a visit to Lord Justice Fitzgibbon. MR. O'CONNOR roseate, M.P., in a letter he ha addressed to the electors of the Kennington Division of Lambeth, states that he is strongly opposed to the doctrine of perpetual hatred between England and Ireland, and that he believes the true solution of the Irish difficulty is to be found in Mr. Gladstone's manifesto. COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN WALES.—AG alarming explo- sion occurred on Thursday afternoon, at Elliot Pit, New Tredegar, caused by the fall of the roof liberating a large quantity of gas which became ignited. Two horses were killed and twelve men injured. Seven of the men were , badly burned. The pit had only recently been sunk, and I amongst the injured is Mr. William Williams, by wham the pit was sunk. Great damage was done by the explosion to , the workings. MR CHAMBERLAIN AY BHADFORD.—Mr. Chamberlain , was entertained on Friday morning at breakfast by the members of the Bradford Liberal Club. Among those pre- sent were Mr. Hoffmann, the chairman, Mr. Lyulph Stanley, M.P., Mr. Barran, M.P., Mr. Wills, M.P., and Mr. Theo. Fry, M.P. A welcome having been given to the right hon. Igentleman. Mr. Chamberlain, who was loudly cheered, [thanked the members for the hospitality which had been offered to him. HORRIBLE MURDER BY A MOTHER.—At the Greenwich Police Court, on Friday, Martha Howard, twenty-seven years of age, a married woman of Forest-hill, was re- manded, charged with the wilful murder of her female child, aged five months, by striking it with a chopper. The police were called to the house occupied by the prisoner and her husband this morning, when the prisoner said "I have kil- led my child ; I want to be hanged." She had been pre- viously discovered with the child on her lap, with the bead altnost severed from its body.

EGYET.—DERVISLIBS ADVANCING. CAIRO, FRIDAY.—An official telegram announces that the Dervishes are advancing. It is reported that a force of one thousand has arrived at Hafir, eighty miles distant from the farthest station of the British troops. THE CHOLERA. The official cholera bulletin issued on Friday morning reports 490 cases and 170 deaths la Spain on Thursday. A Rome correspondent says that an outbreak of cholera has taken place at Ferrara, where nine persons have been attacked. One hundred and sixty-five:fresh:cases have oc- curred at Palermo. THE RISING IN THE EAST. VIENNA, FRIDAY Arrsarroox.—The Talleyenzeine Zeitung states that the War Office have asked the Burgomaster of Pesth for an estimate of the number of soldiers the town could billet. COFENRAGEN, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.— The Bulgarian deputation to-day had an interview with M. de Giers. ATHENS, FRIDAY EVENING.--Military preparations are actively continued.

WORE IN COMMITTEE. The Highway and Sanitary Committee appointed Mr. Norman chairman. It was recommended that Mr John Dobson's tender for rebuilding the boundary wall in Canon. street for the sum, for £lO he accepted. Plans of three cottages to be erected in Taylor's-road, for Mr. S. Taylor ; small noble to be erected at rear of shop in High-street, for Mr. W. Blythe ; additions to stable and hay loft at rear of house in Moughland-lane for Mr. P. Speakman ; alteration of house in Irwell-lane, for Mr. W. Kirkman, were approved. Mr. Lake was appointed chairman of the. Canal Boats and Hospital Committee ; Mr. Dobson chairman of General Purposes Committee ; Mr. Fisher chairman of Finance Committee ; Mr. Pritchard chairman of Parliamentary and Legal Committee ; and Mr. Lightburn chairman of Health Committee. The Finance Committee reported that daring the past month the treasurer bad received general district rate £514 6s id. market rents and tolls £27 14s 10d, slaughter houses £1 13s 6d, total £543 14s sd. Accounts amounting to £242 17s 4d were passed for payment. It was recommended that the wages of the caretaker of the Town Hall be increased from 103 to 1.6 s per week. These minutes were passed. THE LAW CLERK'S POSITION.—LIVELY DISCUSSION. The Finance Committee recommended "that Mr. W. H. Linaker be requested to resign his appointment as law clerk to the Board." Mr. Fisher moved, and Mr. Dobson seconded, the confir- mation of the minute. Mr. Imison moved that the recommendation relating to the law clerk be omitted. He was very glad that the recom- mendation was at last to be discussed in an open, manly, and English fashion. At the two meetings held previously, be had endeavoured to show, but unsuoceesfully, that in the first place, assuming for the sake of argument that Mr. Linaker had been guilty of the charges which had been pre- ferred against him, the punishment that it was desired to inflict upon him was out of all proportion to the character of his offence. In the second place, as there was an action pending— The Chairman said he could not allow Mr. Lnison to discuss the private concerns of any member, and suggested that he should get a seconder to his amendment. Mr. Lake: Surely, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Imison is entitled to proceed with his arguments before he asks for his secon- der. I think there is A good deal in what he says, that his arguments may obtain a seconder. The Chairman : Very well. Mr. Imison : However just your line of conduct may be, as there is an action pending-- The Chairman: We must not go into any action. After further contention, Mr. liaison went on to review the proceedings in committee, and went on to say that while it is their duty, Rs the chairman said the other day, that they should defend their colleagues against charges from their servants, it was equally their duty to defend their servants against malicious action on the part of members of the Board. (Hear, hear, from Mr. Meadowcroft.) The position of a public servant would become such a one that no hie:- spirited, high-minded man would take it if he felt that the tenure of his office depended on the goodwill of the indi- vidual members of the Board he served. And, therefore, it was their duty to protect him against any adverse influences on the part of two or three members. He concluded : If you (the chairman) are able to show that the public have suffered, and that Mr. Linaker as failed in any of the duties he owes to them, it would be a good reason for the Board to ask him to resign ; but when it is a purely private matter, relating to what Mr. Linaker has said against one or two members, then I say it is an insufficient reason, and I think all the members of the Board may fairly say that it is a case for forgiveness on all sides. Mr. Grica said he would second the amendment, for the special reason that at the meeting of the committee the other day some members voted contrary to their intention. This fact had been freely expressed in the town. After a short conversation, Mr. unison asked to be per- mitted to amend his proposition to adjourn consideration of the matter for two months until the trial of the action brought by Mr. Linaker against the chairman had been de- cided. Be nine votes to four he was permitted to do so.— Mr. P. Speakman seconded the amendment. Mr. Meadowcroft expressed his dissent from the remarks of Mr. Liaison, which were altogether uncalled for and un- just. A more unsatisfactory and ill-founded declamation, in which membe's of the Board are charged with personal animosity, with hatred, and with a desire of revenge, he never heard during the whole of his experience. The Chairman : There were none. Mr. ltfeadowcroft : There was no secret meeting, because all the members were called together. What they had done bad been merely to state the true facts to the Board. Mr. Timmins (thought the Chairman should ask Mr. Imieon to withdraw the remarks he had made. He (Mr. Timmins) had at at that Board between twenty and thirty years, and he had never heard stronger remarks made in his life. The Chairman said he had no desire to ask Mr. Imison to withdraw the remarks; the public would be able to judge of the justice, and to see how they were supported. The Highway and S anitary Committee, which met twice a month, was a private meeting. but no one—he was going to say—had boon ignorant enough to call it a mivate meet- ing before. Mr. Imison had not told them what was the real subject. If he understood the qeestion, it was that the Board found, on investigation, that one of their officials had made statements, and reiterated those statements, which had been found to be untrue. It was a question as to what they expected from their officials. If they departed from a principle which existed when be took that chair, which was that they should expect truthful statements from ser- vants, then they must put somebody else in. They would weaken his position as chairman of that Board if they told their officials that they did not expect them to make reliable statement*. It was the duty of the Board that they should deal with a case of that kind. Mr. Lake said he had not the slightee• sympathy with the expressions that had fallen from Mr. liaison in favour of striking out the recommendation entirely, because he felt, and he was sure that every member of the Investiga- tion Committee most feel, that there could be no other out- come ,ben the law clerk refused to apologise. Some reference had been made to the feeling outside, and he thought It would be well to postpone the matter, so that it might not be said that Obey had been swayed by the know, ledge that such an action as that referred to was about to take place. The amendment was then put to the meeting, and ten members voted in its support.

WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. Tha monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, on Friday morning. There were present Messrs. Broadbent (chairman), Derbyshire, Jolley, Grange, the Rev. , G. F. Roberts. John Houghton, William Houghton, W. Long, J. Rylands, R. Owen, Isbell, and swinton ;S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), 1 and J. Rawlings (inspector). THE SCI.VENGING OF STREETS. Mr. Moore, who has property in Warburton-street, off Winwick-road, waited upon the Authority, and asked whether Warburton-street had been completed to the satis- faction of the Authority. They sent him notices three years ago to make his share of the road.—The CHAIRMAN asked if Mr. Moore complained that other people had not done their ehare.—Mr. MOORE said it was not for him to say that. What he wanted to know was whether the street had been completed to the satisfaction of the Authority, and if it had not, why not ?—The SURVEYOR said the matter came before them at the last meeting, and he mentioned at the tune that Mr. Moore bad done his share, but some other parties had not done theirs. He had given those parties notice, bat had done nothing further. If the Authority took the street over they would have to scavenge it, and they would have to consider whether they were in a posi- tion to do that. The inattention of the people who had not completed the street was only with regard to very small matters.—Mr. Moore thought that if he had done his share the street ought to be kept clean.—Mr. Owen said that was the question. The subject would have to come up whether the Authority would start scavenging or leave it over a little longer. The streets were not in an unsanitary condi- tion, and unless it was in an unsanitary condition they could not be compelled to take the street over.—The CHAIR- MAN explained to Mr. Moore that the Authority was not at present prepared to take the street over, and the subject dropped.

THE PENKETHP DRAINAGE. The CLERK said that with regard to the Penketh drain- age:scherne, Mr. Turner, of Penketh, had waited on the Local Government Board as to their objection to the plans, bu he bad not been able to sae the superior officials. He (the clerk) had consequently written to the Local Govern- ment Board asking them to specify their objections, but as yet no reply had been received. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. SEPETON reported fer the month ending September 30th, that the blithe were—males .10, females 11 ; deaths— male 1, females 5. The death rata from all causes was equal to 5.6 per 1,000, against 161 in the corresponding month of last year. The death rate from zymotic diseases was nil, against 6, the average rate of last three months There were not any deaths reported under the zymotic or preventible diseases head, and two deaths only bad occurred under one year. That was an exceedingly small infantile mortality for this season of the year. With reference to Morris Brook, Grappenhall, be reported that he had again examined it, and found it much in the same condition as reported to the Authority in Sept., 1883. The bed of the brook was quite black with the tanning liquor and lime water. He recommended that the waste liquor should be passed through two settling tanks and two filter beds before it was turned into the brook, the filter beds to be made of one foet each thick of coke, fine gravel, and sand. He had examined the brook near Messrs Pierpoint and Bryant's skin yard at Latchford, and found the stream polluted bY refuse lime water and the washing of skins. Ile would make the same suggestions, however, as for the improve- ment of Morris Brook.—Some discussion took place on the subject of the pollution of brooks, and it was stated by Dr. Sephton that he was at present making experiments in order to, if possible, find a method of preventing nuisances. The matter was posponed to allow Dr. Sephton au oppor- tunity of reporting as to his experiments. SURVEYOR'S REPORT.

Mr. OWEN reported that during the month inspections had been made of the following new buildings :—Mr. Hind- ley's house, Padgate ; Mr. Hunt's new stables, dtc., Pen- iceth ; addition to the Friends' School, Liverpool-road; and Mr. Lloyd's houses, Weltield-street, off Lovely-lane. He had in one instance had to threaten proceedinza if a house was occupied before the drains were laid, and the closet provided ; and in another case he had given notice that he would not issue a certificate of habitation with the well in the present position, as it was not sunk where shown on the plans submitted, and in within the prescribed' distance from the as'apit required by the bye-laws.—This report was adopted. This was all the business.

div.head: WIDNE3 REVISION COURT:
div.p: WIDNE3 REVISION COURT:

• • -- - - - A court for the revision of voters in the Widnes district of the 'Widnes Parliamentary Division was opened yesterday at the Sessions House by Mr. Cot- tingham, revising barrister. The Liberals were re- presented by Mr. H. B. Shores, assisted by Mr. T. G. Middlebrook, and the Conservatives by Mr. Wood- north, assisted by Mr, Whiteside. The Irish Na- tionalists were represented by Mr. J. Denver, assisted by Mr. Quinn. There was a good attendance during the day. The number of voters in Widnes township alone have been increased from about Soo to upwards of 4,000, and the business of the court is expected to extend oyer four days. The chief matter of interest arose on the appearance of Thomas Daniels, of Mersey-read. against an objection made to his vote by the Conservative party. Mr. Wood- north said he sent certain notices to the assistant overseer containing the names and addresses of parties objected to. The Assistant Over- seer had objected to every person of tho same name, no matter what their addresses might be. In conse- quence of this about 120 10 130 people were objected to by the Overseer, but not by either of the political parties. A card was printed in the name of the Assistant Overseer. After some inquiry, the Revis- ing Barrister eventually decided that Daniels had come their unnecessarily, and he declined to allow costs. At the evening sitting the court was crowded.—Thomas Miller, of Carlile•street, bad been objected to by the Liberals. In answer to the Revising Barrister, he said he had lived in the street for 13 years. Mr. Shores said the only sign Upon the end of the street was Carlile-terrace. The Revising Barrister said he should allow the vote. Miller: Any expenses? He was allowed half a crown.— Immediately afterwards five Conservative objections were found to be frivolous, but the claimants claimed no ex- pense..

div.head: F RODSII AM.
div.p: F RODSII AM.

LECTIIRE.—On Tuesday evening the Rev. D. Schofield delivered his popular lecture on "The importance of little things," to a large and appreciative audience, the chair be- ing token by the Rev. R. P. Bdrwick. of Frodsham. The collections, which amounted to over £3, will be applied in aid of the trust fund. FIVE CROSSES WESLEYAN CIIAPEL.—The opening ser- vices in connection with the above chapel were brought to a close on Wednesday, when a sermon was preached in the afternoon by the Ray. George Woods, of Runcora, and in the evening the Rev. Charles Garrett preached to a large congregation The collections on Wednesday realised £54, making a total of £217 lOs received at the opening ser- vices. The total cost of the chapel was £1,700, and the debt now remaining is only £.302 10s, a fact which speaks well for the energy of the Building Committee and the lib- erality of the friends who have contributed to the fund. MUTUAL IMPROVEUENT SOCIETY —On Thursday evening the inaugural meeting of this society was held in Trinity Scfmol-room. The Rev. E. Mosscrop, president. occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. The proceed- ings took the farm of a fruit banquet. and during the even- ing there were addresses by thee president, Mr. W. Robinson, sled Mr. Richard Proud, and selections of music at intervals by a choir conducted by Mr. T. Sant. Solos were con- tributed by Mrs: Mosscrop, Mr. Stuart, and Mr. James Kent. Mrs. J. C. Harrop accompanied on the piano. A most enjoyable time was spent, and the secretary (Mr. Jas. Kent) enrolled a good number of members. BRITISII AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.—Tho fifty-third annual meeting of the Froctsham branch of the above society was held in the Town Hall, Frodsbam, on Monday evening, when the Rev. H B. Blogg, MA., presided. There was a moderate attendance. The meeting opened with singing and prayer, after which the Rev. E. Marsden, vicar of Aston, read the financial report, from which it appeared that the Frodsham branch had contributed £54 to the society during the past year. Addresses were also given by the Rev. J. Birch, of Wrexham, the deputation, who at- tended in place of the Rev. Jelinger E. Symons (district secretary), who was unable to be present through sickness ; , Rev. J. Lewis (Free Church), and Rev. 'l'. Lagar (Primitive Methodist.) A collection was made at the close of the meeting in aid of the funds of the society, and a vote of thanks was accorded to the deputation.

ITHE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, Sep. 26th, 1885.—The mean temperature was 50.5 Fahr., and therefore 5•8 degree colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 68 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 23rd inst., and the minimum temperature. 35 Fahrenheit, on the 26th inst. The rainfall measured 0•321 n. The general direction of the wind was W. During the week, which was 0 e 39th of the current year, 32 births and 17 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 19.4 per 1,000, against 19.1 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 18.6 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from erysipelas, 1 from croup, •2 from phthisis, 1 from cancer, 3 from brain disease, and 3 from heart disease. Two cases of whooping cough were repor- ted under the requirements of the Act of Parlia- ment. JOIIN H. GORNALL. Medical Officer of Health. .

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSHENT
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSHENT

COMMITTEE A meeting of the above committee was held at ho Work- house on Friday morning. There were present Messrs. J. 'Wands (chairman), C. Broadbent, W. Long, W. Darby- shire. U. Appleton, and John Houghton ; S. Suttoh (assistant clerk f, and W. Owen (valuer). THE LION HOTEL ASSESSMENT.—Mr. Brook, solicitor, appeared on behalf of the Lion Hotel (Warrington) Com- pany, Limited, to appeal against the assess Dent of the hotel. The present assessment is—house, gross £l5O, rate- abl.. £127 103 ; stables, shed, and yard, £l5O gross, and £127 lOs rateable. He (Mr. Brook) asked that the house, stables, &c., be assessed together and not separately, as they were not separate tenancies. He took it that the Carriage 'Company had been assessed separately on the assumption that there was a separate tenancy, but that was not so. The Carriage Company paid no rites and taxes, and they were not in any sense tenants. He contended that the total as- sessment of £255 was very much in excess of what it ought to be. The business carried on at the Lion tint.! had been affected by two circumstances, one being the establishment of clubs in the town, which bad taken away the local con- nection and businees, and the other was the facilities af- forded by the Cheshire Lines to people who camp to War- rington to get back to Manchester and Liverpool the same day, which had entirely taken away the outside business. Both of these circumstances arose since the hotel was taken over by the company, and the business now carried on was an unprofitable and losing buciness. Mr. Brook mentioned that the Patten Arms Hotel was assessed at £l4l only, though the only advantage the Lion Hotel had over the Patten Arms was a large ballroom, which did not bring in much profit. The last time the hotel was let,he said, the rental was only £9o.—lt was agreed that Mr. Owen, the valuer, should re-assess the Lion Hotel, and report to the com- nai ttee, VALUER'S REPORT.—Mr. Owen reported that he had made inspection of the following properties :—Messrs. J. H. Fleming and Co., warehouse, Friar's Green, assessed at gross £4O 10s, rateable £32 10s, the assessment of which should be reduced to the actual rent, gross £2O. rateable £l7. Mr. Wm. Bellian, 22. Lovely-lane, assessed at gross £lB 44, rateable £l5 101 ; be was of opinion that assessment Should be confirmed. With regard to Mr. Was Bellian's workshop off Cartwright-street, assessed at gross £l4 14s, rateable £l2 108, he was of opinion should be reduced to gross £lO, rateable £8 10s. The reductions decided by HIP committee at their previous meeting would make the asaess- tnent of the respective fustian cuttiao shops belonging to Mr. J. Platt, as under :—Rylands'•yard, gross £2B, rateable £24 ; Cockhedge-lane, gross £6O, rateable £57 ; Aikin- street, gross £65 15s, rateable £56. With regard to the shops in Lythgoe's-lane on which he (Mr. Owen) was to re. part, he had gone over the valuations of the different buildings, and was prepared to advise a reduction of £25 from the gross assessments, making gross £134, rateable £ll4, and dividing them on works and offices as follows : Works, gross £125, rateable £lO6 lOs ; offices, gross £9, rateable £7 10s.—This report was adopted. I This was all the business of public interest.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.—An Ordinary GENERAL MEETING of the members of the above Club will be held in the Clam Roost. WRITE BULL, HORSE- afABEET STREET, WARRINGTON, on WEDNESDAY. OCTOBER 7th, 1885, at 4 p.m. The Business of the meeting will be :- 1. To pass the minutes of the committee meetings on sth and 12th August, and 23rd September, 1885, which contain important memorials on the Rent, Farm Land Assessment, and the Manchester Smith- fie,d Market space questions. 2 To hear a paver read by Mr. John L. Stelfox. entitled "An explanation and criticism of the Agricultural Holdings Act, 1883, and the Ground Game Set, 1880; to be followed by a statement of the demands of Tenant Farmers, and the exposition of an easy, prac- tical, and legal method whereby Tenant Farmers can reduce their rents an 4 rates, and also obtain better prices for their produce." Whereas, in consequence of the completion of the harvest, it Is now convenient for farmers to attend Warrington market ' ' witkout loss to their business, all Tenant Farmers in the dis- trict are respectfully urged to join the club at once, inasmuch es on the reception and support accorded to the club by Tenant Farmers in the district will depend the measure of suc- cess which will result from its operations. If Tenant Farmers will flock to the club In hundreds, so that not a single one shall remain unenrolled, it will then be possible by united action to effect a great agricultural revival, and to remove the prevent dark and serious outlook which threatens agricultural interests with absolute ruin. Farm labourers, interested in agricultural questions, will be welcomed at general meetings of the club. HENRY T. SIELFOX, Hon. Sec. Lymm, Ist October, 1885.
